The claim that no members of the Socialists, Greens, or Renew groups have addressed military emissions is false; MEPs from these groups have repeatedly raised the issue, such as proposing amendments to European Parliament resolutions to close the military emissions gap and advocating for mandatory reporting of military carbon footprints.

Anna-Maja HENRIKSSON

It seems that the parliamentarian has missed something elementary. It is Russia and Putin that have started a war against Ukraine, and that is tragic. That war is ongoing every day, and we must make sure that we do everything to support Ukraine, so that we in Europe do not buy Russian gas and oil.

We can in our own way support Ukraine through our own actions in our countries, and it is our task to ensure that Ukraine can also one day become a member of the European Union.

Kateřina KONEČNÁ

This is not about Ukraine at all. You were not able to vote that you disagree with how aggressively Donald Trump is acting in Iran. And weapons are used there too. The climate is also being destroyed there. You were not able to vote that you disagree with the genocide in Palestine. Weapons are used there too. Simply until you agree that peace policy is the most environmentally clean policy, and you will blame only one part of the economy or sector, it is hypocrisy and you are just pretending something.

Anna-Maja HENRIKSSON

It is of course the case that it would be very good if we had peace in the world. But that does not mean that we can close our eyes to the environmental catastrophe that is happening in the world now, the climate catastrophe that we have.

We must work on many levels every day. We must combat climate change. We must get rid of fossil fuels. We will invest in the green transition, and we will work for a world where people are respected – democracy, human rights – and that every country has the right to its sovereignty.

Laurent CASTILLO

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues, in the face of heatwaves, air conditioning is not a luxury, it is a public health issue. Since 2017, nearly 40,000 French people have died from the consequences of heat. Yet, only 24% of homes are air-conditioned, compared to over 50% in Italy. When temperatures go wild, schools, hospitals, and retirement homes must be effectively protected.

In Nice, we have chosen a major action plan, an air-conditioning action plan for our city. Adapting to climate change does not mean giving up on fighting it. Adapting means investing in nuclear power to produce decarbonised electricity. Adapting means making our buildings livable both summer and winter. Above all, it means protecting the lives of the most vulnerable.

True ecology is not the one that makes people feel guilty, it is the one that protects. True ecology never chooses between the planet and people, it protects both.

Marta TEMIDO

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, "extreme heatwaves are a public health emergency," said the WHO Regional Director for Europe yesterday.

We already knew that. High temperatures have a direct impact on increasing morbidity and also mortality. Excess mortality due to heat was over 7,000 deaths, just in the month of June, in three European countries.

But, beyond the firefighting resources that the European Union has available to support all countries, we need to do more. The rollback of global warming reduction policies, of environmental deregulation, comes at a heavy cost. It is measured in preventable illnesses, it is measured in preventable deaths, and climate adaptation and mitigation measures are the long-term key.

For many in this hemicycle, you only have to look at it, fires are something that happens because cattle farming was ended, vector-borne diseases happen because they come on planes, from strange places, carrying mosquitoes on board. And climate change is ideology.

Until we agree on the facts, we will not catch up with our losses.

Mathilde ANDROUËT

Madam President, six days of heatwave in June in France, 2,025 deaths. And while some are still discussing, others are acting. In Madrid, the metro is air-conditioned. In Barcelona, climate shelters are accessible within a few minutes on foot. In Greece, employers must provide cooled spaces for their employees. These countries have understood a simple thing: protecting the population against the heat is not a luxury, it is a public policy.

In France, we are lagging behind. Too many schools, EHPADs [residential care homes for the elderly], too many hospitals, too many homes remain unsuitable, and yet the heat kills. It strikes children, the elderly, the sick, workers. Faced with this, we are proposing a 'Climate Plan': the right to coolness for everyone. Cooling priority public buildings and helping families adapt their housing, developing insulation and reversible heat pumps, and also producing this equipment at home. Every euro invested must protect the French people, revive our industry and create non-relocatable European jobs.

This is our line. Neither climate denial nor punitive ecology: a protection ecology that adapts and, above all—above all!—saves lives.

Paulo CUNHA

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, Dear Colleagues, there is an inevitable relationship between climate change, heatwaves and fires. This circumstance is increasingly less cyclical and more structural, which explains the permanence of this very sequence.

The question that arises is: what to do?

There are two very relevant levels of action. First, mitigation: continuing to invest in reducing causes, combating climate change; but the second is the level of adaptation. We cannot be naive to the point of thinking that mitigation will happen in a flash and we have to prepare ourselves for this circumstance.

What to do? Prepare the most exposed communities, reinforce the resilience of territories, modernize and empower civil protection authorities. Investigate or invest increasingly in research against fires.

But it is also necessary to strengthen European-level action, namely the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism and RescEU, as well as the sharing of resources and operational cooperation.

Only with an active and prepared European level can we be successful in combating the scourge of fires.

(The speaker agrees to answer several blue card questions)

Catarina MARTINS

We are discussing the civil protection mechanism in Europe and I have argued that we need to include early recovery in a solidarity mechanism.

In Portugal, we are having fires in forests where the timber from the storms is still lying around and we still have populations without electricity and even difficulties with communications.

The groups here in the European Parliament have had a consensus on the need for early recovery, except for your group, the EPP. And so I ask you, when you defend more European solidarity here, don't you think we should do everything and ensure this early recovery to clear the territory and restore electricity and communications with solidarity and quickly?

Paulo CUNHA

I reiterate that the commitment to mitigation is crucial, but that does not mean we should not prepare for circumstances that are inevitable.

Unfortunately, climate change is a reality and its impact in terms of fires, particularly forest fires, is also a reality. And for this, the adaptation and preparation of communities are central.

What my political group advocates, and the European Commission has been doing, is to invest in funds like preparedness, which help communities become more resilient, better prepared to better overcome these circumstances.

Bruno GONÇALVES

Mr Member of the European Parliament, I am not going to nationalise the issue here, as the PSD did in the past with PS MEPs, I am actually going to Europeanise it. You spoke about the civil protection mechanism and we are together, not only in that action, in that activation and in what concerns aid to Member States, but it is just that here in this House, in 2023, European legislation against deforestation was approved.

In the last year, that legislation came back here to be ratified or to be postponed. Unlike this group, which voted in favour of ratification, your group voted in favour of postponement.

Therefore, the question I leave you with is: instead of a civil protection mechanism, wouldn't it be better to have a mechanism to protect MEPs, one that is in favour of prevention, and avoid what is happening in Portugal today?

Paulo CUNHA

The political group to which I proudly belong has had a very consistent position on this as on other matters. What we cannot defend is a regime of deforestation that is not compatible with other dimensions that need to be safeguarded.

I have argued, on many occasions, that the concept of sustainability presupposes not only assessing the environmental impacts of economic measures, but also the economic impacts of environmental measures.

That was what we talked about when we dealt with a topic like the one suggested here and, therefore, consistency, a sense of responsibility and, above all, a dimension of sustainability that is more appropriate to the circumstances in which we live.

Pascal CANFIN

Madam President, I would like to tell the far-right deputies of this hemicycle that they bear a very heavy share of responsibility for the current situation. You have voted against all the texts – all the texts! – that allow us to reduce the worst effects of climate change. You voted against the very principle of having a European climate policy to reduce emissions, and therefore to reduce the climate shock. You therefore bear a very clear share of responsibility for the fact that there are, for example, in France, 12 million people – 12 million people! – whose houses are cracking, breaking apart, and losing all their value due to the impact of climate change.

You bear a heavy responsibility for the fact that thousands of farmers are losing all their harvests, in the south of France, due to the multiplication of forest fires, due to climate change. Take responsibility, at least! Take at least this responsibility! Say it in front of all French and European people! And please, stop, stop this climate-skeptic policy, which is unbearable today in Europe!

(The speaker accepts a blue-card question)

Alexander JUNGBLUTH

Blue Card. - Thank you, dear colleague, for allowing the point of order. You just said that the responsibility for environmental disasters and forest fires lies with the right. I have a question: Which specific law do you know that you believe failed to be passed because of a vote by the right? I would argue that all laws were passed, and in the end the conclusion is simply that your laws are ineffective.

Pascal CANFIN

Sir, your political group and all the far-right political groups voted against the nature restoration law, which precisely makes it possible to have wetlands that help limit the impacts of climate change on water stress or forest fires. You voted against the very principle of having a European climate law that respects the Paris Agreement. You voted absolutely against all texts on industry, on the automobile, on everything, on agriculture, which would make it possible to limit the absolutely dramatic consequences of climate change for Europeans.

Take responsibility, have at least the honor of taking this responsibility!

Oliver SCHENK

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues! In recent years, many of us have had the experience in our home countries of having to cope with extreme weather events. In my home region of Saxony, too, we are experiencing this development firsthand: the major forest fire in the Gohrischheide last year was Germany's largest forest fire. Therefore, a big thank you goes out at this point to the many thousands of emergency workers, firefighters, and disaster relief personnel who stand by our side and help us in these situations.

Precisely for this reason, however, it is right for Europe to further strengthen its disaster preparedness and the idea of preparedness. With the Union Civil Protection Mechanism, joint firefighting aircraft, and satellite data from the Copernicus program, the European Union creates genuine added value. Europe helps to identify dangers earlier and to act together more quickly in an emergency.

At least as important, however, is prevention. We need more resilient forests, new water supply concepts, modern early warning systems, and investments in civil protection. Europe can provide support here, but responsibility begins locally with a preparedness strategy that protects people, secures infrastructure, and makes our regions more resilient – and that is precisely what we will also have to pay attention to in the negotiations on a new EU budget as this august House.

Pär HOLMGREN

Madam President! Then it was time again – a new heatwave here in Strasbourg. The previous one we had about two weeks ago is actually one of the worst we have ever had in several of the EU's countries.

But the EU and the member states can do a lot to make the climate crisis at least less catastrophic. Today, we from the Greens group have sent a letter to you in the Commission with our demands to protect us in Europe from the consequences of extreme weather.

We must invest more in nature-based solutions, ensure that climate resilience is included in all legislation, take full responsibility for all climate adaptation work in all sectors of society, set clear targets for the 36 largest identified risks, and last but definitely not least, protect the workers who risk being affected by the extreme heat.

In short, we need a very strong climate adaptation law for the EU.

Barbara BONTE

Mr President, the heatwave at the end of June was not the first we have encountered and will not be the last. Precisely for that reason, our focus must be on climate adaptation. Make houses, offices, hospitals, nursing homes, schools, and daycare centers more resilient to that extreme heat. And that is why we must, first of all, stop demonizing air conditioning. Air conditioning is not a symbol of climate indifference. On the contrary, it is a necessary tool to protect the elderly, the sick, young children, and caregivers when temperatures soar. Air conditioning saves lives. They are therefore vital.

What we certainly should not do is follow the example of the Commission, because during the heatwave in June, employees on the lower floors of the Commission building actually had to work without air conditioning, while the offices of the Commission President and the other Commissioners on the upper floors were indeed cooled. Orwell would say: “All floors are equal, but some floors are more equal than others.” That sort of thing is called hypocrisy and sums up the Commission's policy very well.

Tiemo WÖLKEN

Madam President, dear colleagues! Climate apocalypse cancelled – that is how the AfD was still rejoicing in May. I would say that has aged like fresh milk in a heatwave. Not two months later, and we have temperatures of over 40 degrees across Europe, wildfires, power outages, heat-related deaths, looting. And science is in agreement: this extreme heatwave would be unthinkable without human-made climate change, without the climate crisis, and it affects the European Union directly.

What comes to mind on the far right? Air conditioning. Wow! Have you ever worked on a construction site during this heatwave? Delivered packages? Nursed the sick? No, you haven't, you are sitting here in the air-conditioned chamber.

We need investments in our hospitals, in care facilities, in production halls – yes, but we also need civil protection; we need more renewable energies; we need resilient infrastructure. And at the same time – and I know thinking about two things at once is hard for you – we have it in our hands to ensure that this hot summer remains an exception and not the beginning of the climate crisis. The Green Deal must be pursued consistently, emissions must come down. Adaptation alone will not save us. When will you finally grasp that?

Ana VASCONCELOS

President, Commissioner, Colleagues, I will address you in Portuguese.

More than 1,300 Europeans lost their lives, above the usual number, between June 21 and 29, due to the heatwave. It is estimated that around 44,000 lives are lost every year due to high temperatures in Europe.

Fire prevention and climate resilience are among the most important agendas of this term, and I want to focus on a particular climate adaptation measure: affordable air conditioning for all Europeans from north to south. It is not a luxury, it is a necessity.

Only one in five homes in the EU has air conditioning. In the United States and Japan, nations facing summers similar to ours, it is nine out of ten. In several European countries, installing an air conditioning unit at home can require permits, municipal approvals, and the consent of the majority of the condominium.

A Union that considers adaptation to climate change urgent cannot consider technologies like air conditioning a dispensable luxury because it consumes a lot of energy. It must and has to treat it now as a climate adaptation measure.

(The speaker agrees to take a "blue card" question)

João OLIVEIRA

Madam Deputy Ana Vasconcelos, you spoke to us about air conditioning regarding the mitigation of heat, but I wanted to ask you a question about water resource management and access to European funds for the improvement of water networks, water supply and sanitation, which in many circumstances see their possibility of using European funds limited in order to have better efficiency in the management of water resources, issues so absolutely essential to cope with the situations of drought and excessive heat that we have.

Does the Deputy think we should continue to deal with these kinds of restrictions in access to European funds by public entities that have this responsibility for water and sanitation management?

Ana VASCONCELOS

Mr Member of the European Parliament, Southern Europe, including Portugal, has been among the largest beneficiaries of European funds to manage water resources. In fact, it is thanks to the mismanagement of these funds that we have not had a good performance in managing these resources and in the availability of water to our citizens.

Therefore, yes, we must better manage our resources, European resources and national resources, for the provision of quality water and to avoid water losses due to poorly maintained infrastructure.

Annalisa CORRADO

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, honourable colleagues, during the most recent heatwave we counted more than 1 300 victims in Europe, some due to illnesses caused by working in unsustainable conditions, some due to pre-existing vulnerabilities or sudden illnesses that clogged our emergency rooms, some for having dived into dangerous basins or watercourses.

The cities that have taken this issue seriously - coincidentally none led by far-right deniers - are saving lives, creating climate refuges, enhancing urban greenery, removing asphalt, unsealing the soil, lives are being saved, especially those of the most fragile and the most lonely.

And let us also think of prisoners, of those who do not have a home or who have one that is a fridge in winter and an oven in summer. And this is where strategies to combat the climate crisis, the social crisis and their effects come together. Investing in sustainable housing cuts emissions, creates social cohesion, creates stable jobs, boosts European industrial supply chains, such as that of heat pumps, saves lives and their dignity.

We have the tools, it takes political courage.

Tiago MOREIRA DE SÁ

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, Gaston Bachelard wrote that fire is the greatest ambiguity of human experience. Ever since the first man gazed at a flame, we have understood why.

Fire warms and destroys; it illuminates and consumes; it shines in Paradise and burns in Hell. But above all, fire has always been the symbol of the trial.

In all cultures, the trial by fire represents the decisive test, the one that reveals true value. This is how, for centuries, the authenticity of gold was measured. Only true gold resists fire.

Gold and the firefighter share the same essential truth: it is not the fire that makes the gold. Nor the firefighter. Fire merely reveals what each is made of. Whenever they step into the flames to protect others, the homes of others, the lives of others, Portuguese firefighters go through the trial by fire once again. It is there, face to face with the flames, that it is proven that those men and women are authentically made of gold.

Portugal is in iron and fire. The European Union Civil Protection Mechanism can help, but only Portuguese firefighters can prevent 900 years of existence from burning.

(The speaker refuses a "blue card" question from Marta Temido)

Letizia MORATTI

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, honourable colleagues, this summer millions of Europeans are still living through suffocating days. Elderly people who cannot leave their homes, children who have to give up playing in parks, families evacuated due to fires, firefighters risking their lives.

This is no longer an emergency, it is a reality.

Europe must continue to combat climate change through mitigation, relying more on incentives than on penalties, but it must – alongside the reduction of emissions – think about a major adaptation strategy.

We must continue to prevent climate change, but alongside this we must protect people from the effects of climate change.

The three billion trees planned by 2030 are an important signal. Europe must strengthen its reforestation strategy: one billion more trees in cities to lower temperatures by 2 to 8 °C, more forests where fire has destroyed entire territories, more greenery in areas threatened by desertification.

Adapting to climate change does not mean surrendering, it means defending health, defending security, defending the future of our children. It is a responsibility that Europe must assume today.

Francisco José MILLÁN MON

Madam President, last year southern Europe suffered an unprecedented fire season marked by so-called sixth-generation fires. This year's data is not looking good either, quite the contrary.

I welcome the fact that the European Union is reacting. Last March, the Commission presented the first Communication on the integrated management of wildfires and has also increased the deployment of resources. This is a step in the right direction, and other public administrations should follow this line.

In this regard, I want to praise the importance that the Xunta de Galicia has been giving in recent years to wildfire prevention and extinction. In this year 2026, it is further strengthening a system that is a true benchmark not only at the national level, but also internationally. For this year 2026, the Xunta has improved systems at all levels —prevention, surveillance, extinction—, material and human resources available have been increased, and the largest budget in history has been approved: more than 213 million euros, 18% more than last year.

Juan Fernando LÓPEZ AGUILAR

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, from the intensity of this debate and the controversy it has sparked, it is clear that the European Union is the region of the world most affected by global warming and has a tragic mortality toll this very summer, but lowering standards in European ambition regarding the digital agenda and the migration agenda is undoubtedly harmful and, in my view, suicidal. But nothing is more unjust than lowering standards in the fair green transition, and that cannot happen, under any circumstances, by reducing the necessary financial allocation within the multiannual financial framework so that the European Union can maintain its ambition in the incorporation of renewable energies and in combating the carbonization of the European economy that has contributed to global warming. It is essential that there are resources to protect citizens and, especially, the working class who cannot bear this heat.

Romana JERKOVIĆ

Madam President, dear colleagues, for years, decades even, we have been warning about the impact of climate change. Yet here we are. Every summer is hotter, every wildfire season more devastating, and our response is still too slow. Why? Because of those who repeatedly choose to ignore the facts. Unfortunately, some of them are today here in this plenary.

Heatwaves and wildfires are no longer exceptional events. They are Europe's reality. Families lose their homes, workers face unbearable conditions and firefighters risk their lives.

Europe must do more, because no Member States should be left to face these disasters alone. There is no credible strategy against heatwaves and wildfires if at the same time we weaken climate policies or dismantle the Green Deal. Every delay and every vote against climate action has consequences that are measured in lives lost and communities destroyed.

Sebastian TYNKKYNEN

Mr President, here is EU news: heatwaves hit Brussels and the rest of Europe, and the air conditioning in the Commission building was partially turned off. Now, sweating profusely, people are demanding EU heatwave strategies and EU-level responses. But what do a hot day in Finland and a heatwave of over 40 degrees in Spain have in common? Practically nothing, and that is why the solutions must be different, too.

Rescue services, healthcare, construction, and preparedness belong to the member states. They know their own conditions better than any bureaucrat sweating in Brussels. But when the thermometer rises, it seems that a fever for power rises in Brussels, too. When it comes to climate action, we can certainly discuss China and other exploiters, but when it comes to preparedness solutions for the present moment, the solutions must remain in national hands.

Maria OHISALO

Madam President, the five biggest fossil fuel companies – TotalEnergies, BP, Chevron, ExxonMobil and Shell – together generate roughly EUR 8 trillion in revenue every year. According to the Commission's own estimate, making Europe heatwave proof would cost EUR 70 billion a year – just 7 % of these companies' revenue. These same companies have spent decades profiting from the very emissions now killing people all over the world and in Europe. So my question to the Commission is: will the Commission make the companies causing the climate crisis pay the bill for making schools, hospitals and care homes safe in hot weather?

Marc BOTENGA

Madam President, listen, it has been said, but 1,222 people died in Belgium because of the heat. If it had been a military attack, how would you have reacted here? If there had been 1,200 people dead in Belgium because of a military attack? That would have been a state of emergency. You would have mobilized all the troops, all the forces, all the funds to react to that. And here, today, what do I hear from the Commission? "Don't worry, in a few months we will come up with a new action plan."

But in the meantime, the funds for militarization, for war, amount to hundreds of billions for fighter jets. Where are the hundreds of billions for our nursing homes? For the hospitals? We now have to put emergency blankets in Europe – emergency blankets! – on the windows of our hospitals so that patients don't die of the heat! Workers who have to work at 40 degrees. Where is the emergency plan? How are we going to save them?

And there, the far right even denying the obvious, it's a disgrace! But the government coalition, the ruling coalition here, also has questions and responsibilities to which it must respond.

Željana ZOVKO

Madam President, congratulations Commissioner on the increase of the EU Rescue mechanism Fund by 11 billion euros.

As the rapporteur for the opinion of the Committee on Development, I think this is crucial. In 2019, this house had no interest at all in us doing anything in that regard, but we are still not investing in what is fundamental, and that is firefighters. No one is helping firefighters to procure equipment; last week in Mostar, meaning, we use this equipment for cross-border firefighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. Desperate, a firefighter came and said: „We can't go on. We can't do any more, we don't have equipment”. Meaning, fires are also coming to Croatia, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, 11 billion, we are discussing here, we are still doing nothing for prevention.

We are using nothing, and in 1956 in Mostar 46 degrees was recorded, there was heat and there will be, but our inaction still exists here.

Alicia HOMS GINEL

Madam President, protecting people from heatwaves also means protecting workers; because preparation for heatwaves starts with not forcing anyone to choose between their salary and their health.

That is why it is incomprehensible that the Partido Popular in Spain proposes precisely to cut benefits for those on sick leave, as if doctors had no criteria or as if, for example, suffering a heatstroke were not serious enough. Is that your recipe for protecting workers when extreme temperatures are already putting their health at risk? Because climate change does not understand ideologies, but it does understand consequences.

Quality work must be safe, healthy, and adapted to the reality of the 21st century. And that, in 2026, involves protecting those who work against extreme heat, establishing common minimum standards of prevention and protection, and guaranteeing income when it is not safe to work. That is the difference between those who understand adaptation as a cut and those who understand it as an expansion of rights.

Kai TEGETHOFF

Madam President, Commissioner, colleagues, the data is clear: the next climate refugees will be us. It will be families in Spain, Portugal or Italy forced to leave towns their grandparents built because the climate is just too hot. In Andalusia right now, experts are using crop planting methods once reserved for the Sahara, because that's what Europe's soil is turning into.

Yet some still prefer just distracting citizens. Today we again listened to some of your climate lies that, in the end, only serve and protect the wealthy – those who are building climatised luxury bunkers because they know what's coming. As do you. You're just fooling your own voters.

We need a European plan to work with nature to update our infrastructure before our own citizens are forced to flee it. Let's stop pretending the danger is somewhere out at the gates. The danger is right here in our own ranks.

Sunčana GLAVAK

Madam President, dear colleagues, wildfires are a security, economic, and climate challenge.

I come from Croatia, a country that has been devastated by fires in recent years, and we know very well what it means to protect lives, homes, and nature. Thanks to a strong civil protection system, professional and volunteer firefighters, and an aerial firefighting fleet, we have shown that good organization ultimately saves lives and property. That is what we call prevention.

Now we must raise that level of preparedness to the European level. We need greater joint capacities through RescuEU, faster cross-border assistance, increased investment in prevention, forest management, and modern early warning systems. Investing in resilience is not just climate policy. It is a security policy for European citizens, and that is why we must discuss this before the next season arrives, because otherwise we will say again: the fires are here, the warm weather has come.

No, we must think about that today.

João OLIVEIRA

Madam President, Commissioner Lahbib, the prevention and fight against fires require the valorization of the rural world, they require investment in public services and civil protection structures.

When competitiveness is defended, small businesses and small producers are crushed. When militarization is defended, diverting resources from the CAP and other European funds that should support productive sectors, family farming is ruined, and all this contributes to the desertification of the rural world, turning the territory into a powder keg.

When budgetary limitations are imposed on State investment in public services, the capacity for action of health services is conditioned, the response of civil protection is conditioned.

All of this is absolutely essential to be reversed. We need better planning, we need a better approach to fire prevention issues.

But none of this can be done if there is not on the part of the States the capacity and the means to face their responsibilities, including in these areas that I highlighted.

Thomas BAJADA

Madam President, but are we truly prepared? We are still talking about heatwaves as if they are tomorrow's problem. But they are not. People are struggling to sleep, children cannot go to school as usual, workers are working in dangerous temperatures and thus this is a social emergency. People do not need more debates, they need protection and action today. Let us insulate our homes, protect schools and hospitals, more shaded spaces in our cities and this very Parliament, a year ago, called for access to drinking water in public spaces. These are practical measures that save lives and thousands of people have already lost their lives. Dear Commission, enough with strategies, people want tangible action. I am waiting for a climate resilience framework that works, not in ten years' time, not next summer, but now.

Kostas PAPADAKIS

Madam President, thousands of dead from the heatwave in Europe. The European Union and governments, after bleeding billions of euros from the peoples to feed the predators of green conglomerates under the guise of climate change, now appear provocatively surprised and unprepared. At the same time, they are already budgeting hundreds of billions for military preparation, suffocating even the most elementary needs concerning the peoples, such as in infrastructure.

In the era of artificial intelligence, peoples and workers in workplaces melt in inhuman working hours and high temperatures. They mourn losses and destruction from natural phenomena for which climate change is always put forward as an alibi, while forestry services and firefighting—as in Greece—are stripped of infrastructure and personnel. You claimed that the capitalist market and competition would solve high prices, energy poverty, low wages—and ultimately the people live in unimaginable deprivation for the 21st century. From everywhere shouts the need for the new world of socialism, overthrowing the rotten, outdated capitalist system of war, profits, and exploitation.

Rosa SERRANO SIERRA

Madam President, honourable members, Europe needs a budget commensurate with the climate emergency. Summer has just begun and Spain is already in flames. And facing regional governments that make pacts with climate change deniers and cut resources allocated to address this crisis, there are we Socialists, who defend investing where it really matters: in prevention, in emergency services, in adaptation and in effective European solidarity, especially in rural and depopulated areas where our farmers, our families, our neighbours — like mine from Leciñena and Robres — risk their lives when they try to contain the flames with their own means. Let us give priority to the climate adaptation and prevention agenda. Let us act now. Let us save lives and also save European heritage.

Hadja Lahbib

Madam President, I will be very brief in one minute. I just want to correct some information. First of all, thank you for this very hot debate. The EU must be an added value, some of you said – and that is exactly the spirit of the preparedness strategy that we presented last year. I would like to add that it is not a strategy that started last year: the rescEU capacities and the ERCC, the Emergency Response Coordination Centre, have existed since 2000. So we didn't start it last year from scratch.

Our rescue capacities must be a permanent reserve, some of you said. It is a permanent reserve. It is not during the summer that we activate. This is a reserve that we can activate when Member States are overwhelmed and, through rescEU and the European Civil Protection Pool, we have 22 firefighting aircraft, 5 helicopters and 22 certified ground firefighting teams available across 10 countries.

So I would like to thank you for this strong debate, and I hope to have such commitment in the autumn, when the temperature goes down and we need your support for the next efforts.

Thomas Byrne

Madam President, thank you, and I want to thank the honourable Members and indeed the Commissioner as well. This has been a timely debate on a very, very important topic.

I should say as well that it is important to remember those who have died and those who have suffered because of the unprecedented heat wave that we have just experienced in Europe. And it is a reminder of the urgent need to tackle the causes and consequences of the climate crisis. The presidency will support continuing work in this regard, alongside risk management and preparedness to extreme events.

I should acknowledge that many Members from southern Europe spoke during the debate, and we must acknowledge the suffering and deaths there. But there was not just Members from southern Europe; we see that this has been an issue in other Member States of the European Union, and it is an example of where best I think the European Union can show solidarity and action.

The Council has been acting on two main fronts countering the effect of climate change. One is to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, which we know from the science lead to negative impacts of climate change. The second is to adapt to climate change.

Regarding the mitigation of emissions, I would like to stress that the EU has one of the most ambitious and necessary climate policies in the world. Our task for the following months and years is to ensure that the implementation of the climate measures supports and enhances the competitiveness of the European economy and indeed not just contributes to climate resilience, but contributes to economic resilience as well.

With the increasing economic costs of extreme weather events such as wildfires, heatwaves and floods, it's increasingly clear that the cost of inaction against climate change exceeds the cost of timely climate measures. On the front of adaptation to climate change, the recent analysis by the European Environment Agency has acknowledged uneven progress in national adaptation policies and identified gaps between the plans and implementation across European countries.

Indeed, to address these challenges, the Council looks forward to a proposal for a European Union framework for climate resilience, which the Commission is expected to propose in the fall.

Sophie WILMÈS (Chair)

The debate is closed.

Written Statements (Rule 178)

Γεώργιος Αυτιάς

tós – Every summer Europe is tested more and more by extreme heatwaves and devastating forest fires. From Greece to Portugal and from Spain to France, our citizens expect the European Union to be better prepared.

Solidarity through rescEU is invaluable, but on its own it is not enough. We need a more ambitious European approach that will strengthen prevention and preparedness.

That is why I call on the European Commission to create a European mechanism for joint procurement for civil protection, along the lines of the joint procurement we are developing in the field of defence.

With joint European orders, member states will be able to procure fire engines, aircraft, firefighter equipment and modern means of dealing with natural disasters at a lower cost, faster and with greater interoperability.

Natural disasters know no borders. Our response cannot be limited to national borders. A stronger Europe in civil protection means a stronger operational capacity for National Authorities and greater security for citizens and their property.

Viktória FERENC

Record highs are raging across Europe, heatwaves are devastating, and more than 1,300 people have lost their lives due to the heat in recent weeks. In Hungary, too, thousands of people have suffered from the extreme heat. Yet the European Commission is tightening the quotas of certain climate gases for the coming years with a new implementing decision, thereby further increasing the cost of cooling equipment and air conditioners.

Instead of helping people to adapt—for example, with more affordable air conditioning equipment—the Commission makes decisions that endanger people's health and safety for abstract green ideological goals.

This is not climate protection, but green fundamentalism. Environmental protection cannot happen at the expense of people's safety and health. Rational, affordable adaptation solutions are needed that serve both the protection of the environment and the people.

Nicolás GONZÁLEZ CASARES

Fires and heatwaves have become two of the most destructive and lethal threats facing Europe. Directly aggravated by the climate emergency, heatwaves are increasingly frequent, intense and prolonged, causing thousands of deaths and creating the perfect conditions for wildfires to spread with unprecedented virulence. Our solidarity is with the victims and those affected by these phenomena.

Preparing for these threats involves anticipating, knowing and preventing risks, understanding early warnings and knowing how to act before and during an emergency. Regional and local authorities play an irreplaceable role in this area, as they are the ones who best know the territory, the vegetation, local climatic conditions and the specific needs of their communities. Likewise, the activation of early warning systems and citizen education on evacuation and self-protection are responsibilities that can only be effectively exercised from proximity. Every euro invested in prevention saves up to six in response and recovery.

From the Government of Spain and the Union, resources will continue to be reinforced, including RescEU, in application of the new fire preparedness plans.

Today, Slovenia is under a high fire risk due to extreme heat. Meanwhile, France and Greece are already battling extensive forest fires—in the far south of France, around 10,000 people had to leave their homes, while a fire west of Athens is forcing residents to stay indoors. This is not an exception, but a new European reality.

Slovenia understands this, primarily because of the largest fire in 2022 and the historic floods in 2023. Over the past five years, we have thoroughly reformed the protection and rescue system. Therefore, we call: to combat heatwaves, we need comprehensive action—from climate-adapted construction and building renovation, the strengthening of the European Civil Protection Mechanism and RescEU, to binding protection of workers against heat and, above all, a decisive reduction in emissions to limit further temperature increases.

Solidarity works. Now we must strengthen it.

Every summer the same images are repeated: columns of smoke, blocked roads, residents watching the wind and firefighters pushed to the limit. But fires do not start when the flames appear; they start much earlier, when the countryside is abandoned, paths are closed, undergrowth accumulates and grazing and rural activity disappear.

Asturias, my region, knows this well. Last summer more than 6,000 hectares burned. We did not only lose vegetation: we lost landscape, farms, memory and a future for our villages.

Europe has reinforced its emergency resources, coordination and response capacity. That solidarity is essential, but we cannot limit ourselves to acting when everything is burning. The Union must continue supporting surveillance, forest management, paths, water points and cooperation between administrations.

But Europe cannot replace the responsibility of Member States, which must turn European funds into concrete actions on the ground. And Spain has not made sufficient use of these resources.

Prevention may not offer great photographs, but it saves homes, jobs, hectares and lives. The resources exist; what is lacking is political will and management capacity to act during winter and spring, before regretting in summer what was not done in time.

Discussion transcript

Objection pursuant to Rule 114(3): Trajectory to decrease the contribution of high indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels to renewable energy targets

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

The first vote is on the objection pursuant to Rule 114(3): Trajectory to decrease the contribution of high indirect land-use change-risk biofuels, bioliquids and biomass fuels to renewable energy targets (see minutes, item 10.1).

Dubravka Šuica

Mr President, honourable Members, I would like to encourage honourable Members to support the Commission Delegated Act on indirect land-use change and to vote against the tabled objection.

In the latest review, it was found that both palm oil and soy beans qualify as feedstock with a high risk of indirect land-use change and therefore the Commission was obliged to revise the delegated act accordingly. This Delegated Act is supported by robust scientific analysis and latest available data and is legally required by the legislative framework agreed by the co-legislators.

Updating the scientific data to determine which feedstocks are classified as high risk is also needed for the EU to comply with the findings in two WTO dispute settlement cases, and the WTO. Should the Delegated Act be blocked, then the EU risks being subject to substantial sanctions, which could target our agricultural exporters.

It is important to underline that the categorisation of soy beans as high-ILUC risk feedstock does not represent a ban. Member States are still free to promote and support biofuels, including from soy beans, as they consider most appropriate. Only the amount of fuels that is counted towards the targets in the Renewable Energy Directive is gradually reduced until 2030.

I would also like to stress that only a small share of biodiesel consumed in the EU is produced from soybeans and the vast majority of it is grown in third countries. Therefore, although some operators in the EU may need to adapt, the economic impact of classifying soya as high ILUC on EU producers and crushing industry should remain limited because the EU livestock sector continues to rely on soyabean and there are alternative outlets for soya oil, including food, feed and industrial uses. Strong global demand and high soyabean oil prices, together with possible lower EU imports and export opportunities, should further help limit negative effects on suppliers and the soya industry.

Independently from that, work is currently ongoing on ways to review the low ILUC-risk certification procedure, so that producers of soy beans that receive such certification will be exempted from the categorisation of a feedstock as high-ILUC risk, and we will further assess in setting-up the renewable energy framework for the decade ahead how we can further support domestic biofuel production as well as the farming sector.

2026-07-08Vote2 speechesEU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement

Discussion transcript

EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

The next vote is on the EU-Morocco Agreement for scientific and technological cooperation setting out the terms and conditions for the participation of Morocco in the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA): amendment and supplement (see minutes, item 10.8).

Paolo BORCHIA

Mr President, honourable colleagues, we are proceeding with a vote that represents a technical alignment for Morocco's participation in PRIMA, the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area, with a focus on water, agriculture, and food security.

This vote will guarantee its continuity until 2031, with no budgetary implications.

I also take this opportunity to thank my colleagues on the ITRE Committee, who voted for the measure in committee almost unanimously.

That being said, however, I would like to broaden the reflection to the topic of agriculture, given that we cannot look at an agreement with Morocco without extending our vision to a broader framework of relations, particularly on the agricultural front.

In the last two months of 2025 alone, Morocco covered over 70% of extra-EU imports regarding tomatoes, a flow that has quadrupled over the last twenty years.

Therefore, this report would also like to open a reflection on the issue that the Commission should monitor the implementation of these types of agreements, even those referring to research and innovation, with particular attention to agricultural imports, so that the principles of reciprocity and fair competition are respected.

Victor NEGRESCU (Chair)

Jacek OZDOBA

Mr President! We propose an amendment in the following wording (I will read it right now): "The European Parliament demands memory for the 100,000 brutally murdered Poles and Jews in the Volhynian slaughter; firmly rejects the cult of bandits from the Ukrainian Insurgent Army and Stepan Bandera, who are responsible for genocide and cooperation with Hitler; calls on the Ukrainian authorities to immediately cease their state commemoration and glorification; cultivating the memory of genocide perpetrators is contrary to morality and European values; therefore, we call on the Ukrainian authorities to unequivocally reject the glorification of persons responsible for genocide; emphasizes that Banderite ideology is a mirror image of Nazi ideology and - like Nazism - Banderism must be recognized as a banned ideology in the European Union."

Gilles PENNELLE

Mr President, the prospect of Ukraine's accession to the European Union would constitute a major threat to our nations' agriculture. Our farmers have already been suffering the consequences since 2022. The liberalization of Ukrainian agricultural imports, which only the Patriots group fought against from the very start, has led to the massive influx of sugar, cereals, and poultry onto the European market, to the detriment of our producers' incomes.

Yet the Commission wants to go further. In its new vegetable protein strategy presented yesterday, it confirms its abandonment of the ambition to see European agriculture satisfy our needs for vegetable protein, in order to worsen imports from Ukraine.

I therefore propose the following amendment to create a new paragraph 32: "stresses that the Commission, in its latest protein strategy, proposes to rely on Ukraine's agricultural production capacity to remedy the shortage of vegetable protein in the Union, instead of favoring the development of European production".

Petras AUŠTREVIČIUS

Mr President, colleagues, let me move the following oral amendment:

Sergey LAGODINSKY

Mr President, I would like to draw your attention to some of the chants that were uttered here from that side of the Chamber, when somebody dared to stand in opposition to one of the oral amendments.
