2026-07-07Plenary debate74 speechesUrgent measures to strengthen the competitiveness and safeguard quality jobs in the EU’s automotive sector

Discussion transcript

Urgent measures to strengthen the competitiveness and safeguard quality jobs in the EU’s automotive sector

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Sabine VERHEYEN (Chair)

The next item on the order of business is the debate on the Commission statement on urgent measures to strengthen competitiveness and secure high-quality jobs in the EU automotive sector (2026/2806(RSP)).

I would like to remind speakers that, given the test measures currently being carried out and the set time for the conclusion of the debate, speaking time should be strictly adhered to. I believe you are sufficiently familiar with the rules on blue cards and catch-the-eye by now.

Stéphane Séjourné

Madam President, honourable Members, the European automotive sector is facing mortal danger. I warned of this finding more than a year ago and today, manufacturers, equipment suppliers, it is the entire value chain that is under strain, and the future of millions of jobs at stake – let us be clear, behind these jobs, it is prosperity, it is the social cohesion of many of our territories, in particular rural territories...

These sectors are facing at the same time a technological lag, supply chains weakened by geopolitical instability, financial balance sheets weighed down by customs duties, restrictions on access to foreign markets, and China's predatory strategy to dump overcapacities in Europe.

The result is unequivocal: losses of market share for our manufacturers, the massive import of Chinese models, which today represent more than 15% of electrified segments in Europe, European factories running below capacity and the specter, obviously, of mass redundancies. The European Commission fully measures the urgency of the situation.

Since the beginning of this mandate, we have been working to build, around the strategic dialogue with the entire sector, a genuine industrial policy for the sector. With the automotive package in December, complemented by the industrial acceleration proposal in March, we are deploying for the first time a strategy across the entire value chain of the automotive sector. With the CO2 emission control rules, we are introducing flexibilities while maintaining our consistency on our objectives. With the fleet decarbonization regulation, we are protecting an essential segment for our manufacturers, guaranteeing the availability of second-hand electric vehicles for European households. With the simplification efforts, we are accelerating the deployment of small affordable electric vehicles. With the "Battery Booster", we are financing the ramp-up of our own European battery industry. With the industrial accelerator, we are protecting jobs in Europe, we are stopping the hemorrhage among equipment suppliers and strengthening their place in the electrified value chain.

So, you understand, honourable Members, the urgency of sending clear signals to the sector today, and therefore the collective responsibility of all European institutions when it comes to adopting as quickly as possible these texts, which are on the table. The objective is clear: to break the deadly cycle of the triple European decline – drop in production, drop in market share for our manufacturers, drop in added value in Europe. We owe it to our industry. We owe it to its employees. We owe it to our regions, which are in this automotive segment.

You can count on me in any case to deploy this industrial strategy, just as Commissioners Tzitzikostas and Hoekstra and the entire European Commission.

Massimiliano SALINI

Madam President, honourable colleagues, we must recognise that what is happening in the structure of European industry sees the automotive package as one of the central points, decisive for guaranteeing a future for the entire European manufacturing sector.

Therefore, the European Commission's proposal to revise the regulation on CO2 emissions into the atmosphere for light-duty vehicles is absolutely welcome.

The European automotive industry has invested billions of euros to accept all new challenges, first and foremost the challenge of electrification. Today, our car manufacturers can produce electric engines and internal combustion engines.

The market, however, indicates that the pace envisaged by the ambitious regulation is not being met: we have a 20% electric penetration in May 2026, but forecasts are for 38% by 2030 and 64% by 2035, so intervention is necessary.

What is needed? Enabling conditions are needed. Therefore, first of all, economic accessibility for consumers is required, along with a widespread distribution of charging systems and an adequate European energy system. This will make it possible to have comprehensive European investments that take into account market dynamics and citizens' needs.

The alternative would be to reduce European production and purchase credits, perhaps from non-European car manufacturers, a prospect we cannot accept. We have the modification of the CO2 emissions regulation, which is the fastest tool to obtain the expected results and to adapt to the market through two major technical, legal and industrial assets: flexibility and technological neutrality. We will work in this direction.

Mohammed CHAHIM

Mr President, I am afraid that every six months — I hope not — we will be debating the future of the automotive industry, that another factory will close and the manufacturer of that automotive technology will probably set up a factory somewhere outside Europe.

We have laughed about electric driving for too long. In Brabant we have a car dealer who proudly has a very large sign in front of his showroom stating that electric driving is something for the funfair. But I think many motorists have been sorely disappointed in recent months, having queued in Turnhout, Brecht or Poppel to refuel cheaply in Belgium.

We are suffering from cognitive dissonance. We are clinging to a technology for which we see global demand falling: the internal combustion engine. At the same time, the electric car is gaining ground. Demand for new electric cars and second-hand electric cars is rising.

Behind that development lies a much larger trend. While parties here cling to that technology at all costs, the rest of the world is focusing on electric transport. Ethiopia has banned the import of cars with an internal combustion engine. Laos is going to do the same. Countries in Asia and South America are rapidly switching to electric transport.

It is expected that by 2035 half of all cars sold worldwide will be electric. The question is therefore not when that shift will come, but where we are going to build those cars and where the jobs will be in the future: in Europe or in China?

Klara DOSTALOVA

Madam President, dear colleagues, it is great that the European Commission finally admits in its action plan what the automotive industry has been pointing out for several years. High energy prices, rising production costs, disrupted supply chains, and growing competition from third countries are threatening one of the most important European industrial sectors. Unfortunately, a correct diagnosis does not yet mean the correct treatment. The Commission talks about competitiveness, but at the same time maintains a regulatory framework that systematically weakens our competitiveness. It talks about simplification, but adds further administrative costs. It talks about innovation, but increasingly prescribes which technologies should be used instead of letting innovation arise through natural competition. European automakers do not need more strategic documents. They need cheaper energy, predictable rules, less bureaucracy, and a truly technologically neutral environment. If European businesses produce at significantly higher costs than their competitors in China or the United States, the quality of our engineers or the experience of our workers will not be decisive. Costs will be decisive. Dear Commission, do not waste time with further plans. Start removing the obstacles that you yourselves have created for European industry.

Elena DONAZZAN

Madam President, honourable colleagues, Mr Commissioner, thank you for your clarity, your firmness and your analysis.

It is on the prescription that we have differences, because, as you were recalling, but I recall even two years ago, July 2024, a debate was held here on the automotive sector. What has changed? Nothing with regard to the Commission's direction – little, I would say – while the market has definitely worsened: China has invaded our car market and we are witnessing the loss of jobs. You yourself, in the Committee, recalled that we have already lost 200,000 jobs. One of the largest European companies, Volkswagen, is announcing the reduction of a further 100,000 jobs, usually men with families.

This is an impoverishment of Europe. And, on the other hand, the closure of factories and the impoverishment of the entire supply chain – as you well remembered – of the supply chain. A supply chain that is a wealthy supply chain, which has invested, which has also invested in containing environmental damage, which is expected from an industry.

But it is on the prescription that we are missing the mark. We strongly call for technological neutrality. The market is not asking for electric cars, the market wants to be free, consumers are free, we are in a free Europe. We need to ensure that all technological neutrality also applies to fuels and we need not to penalise a sector, such as that of trucks, of heavy transport, which we delude ourselves can run on an electric battery made in China.

Sigrid FRIIS

Madam President, morning. Let's start with some good news.

June was an all-time high for electric car sales in the EU. We are setting records as we speak. Across Europe, more and more people are choosing electric cars. They are getting better, cheaper and more accessible. At the same time, let's be honest, high fossil fuel prices make the shift even more attractive.

If we don't prioritise producing electric vehicles for European citizens, China seems more than ready to. Our European competitiveness, industrial strength and jobs depend on accelerating that European transition, not hitting the brakes to slow it down.

Yet, some in this House want to reopen old debates or weaken the regulatory framework – the certainty that Europe and our European industry needs. They claim it will protect the European car industry, but in reality it will do the opposite. It will mean less innovation, fewer investments and an industry that falls even further behind China.

We cannot secure the jobs of tomorrow with the industrial policy of the past. Europe will not help its workers by pretending the global market is standing still. We need to support you. We need to be brave, give our companies a clear, stable, ambitious framework.

Sara MATTHIEU

Colleagues, can you look the people at Volkswagen straight in the eyes today and claim that the future of their job lies in diesel and petrol engines?

What is happening at Volkswagen today is terrible. One hundred thousand workers are fearing for their job. These are people who have often worked for the company all their lives; it has become their family; they have become friends.

This reminds me of the round of layoffs we saw at Audi in Brussels. There, too, people suffered greatly from the layoff round. A couple who had been working there for 33 years testified how coldly they had to say goodbye, via a letter, a security guard escorting them to collect their things. They were not even given the opportunity to say goodbye.

Had Volkswagen's CEOs put more time into competing with China in the electric vehicle market instead of installing defeat devices, those people would still have a job today. Let us not make that same mistake again.

Martin SCHIRDEWAN

Madam President, Commissioner! Mercedes-Benz employees are resisting working longer hours without wage compensation while excessive dividends are paid out to major shareholders. Volkswagen management has announced drastic job cuts; four plants are to be closed in Germany alone. And Group CEO Blume is so brazen as to pocket over 10 million euros every year that was earned by these employees.

The automotive industry faces major challenges: international competition, the transition to e-cars, digitalization. But management's ongoing failure only exacerbates this crisis. Plants are now even to be used for rearmament: missile defense systems instead of Volkswagen and tanks with the Mercedes star, if it's up to Mr. Blume and Mercedes boss Källenius.

Not with us! Stop the course of cuts at the expense of employees! We demand future investments to secure locations long-term, with employment guarantees. Stop the attacks on working hours and collective agreements!

Milan UHRÍK

Madam President, colleagues. It is clear to me that green fanatics in Brussels, such as Mr. Hojsík, would most of all ban all normal cars and basically hate drivers. But the reality is that today, in today's world, an ordinary family simply has no chance without a car. And because of your measures, those cars are increasingly expensive and out of reach. Now Volkswagen has announced that it plans to lay off 100 thousand people and plans to reorient itself towards weapons production, because the Green Deal simply does not apply to weapons. So please, do not blame some Chinese people here now for overtaking us in automobiles. Blame first of all yourselves for allowing this, because that is the reality and that is the result of your work. Look at what has happened here over the last few years. First you came up with the ban on internal combustion engines, which has not been repealed to this day. Then you promoted the Euro 7 standard, which even engineers described as technically unfeasible. Most recently, you are pushing mandatory tachographs even for small vans. For people, for ordinary people, you want to make fuels, petrol, diesel more expensive through ETS 2 emission allowances. You force companies into purchasing a mandatory share of electric vehicles that are sitting in European warehouses. And you are even pushing half of women into the management of companies through gender quotas, while I absolutely do not understand what some gender has to do with some management abilities. Please, when was the last time you simplified or deregulated anything? You only complicate and make everything more expensive. And that is what we want to stop, and that is what we want to fix.

Stéphane Séjourné

Madam President, let us first return perhaps to the competitiveness factors that each of you mentioned in your speeches.

Technological delays, as I mentioned in the introduction, are on the one hand industrial choices—and there have been, in all honesty, bad industrial choices by our manufacturers regarding industrial strategies, and there have also been choices in our ability to conquer a certain number of markets. We are exposed to international competition, with the choice of other countries to focus on their domestic market. I am thinking in particular of China, where a number of Chinese manufacturers are today replacing European manufacturers. On the other hand, these are political choices by our international competitors in markets, hence the opening of other markets abroad, the creation and organization of new trade agreements to find outlets. And then, on our side, work on our internal competitiveness at the European level that must be continued.

Fragilized value and supply chains linked to geopolitics, financial results weighed down by customs duties, with manufacturers who had a global-for-local production concept, with fragmented value chains across the world, which today find themselves in a difficulty where the return of protectionism, the return of customs duties are weakening the economic models of our manufacturers.

Also loss of domestic competitiveness at the European level. Energy prices will probably be the subject of much debate here during this session. Complex European rules and work on simplifying a number of mechanisms to facilitate the marketing of new types of vehicles. In short, the Commission has tackled all the factors of competitiveness.

A final word on some figures you mentioned. In Europe, we have reached 25% market share for electric vehicles and more than 35% if we add plug-in hybrids. Worldwide, we now exceed 13 million electric vehicles produced and, today, we reach approximately 20% of vehicles sold worldwide that are electric. This trend is increasing very sharply, and in the last quarter, it is more than 40% of additional electric vehicle sales in Europe. Why? Quite simply because the market allows the sale of this kind of vehicle. Quite simply because, to drive electric, that is today 80 euros saved for a month of fuel for a certain number of workers. That is 1,000 euros saved for a month of work for a taxi driver in a European capital due to having an electric vehicle today.

So we also have the capacity to convince with vehicles that will arrive on the market, more than 200 new series of vehicles that will arrive on the market this year, vehicles that will be much cheaper and will also benefit from European reforms on simplification, on the capacity to precisely offer the middle classes and working classes a vehicle at less than 20,000 euros. That was the objective we had set ourselves with the small European electric vehicle.

There you have it: to tell you that the Commission, through these three texts that we have presented to you, touches upon all the competitiveness points that we want to debate today. The message is clear: move quickly on the adoption of these texts—to adopt these texts, so that they can enter into force and so that they can also have an impact on our industry and our jobs.

Jens GIESEKE

Madam President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, If Europe's largest car manufacturer wants to cut 100,000 jobs, that is more than a corporate decision; it is a desperate cry for help. The automotive industry is one of Europe's key industries; when it loses competitiveness, Europe loses – and that is exactly what we have been experiencing for years.

While China and the USA are massively supporting their industry, Europe has overburdened its industry with bans and bureaucracy. This shows that a genuine course correction is needed. Only an economically strong industry can master the transformation and preserve jobs in our regions. Therefore, we must reduce bureaucracy, accelerate procedures, and expand charging and hydrogen infrastructure. And we need CO2 fleet limits that are practicable and guarantee technological openness. Whoever wants to promote innovation must not suffocate companies with ever new burdens.

Employees in the industry rightly expect us not only to talk about jobs, but to secure them. This requires an industrial policy that creates trust, enables investment, and strengthens Europe as a production location. Our goal is clear: climate-neutral mobility – but with European vehicles, European innovations, and European jobs. Therefore, I would like to make an appeal today to all democratic and responsible forces in this House: Let us work together to lead Europe's automotive industry back to the top of the world – for employees, companies, and our prosperity.

(The speaker agreed to take a blue-card question.)

Piotr MÜLLER

Mr. Deputy, you are saying here that the automotive industry is in a difficult situation. I agree with you completely. At the same time, however, you were talking here about accelerating climate targets. I would like to understand your statement. Do you think that accelerating climate targets in Europe is supposed to help the automotive industry? Did I understand you correctly? Or rather, should we approach this in a more pragmatic way, and are the targets that you set not long ago in this chamber de facto the reason why the automotive industry is in such trouble in Europe (among other things, the ban on the registration of combustion engine cars from 2035)?

Jens GIESEKE

Blue Card. - I believe you obviously misunderstood me there. I did not say that we have to accelerate the climate targets, but rather I said that we must be open to different technologies and find practical ways to ensure the transformation. That means no acceleration, but sticking to the targets while allowing a mix of options and a competition of technologies. In this respect, I believe this is an approach that we can jointly support.

Gabriele BISCHOFF

Madam President! It is certainly clear that employees did not cause this crisis. Commissioner Séjourné said that - we are also dealing here with massive management errors that we cannot conceal here, and at the same time with a lack of innovative capacity. And if we want to tackle that, we must accelerate with the industrial accelerator.

We need a 'made in Europe', and we need it relatively quickly. And again: If, due to the errors committed in management, the employees are now made to pay the price, then that is disgraceful.

So far, we as the EU have also not delivered on the promise of fair transitions. Remedial action must be taken here; all measures to support employees. We have SURE; we have the experience that it works. Are we ready here to use that? Even if we provide public funds, then not without conditions. Good work, finding collective bargaining solutions for this crisis - that is the order of the day.

Paolo BORCHIA

Madam President, honourable colleagues, I am appalled by the fact that in this Chamber no one is asking the question whether all-out electric vehicles can be compatible with the limits in terms of electricity generation.

If we analyse the context, we have an American market closed to China, stagnant domestic Chinese demand and, on the other hand, Europe which has become an outlet valve, a conquest ground, for Beijing's industrial overcapacity.

Therefore, the title of this debate seems to me to sound a bit like a mockery: we talk about quality jobs, but here we will be lucky if any jobs are left at all. I recall that in a few days Volkswagen will evaluate an industrial plan that provides for the cut of 100,000 jobs and the closure of four plants.

So, at this point, I wonder if anyone here thinks that a price must be paid, but above all: do you all feel calm? Is there anyone who feels responsible?

Piotr MÜLLER

Madam President! The automotive sector is extremely important for the whole of Europe. We know very well what supply chains look like, how many member states are involved in this industry when it comes to the earning opportunities it provides. I am therefore surprised today in this chamber when I listen to this discussion, because I have the impression that practically nothing can be done. That is, you believe that, for example, the climate targets for 2040 – 90% – are supposed to help the automotive industry, that the ban on registering combustion engine cars from 2035 is supposed to help our industry. Or that the fact that we have energy prices in Europe two or three times higher than in the United States or China is supposed to help this sector?

Today in this chamber I have the impression that many people think everything is fine. And you will talk about state aid for plants, and I would prefer that today you spoke about abandoning these high climate targets that currently exist, about abolishing the ETS, about abolishing the ban on registering combustion engine cars after 2035. This needs to be done, because otherwise the European automotive industry will simply collapse.

Jan-Christoph OETJEN

Madam President, Commissioner, dear colleagues! Hundreds of thousands of jobs at car manufacturers and suppliers are in danger because we are currently not competitive in Europe. And, dear friends, the rules we have had up to now, namely the phase-out of combustion engines in 2035, are exacerbating the crisis at car manufacturers. The future is electric – yes, but it is not coming as quickly as some people here thought, and it will not be 100 percent electric either.

Our rules that we have given ourselves are not flexible enough; today they are strangulating our automotive industry. That is why we need more flexibility. Not all the proposals presented by the Commission are dedicated to this goal, but I believe that as part of the parliamentary procedure we can work on expanding this flexibility that was proposed by the Commission.

We need technological openness so that we can use alternative fuels to reduce CO2 in Europe.

Michael BLOSS

Madam President, Commissioner! The combustion engine was great and good engineering, and the employees in the automotive industry can be proud of that. But quite honestly, the combustion engine is a thing of the past. The fact that Volkswagen, Bosch and many others are cutting jobs is because we are not fast enough in switching to e-mobility, and because others are taking the bread out of our mouths.

Since 2017, sales figures for combustion engines have been falling – down by 30% since 2017. And even in Germany today, more electric cars are sold than petrol cars. Your nostalgic clinging to the combustion engine ultimately destroys jobs, because the cars of the future are electric, they are digital, they are affordable; and either we build them, or they are built in China and our factories close.

We can build world-class cars – we have shown that for 100 years; but for world-class, you have to look ten years into the future and not 50 years into the rearview mirror.

(The speaker agreed to answer a blue-card question.)

Idoia MENDIA

I wanted to share with you whether you consider that what we need, taking into account the regulations we are processing, is truly greater support for our businesses, a clear definition of 'Made in Europe', unique and harmonised, easy to apply and, above all, easy to audit, and, above all, that any origin definition must be clear, stable, and easily verifiable.

Likewise, I believe we need framework conditions that favour industrial investment in Europe, thus promoting quality jobs. And also whether you consider that we must strengthen the development of strategic European value chains, especially in the field of batteries, as a way to safeguard the electric car.

Michael BLOSS

Thank you very much. What I think is that we see an amazing rise of the sales of electric cars in Europe, much better than expected: 40 % growth rates.

And in this very moment, to cut down on our legislation, it just doesn't make sense. I mean, the market is much further than the right part of this House. So, there's the first mistake: we are acting against the market.

The second is we want to be naive and stay in the old world. China is doing a lot of industrial policy to strengthen its electromobility and its battery sector. Europe should do the same. If we don't do it, we will lose our industry.

Marina MESURE

Madam President, 50,000 is the number of jobs destroyed in the automotive sector in France since 2017. If we do nothing, thousands more will be sacrificed tomorrow. This is the reality of the earthquake hitting our industry, and the longer we delay in reacting, the heavier the bill will be for our entire society. I am speaking here of our entire society, because, with all due respect to the right and the far right in this hemicycle, in the face of climate change and successive heatwaves, the electric transition is no longer negotiable. It is a vital urgency, given that 30% of our emissions depend directly on the transport sector.

So yes, we must invest massively, but obviously not to fuel speculation, as we have been able to see: public money must truly serve to protect employees, to transform our industry, and not to enrich shareholders. To succeed, we obviously need a shield, a true "made in Europe" approach in the automotive sector, in order to master our batteries and our technologies. In this sense, current plans do not go far enough regarding local preference and aid for the acquisition of affordable electric vehicles for all citizens. Therefore, we must break away from these lethal free-trade logics and truly protect our market and our industry.

Stéphane Séjourné

Madam President, perhaps a word to tell you that the objective is indeed to stop the bleeding and to reposition our industry in a sector of the future, of innovation, with improved competitiveness conditions, including internationally.

A few messages on the Commission's proposals: we have proposed having a definition of a European car to be able to positively discriminate, when European public money is committed, in the framework of public procurement, in the framework of purchase subsidies, so that there is a European purchase preference from the moment the consumer wishes to benefit from this particular taxation.

I find it normal today, in view of the observation you are all making here, in this hemicycle, that the public money collected through taxation can benefit above all the creation of demand, in Europe, in particular segments, notably in the segments of electric vehicles. This is the proposal we have made, with 70% of European components in an electric car (excluding battery), with 50% of European components for the electric propulsion chain and 50% of European components for electronics.

Here is the proposal on the table, on which you must debate, but which is part of the solution we are proposing to you – not the whole solution, but part of the solution that we are proposing to you in the framework of this text.

One last message: this text must absolutely reach its destination as quickly as possible – and the urgency of the situation demonstrates that the vote on the industrial accelerator is also a question of urgency for the automotive sector.

Volker SCHNURRBUSCH

Madam President, Commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the Commission is worried about the competitiveness of our automotive industry, about securing jobs. Seriously? Who drove this great industry against the wall? Why are our businesses in the deepest crisis of their history? Why are tens of thousands of workers being laid off? But that is also the result of your policies. You have presumed to intervene in a market that worked: there were cars for every budget, for every purpose, for every taste. But now Ms von der Leyen stands up and demands that small battery-powered cars be built.

Politicians have no business prescribing to our entrepreneurs what cars they should build. Politicians are supposed to create a framework for the market, nothing more. Now plants are being closed in Germany, jobs are being cut, production is being relocated to China and the USA. Does this look like the success model in Europe? No! This Commission relies on saving the world instead of a market economy. It relies on prohibitions instead of technological openness. It relies on rotten compromises instead of fair framework conditions and drives energy prices to heights that stifle any competition.

It is not too late yet. 50,000 jobs can still be saved in Germany alone if you bid farewell to the combustion engine ban. Bid farewell to green daydreams, because with the fight against our industry you do not change the world climate, you only worsen the investment climate. Europe has become a no-go area for innovation, and unfortunately that is also your fault.

(The speaker agreed to answer a blue-card question.)

Yvan VEROUGSTRAETE

Dear Sir, you speak to us about the market economy, but do you not have the impression that the market economy, precisely, is giving the victory to electric vehicles today? You speak about the market economy, but in fact you deny the very reality of the market.

You also speak about energy, increasingly expensive energy, and you defend the fact that we continue to buy this energy dearly rather than switching to an energy that allows us to have our sovereignty and a cheaper price -- and which is electricity.

There are two paradoxes here that it seems simply impossible to justify to me.

Volker SCHNURRBUSCH

blue card". - Thank you very much for the question. You will allow me to reply in German again.

Ofচন্দ্র course, the market also provides a market for electric cars; there is absolutely no question about that. We have never rejected the idea that there should be electric cars, but we have always said that there must be both or several types of drive systems. Because electric cars are very, very well suited for many purposes - the Commissioner also said so, for taxis, for example, for courier services, for the postal service - but they are simply not suited for all purposes. And the success, the alleged success, is also due to subsidies, high subsidies with which the state has intervened in the market. And that is not a market economy, that is a planned economy, and we reject that.

Erik KALIŇÁK

Madam President. For an hour now we have been speaking here about urgent measures to save jobs in the automotive industry, which has always been one of the pillars of the European economy. But in recent years, Stellantis has had to suspend lines in Poissy, Eisenach and other places. Audi has completely closed its plant in Brussels. Mercedes is interrupting the production of its electronic GLC in Bremen. And Volkswagen, for the first time in history, is considering closing as many as four German manufacturing plants, which would mean the dismissal of 100 thousand people. These are not accidental problems or temporary difficulties of the transition to electromobility. It is a consequence of the fact that European production is no longer competitive, and the key cause, which is hardly heard about here today, is expensive electricity – twice as expensive as in the United States and more than half as expensive compared to China. Why is it so expensive? Because the policy of the European Commission, the ideological pressure for the green transition regardless of price and reliability, has deprived us of cheap and stable energy. And instead of solving this root cause here today – we are applauding ourselves for spending billions we do not have on the retraining of dismissed observers or battery subsidies. Please, let us stop endlessly dealing with the symptoms and start dealing with the causes. Thank you.

Raúl DE LA HOZ QUINTANO

Madam President, how much longer are we going to witness, resignedly, the decline of the emblem of European industry?

The situation that the automotive sector is experiencing today in Europe is the consequence of years of many mistakes; also years of political mistakes, years of impossible obligations, unattainable targets, unaffordable energy costs and also unacceptable administrative hurdles. Faced with that, a consequence —a result—: the uncertainty that the sector is experiencing today and the closures and layoffs that we are learning about.

However, the Commission has presented —and they are currently going through parliamentary processing— two initiatives that can help us reverse this situation. The first of them is the automotive package, an initiative that goes in the right direction, but which, to be truly useful and effective, must place the principles of flexibility and technological neutrality as a fundamental axis in its planning and development, without subordination, by the way, to other climate principles. The second of them is the industrial accelerator, a tool that will serve us to accelerate strategic investments, to reduce administrative hurdles, but, above all, to make it possible for investing, for producing, in Europe to be a competitive advantage, to be an added value and never a burden for our companies.

Europe needs today more than ever a strong, innovative industry, capable of growing, of creating employment, backed by public institutions. Otherwise, it is impossible for us to speak either of strategic autonomy or of the welfare state, nor of the generation of employment.

Dan NICA

Madam President, Mr Séjourné, you are the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission and today you are present at an extremely important debate on the automotive manufacturing industry in the European Union.

As we speak, in Romania, Dacia has announced its first collective redundancies in the last 22 years. It is a symptom that shows how serious the situation is for the automotive manufacturing industry and automotive supply co-industry in Romania, and the same situation in the European Union. Why is this and what do those who are watching with great concern expect from us? Because if this backbone is sick - the automotive manufacturing industry - the economy of the European Union is in a very bad situation.

Carbon dioxide certificates: in Romania we pay 80 euros per tonne of carbon dioxide certificates, in China seven times less. Is this not obviously a lack of competitiveness? And I believe that the first measures that should be taken, please consider, I don't know, allocations of free carbon dioxide certificates, in order to bring competitiveness to the same level.

Perhaps all those who do not pay any taxes on the import of cars into the European Union should be subject to CBAM regulation and I believe that all these things must be done now, before it is too late.

Jorge BUXADÉ VILLALBA

Madam President, I have been speaking harshly, but respectfully, about Europe's ruinous automotive policies for seven years.

We are fed up, fed up with the Commission, sick and tired of that little speech about decarbonisation, transition, resilience and climate targets. Every month in Strasbourg there is a debate on the automotive sector and every month production figures fall across Europe.

Europe made the industrial revolution, changed the world, we changed the production and lives of millions of people. The history of our industry is a history of innovation, adaptation and growth. And you, in the last legislative term, destroyed everything. Our cars —the best on the planet— dominated world markets. It was employment, wealth, middle classes, democratisation of movement. Now China produces more than 90% of electric batteries and moves its production to Morocco and Turkey to use triangular operations and enter our market under better conditions.

This is the reality and you are guilty of the closure of companies, you are guilty of 104,000 layoffs in the last two years. I dream of the day when all of you will one day be held accountable and declared as such.

Marion MARÉCHAL

Madam President, dear colleagues, we can say well done and thank you to the political group of Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné, as well as to the various governments of Édouard Philippe, since, from the price of energy to the cost of labor and the ban on internal combustion engines in 2035 to unfair Chinese competition, its left-wing and center political leaders have done everything methodically to bring this European automotive industry to its knees, with the latest victim to date being the emblematic Stellantis site in Poissy, which will no longer produce new cars as of 2028.

Because your Green Deal has resulted in a genuine "Buy China Act": while China was twenty years ahead in the field of electric vehicles, you found nothing better than to roll out the red carpet for it by dogmatically imposing the end of internal combustion engines. Worse still, you are persevering in your mistake by refusing to truly overhaul the dogmatic objectives of this Green Deal. You are thereby worsening a foreign dependence on hydrocarbons, into an even more concentrated, even more critical dependence: that on batteries and rare earths.

In 2019, we had a automotive trade surplus of 23 billion euros with China. Today, it is a deficit of 6 billion euros, and there are still people in this hemicycle to congratulate themselves on this situation.

(The speaker agrees to take a blue-card question)

Thomas PELLERIN-CARLIN

Mrs. Marion Maréchal, you talk to us about sovereignty. Can you just tell me what share of the oil we produce in France is and what share of the electricity we produce in France is? That seems to me to be an important subject, whether we want to move to electrification, or whether we want, like you, to remain dependent on oil and refuse electrification.

Marion MARÉCHAL

This is a completely central subject. You are right because, indeed, political leaders like you have campaigned for years for the Hulot law, which prohibits any new exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons potentially present on French soil, thereby depriving us of another share of sovereignty—since we know that, notably off the coast of French Guiana, there are potentially extremely significant hydrocarbon deposits—and, as a result, here we are indeed largely dependent on foreign hydrocarbons.

But, as I have just specified, the tragedy with the "all-electric" approach as you have built it is that we are replacing one dependency with another, an even more critical, even more concentrated dependency, which is that on batteries, which is that on rare earths. Hence the fact, obviously, that I am talking about dogmatism and that I am talking about ideology, which are paid for in the first place, of course, by employees in the automotive sector.

Thomas PELLERIN-CARLIN

Clearly, Ms Marion Maréchal does not know the figures, so I am going to explain them to her: the share of oil we produce in France is 1%. It is not because of questions concerning the Hulot law, etc. It is simply because of something called geology: we have no oil in France, and the French know it, unlike you.

On the other hand, in France we have electricity: we produce more than 100% of our electricity thanks to renewables and nuclear power. Refusing the electrification of cars means refusing to build a French energy system, and I am very, very surprised that you say yes to nuclear power in your words, but that, when it comes to voting here, you go against electrification, which is essential for the future of our nuclear sector.

Marion MARÉCHAL

Sir, I know the figures perfectly well. The only thing is that I was explaining to you that we could have, contrary to what you are saying, a greater production of French hydrocarbons, but that we forbade ourselves, for ideological reasons - because of the Greens, with the support, moreover, of the centrists and the Macron movement -, from benefiting from them, since we even forbade ourselves from exploring the potential of these deposits, which we know moreover, on a geological level, could exist, not only moreover for hydrocarbons, but also for gas, for example, off the coast of Mayotte. So yes, I regret that.

You are right to say that fortunately there were people like us, for years, to defend nuclear power, because if we had had to count on the center or the left, we would have put an end to French nuclear power.

I am not against the electric car industry, I consider that, on the other hand, when we have a technological lead such as ours, with the internal combustion engine industry, it is obviously dramatic to s...

(The President withdraws the floor from the speaker)

Stéphane Séjourné

Madam President, I will not enter into the debate, and I believe I have very little speaking time left. First, perhaps, a few elements to support the impact, notably of China, on the automotive market. The consequences for our automotive industry are catastrophic and present almost everywhere in Europe. This is not just a German debate, it is a debate for all Europeans across all value chains. And you have a very strong German industry, but you also have an industry, equipment manufacturers, subcontractors, very present, everywhere in Europe, that supply the automotive industry.

In Europe—whether in Italy, for example, where more than half of the plug-in hybrid market is dominated by Chinese models, or in Germany too, where the primary beneficiary of national public aid today is BYD—we have built a model that finances Chinese manufacturers. What we are proposing to you, with the industry acceleration law, is to go back on this and precisely favor European preference, made in Europe, when it comes to European public money.

Andreas GLÜCK

Madam President, dear colleagues! Whoever takes the wrong exit over and over and over again will never reach their destination. Over 100,000 jobs have already been lost in the automotive industry, and that was only the beginning. Incidentally, this is a huge challenge not only in Germany, but across the whole of Europe. This is a direct consequence of the combustion engine ban, which was decided here by a majority. Now there is the opportunity to revise this mistake.

We need the best solutions, not political know-it-all attitudes, no bans. Our task is to set climate targets, not drive systems. Employers and trade unions are jointly demanding precisely this course, and yet Greens and Social Democrats are always only intent on being proven right. If reality now changes, politics must be willing to review its decisions. Whoever makes a mistake and does not correct it makes a second one. Therefore: Let us finally give our engineers the chance once again to develop the best technologies.

Benedetta SCUDERI

Madam President, honourable colleagues, Fiat, FCA, lost almost 50,000 workers between 2000 and 2020, well before the Green Deal.

Therefore, the absence of European industrial policies was already a problem. And what did we do? Nothing.

Were our competitors investing in new technologies? We were giving dividends to shareholders, instead of reinvesting them.

Were wages losing purchasing power? More and more luxury cars were being produced, because they make more profits.

Was the redundancy fund increasing? Production was relocated to pay less.

So, colleagues, let me understand: are we here because we did not invest, we did not plan, we did not understand what the direction of the future was, and your solution is to go back and make all the mistakes of the past?

We must invest in the technologies of the future, become experts in the production of batteries and electric motors. We must support demand and create more infrastructure for electric mobility, create a market for 'made in Europe' – but the real one, the one concerning Europe, Commissioner – we must invest in skills, training workers for the transition.

You talk a lot about competitiveness in the automotive sector, but you do not want to put a euro into it: if you want to help workers, invest in them.

Dario TAMBURRANO

Madam President, honourable colleagues, I do not want to repeat things here that have already been said by colleagues.

The challenges we face are enormous and it will take years, decades, to make up for wasted time, increase people's purchasing power, strengthen the competitiveness of the European automotive industry, and protect workers.

We can, however, adopt small measures right away, with great effects: a technically simple rule with a marginal cost close to zero is the State of Health - the health status of the battery - the performance status indicator that the battery retains compared to when it was new.

For a used electric vehicle, it is one of the main indicators of its real value, because the residual value of the battery is more important than the mileage driven, it directly affects the value of the used car, and it is decisive for corporate fleets that, after a few years, feed the used market.

Let us make the State of Health harmonised, freely visible on the car's dashboard, and mandatory in used car advertisements. More transparency means more trust, more demand, and therefore more jobs and industry in Europe.

Dariusz JOŃSKI

Madam President! Commissioner! Either we save the European automotive industry, or 14 million Europeans will be unemployed, and our continent will become an economic marginalisation. And all of us in this room know, we know very well, that it was Europe that created car brands which for decades, precisely for decades, have set global standards. And today we cannot afford in any way for this continent of ours, our Europe, to become merely a market for vehicles from China and the United States.

Of course we must invest, invest in modern technologies and innovation, but we must also remember ordinary citizens. The fact that they buy Chinese cars is only because they are much cheaper. Simply put, European cars are too expensive for Europeans, and we must also admit that to ourselves. And since we are on the subject of competitiveness, we must focus on independence. Let us not replace our former dependence on Russian oil with dependence on Chinese batteries and raw materials.

And in this whole flood of disturbing information, I also have good news. Well, in Poland we have made a decision – at this rather difficult moment for the entire European automotive industry – to build the first electric vehicle factory. This year we break ground, we begin the construction of the factory, and the first vehicles will roll off the line in 2029. The first 400 thousand units. Why? Because we cannot abandon our own ambitions. That is why we are doing this. But it is also about jobs, about our European and Polish economy. And let us prove to the whole world that the best future of the automotive industry still bears the proud brand Made in Europe.

Jacek OZDOBA

Madam President! Mr. Member, this is the moment. I would even agree with your speech, were it not for the fact—though indeed not yours—but the voting in the last term on EU matters, which are precisely blocking and destroying the European industry.

So now a simple question: would you recommend the same voting to the European People's Party, in the exact same way regarding ETS2? Would you say today that ETS2 should be thrown in the trash?

Dariusz JOŃSKI

We are talking about the automotive industry. It seems to me that everyone here, as far as the Polish delegation is concerned, was unanimous on this matter. However, Mr. Ozdoba, you governed for 8 years. It is a pity that you did not do anything, even though you promised that you would build this car factory, and you didn't even drive the proverbial spade into the ground. So today, at this very moment, you might choose not to speak in this hall.

Thomas PELLERIN-CARLIN

Madam President, at 53 years old, my disabled father found himself unemployed. The automotive component factory where he worked had closed.
