That is where I come from, from this industrial land where we experienced in our flesh what these layoffs do to our families. MPI Lisieux has disappeared, but the Renault Cléon factory still employs more than 2,500 Normands today. These jobs, we can preserve them. What will save them is not the far-right's nostalgia for the internal combustion engine, because, in Cléon, it is the electric engines of the R5 and other electric models from Renault that our workers are manufacturing.

It is true that China threatens them. That is why we must adopt European preference, so that cars bought in Europe are manufactured in Europe, built by European workers. The factory where my father worked closed; the one in Cléon, we can save it.

Anne-Sophie FRIGOUT

Madam President, the Commission, acting like an arsonist firefighter, started the fire – with the ban on internal combustion engines by 2035 to the benefit of China – and now here it pretends to put it out with a teaspoon. So, to clear your conscience, you are organizing yet another debate right here on how to save the competitiveness of our automotive industry. But what cynicism! Because behind your climate objectives, jobs are at stake. There are the employees of the Stellantis plant in Poissy and so many others – the subcontractors, the dealerships, the garage owners... – the families who live off this industry, and who see their future go up in smoke because of your obstinacy. They also have to hear your lies about job creation linked to the electrification of the vehicle fleet, but at the cost of how many jobs destroyed elsewhere?

So, if you really want to save the automotive sector, be more ambitious in your proposals on European preference and for the reconquest of our industry's sovereignty. Because everyone who knows the sector much better than you do states: it is one minute to midnight before the death of this industry.

Ondřej KRUTÍLEK

Madam President, dear Commissioner, we are returning to the issue of automotive repeatedly in this forum. I would like to recall that it was precisely the ECR group who first pushed for the adoption of a resolution at a time when European car manufacturers faced the threat of senseless fines. We also pushed for the acceleration of legislative changes towards the abolition of the ban on internal combustion engines after 2035 and for the establishment of true technological neutrality. Not because of internal combustion engines themselves, but mainly so that we could align European rules with car manufacturers and, above all, so that car manufacturers could deliver to customers what they want from them. That means quality cars with various powertrains at fair prices.

Now we are trying to fix the Commission's latest proposals, and the automotive part of the industrial accelerator is also problematic. And that is precisely what it is about. Either we want to preserve our own traditional production and traditional partnership with reliable partners, or under the flag of climate policy we will fully open the gates to the invasion of Chinese electric vehicles. I wish for the former.

Elisabetta GUALMINI

Madam President, I wrote my PhD dissertation in Wolfsburg in the mid-1990s, on the introduction of flexibility and the four-day workweek at Volkswagen. It was a cyclical crisis that eventually seemed to be overcome.

Today we are talking of a genuine collapse, and the alarm is broader in scope because we are talking of the breakdown of the German social and economic model, the one based on co-determination, high wages, cooperation between capital and labour, and collaborative innovation.

'People's cars' are no longer selling for a variety of reasons. An obsessive push towards electrification without having the necessary infrastructure – how can you fix a goal without the means to reach it? – and the shift in lifestyles and so on and so forth.

So we have the paradox that Germany invested in China hoping to compete with China, but now it will be China that will eventually save Germany buying German enterprises.

So what now? The crisis cannot fall on the shoulders of the workers. It is up to Europe to find a strategy.

Virginijus SINKEVIČIUS

Madam President, Commissioner, dear colleagues. Europe's automotive sector means more than 13 million jobs. And of course, it's one of our industrial engines. But clearly, that engine cannot run on nostalgia.

The market is changing fast, and one in five cars that has been sold in the EU this year is already battery electric. So our task is clear: to make sure that this transition happens first of all within European factories, with European workers and, of course, with leading European technology. And that means, first of all, cheaper clean energy, charging infrastructure, European batteries, stronger software capacity and real support to European suppliers – because the automotive sector is not only Germany, the automotive sector is Europe as a whole.

Weakening targets is not going to bring competitiveness; it will only create more uncertainty and delay investment. So our answer should be industrial confidence and not industrial fear.

Rudi KENNES

Mr President, CEOs are in a panic because the European automotive industry is disappearing. But where was that panic when millions of workers were laid off? I am one of them. In 2010, thousands of colleagues and I lost our jobs after Opel Antwerp closed. Since then, things have only gotten worse. Audi Brussels, Van Hool in Lier and now Volkswagen in Germany.

Time and again, China is blamed. But where is personal responsibility? Profits were not reinvested. Production was relocated and subsidies vanished into the pockets of shareholders. Talk about neoliberal extremism.

Now everyone sees what workers and trade unions have been saying for a long time. This could easily have been prevented. Factories could have been given a new purpose, workers could have been retrained, jobs could have stayed here and we would have been competitive.

Now we are bringing the industry back. Great! But who is going to compensate all the victims of restructurings, relocation and closures? We must never do this again.

Production must return to public hands. We need to draw up a long-term economic plan and invest in the economy and in our workers.

Zala ČERNILEC TOMAŠIČ

Madam President! In just two years, more than 100,000 people have lost their jobs in the European automotive industry. That is approximately 140 people a day. 140 families every day facing the loss of a job. And in the coming years, we can only expect more of them. Why?

Because we decided to force a single technology and ignore reality. Thirteen million eight hundred thousand Europeans depend on the automotive industry. Last year, various types of hybrids outsold pure electric cars by more than two to one. Because people want choice, they do not want ideology.

Meanwhile, China already controls more than 80 percent of global electric vehicle batteries. The rigid "electricity only" approach not only costs jobs, it costs us our industrial sovereignty and hands our future over to others. Of course, we should not be dependent on fossil fuels, but we must not replace one dependency with another. And the urgent measure we need is technological neutrality.

We must open wide the doors to all efficient solutions and let competition and innovation decide. And I don't know why some of you are so afraid of this – because that is the only way we will protect quality jobs, preserve world-renowned European engineering, and actually achieve faster decarbonization.

Because our workers have been powering Europe for generations and technological freedom in the European Union must not be just flexibility – it must be the standard. And now you have the opportunity to change the mistakes that have been made and actually save the European automotive industry.

Christel SCHALDEMOSE

Madam President! Europe's automotive industry is at a crossroads. We can keep protecting the past, or we can invest in the future. For me, the choice is clear: We must simplify the rules for the European automotive industry, but without weakening Europe's green ambitions. If European car manufacturers keep getting stuck in yesterday's technology, we will not only lose even more market share to China and the USA, we will also lose good European jobs.

Therefore, we need to get more electric vehicles on European roads, and many, many more of them must be built in Europe. And yes, it may be that the European electric car is neither the best nor the cheapest right now, but it will never become that if we do not dare to truly invest in the green transition. It is about strengthening our competitiveness, the climate, and good jobs. To get there, it requires political courage, and that courage is about not giving up on the Green Deal.

Antonín STANĚK

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, every time one of the European car manufacturers announces production cuts or layoffs, we should ask ourselves a simple question: "What signal are we sending to one of Europe's most important industrial sectors?" We all want cleaner transport. But we must start from reality. The transformation is progressing more slowly than expected, while the pressure on manufacturers continues to grow. If our responsibility and response are only further regulation and more obligations, we will not save the automotive industry. We will move production and jobs outside Europe. Europe needs less bureaucracy, simpler rules and respect for technological neutrality. Let us give our manufacturers space for competitiveness and innovation. If we want to preserve quality jobs and car manufacturing in Europe, we need a policy based on reality, not ideology.

Jacek OZDOBA

Madam President! Just look at two large countries in the world - apart from the European Union, if we looked at the European Union as a whole: China and the United States. India and Brazil will join them in a moment. Why are Chinese cars cheaper? Because production costs in Europe are higher. If Chinese cars have modern technology, it is simply because energy costs are lower in terms of production costs.

If we look at the United States, energy costs there are also twice as low, and gasoline costs are lower. Well, but what is this chamber doing? This chamber is currently debating what you did in the last term. A simple question about ETS2. After all, you can withdraw from it. In a moment, gasoline costs will be even higher. ETS1 energy costs are getting higher and higher. Modern technologies and artificial intelligence need more energy. More energy means higher costs.

A simple question could be asked, but I would not want to be impolite to the Commissioner: those who came up with this, maybe some of these officials should be verified to see if they are not working, for example, for the American or Chinese industry, because it is impossible to murder European industry like this.

Katri KULMUNI

Mr President, I understand that the automotive industry is a key economic sector in many European countries, employing around 13 million people within this continent. It is clear that if we talk about strategic autonomy, industry is a key issue in it, both for the automotive industry and other industries. At the same time, of course, the major discussions when taking action to combat and counter climate change while trying to help our industry survive should not be mutually exclusive in any way.

We must not create regulations that drive our important sectors outside of Europe, because emissions there will certainly be higher. After all, the atmosphere is a single shared one, so it is important to keep these sectors in Europe, while at the same time taking sensible, technology-neutral actions and being ambitious about them. In Finland, the automotive sector has suffered, but on the other hand, this same Finnish car factory has now started manufacturing armored vehicles as well as diesel and electric buses, so it is not worth fighting on the crest of a recession, but rather being at the forefront of development.

Angelika NIEBLER

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, dear colleagues! For the first time, China's car imports into the European Union exceed European exports to the People's Republic. 250,000 jobs have already been lost in the automotive industry; a further 100,000 jobs are at stake. Jobs are migrating abroad, and investments in research and development are also going abroad. The situation is truly dramatic, but the situation is not a natural phenomenon, but also the result of political decisions that we urgently need to correct now.

What needs to be done? First: We must correct the CO2 targets and allow real technological openness. The CO2 fleet limit values must be adjusted. Quotas for the electrification of fleets are to be rejected; that is nothing other than reintroducing the ban on combustion engines through the back door. Second: We must keep the plug-in hybrid in Europe; the utility factor must be frozen. And thirdly: We need better locational conditions, and that means above all that we must lower energy prices and electricity costs. Today, European industry pays around twice as much as American industry. We must reduce grid fees and levies, use revenues from emissions trading to relieve industrial electricity prices, accelerate approvals and, above all, reduce bureaucracy.

Focusing on only one technology is wrong, was wrong and will always remain wrong.

Giorgio GORI

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, honourable colleagues, this debate comes at a crucial moment, with the automotive package under discussion in the various competent committees.

And there is no doubt that the choices made in the coming months will be decisive for the sector, which is called upon to decarbonise while safeguarding competitiveness and jobs. I am also thinking of component manufacturing, a large part of which cannot be replicated in the electric dimension.

Promoting innovation and accompanying the transformation: to revive the main sector of European manufacturing, substantial investments are needed, including public ones – we have said this and we repeat it – also because, visibly, rules and sanctions alone are insufficient to produce the desired change, especially in the presence of Chinese competition that is extensively subsidised by the State.

But, in the absence of adequate investments, reasonableness is needed. I therefore hope that the negotiations in the coming months will focus on the substance, keeping the decarbonisation objectives firm on the one hand, and, on the other, finding the right measure of flexibility needed to govern the transition process.

François KALFON

Madam President, dear colleagues, Mr Vice-President, European industry is stalled. There is an emergency! Production has dropped by 20% in five years, and 100,000 jobs were destroyed in 2024. Yet here, the right prefers to keep the internal combustion engine, while Europe burns.

Meanwhile, China is accelerating. This year, its market share has doubled in Europe. It sells more vehicles in Germany than the Germans sell in China. To save our jobs, we urgently need 35% tariffs – including on hybrids – and strict local content criteria. Launch the small, accessible "made in Europe" car to boost demand!

Dear colleagues, the choice is simple: invest in "made in Europe" electric vehicles to ensure a peaceful future for the 3.5 million workers in the sector, or look in the rearview mirror – and by 2035, we will have 1 million fewer jobs and ever more pollution.

(The speaker takes a blue card question)

Anne-Sophie FRIGOUT

Dear colleague, no later than this morning, a study by an expert firm came out and it states that one in three car factories in Europe is "useless because of our overproduction capacities". We all know here how this will end if you do not wake up: massive job losses and factory closures, particularly in France—and this has already begun.

So, dear colleague, I have a question for you: do you take responsibility for having sold off our automotive industry for the benefit of China, by supporting unrealistic, detached standards, and the ban on internal combustion engines by 2035? And above all, will you ever finally present, along with your colleagues, your apologies to all the employees and to our manufacturers and equipment suppliers who have found themselves unemployed and in precariousness through your fault?

François KALFON

Dear colleague, I invite you to open the newspapers and see that the number of electric vehicles sold in France has doubled in a year. You are behind the market, you are behind European citizens, and what we are doing with electrification is, on the contrary, catching up with China. You are looking in the rearview mirror, and soon, with your action, the entire European automotive industry will experience a crash.

Alice TEODORESCU MÅWE

Madam President! Grandiose goals that do not take into account the prerequisites for realizing them do not indicate leadership.

Europe cannot afford to engage in wishful thinking or more political castles in the air. Yet the EU chose to do just that during the previous parliamentary term. The combustion engine ban is the clearest example. In the eagerness to drive the green transition, basic questions were ignored. Where is the stable electricity production and charging infrastructure? Does the climate improve from the measures? The answer is no. The ban does not reduce our dependence, it shifts it: from Russian oil to Chinese critical raw materials. That is not a green transition, it is geopolitical naivety.

While Europe stifles its own industry, jobs, and willingness to invest, the world's major climate offenders continue to increase their emissions. Politics must be based on reality. Europe needs technological neutrality, innovation, and competitiveness, not more symbolic bans.

Maria GRAPINI

Madam President, Commissioner, you began your speech by saying that last year you said the automotive industry is in mortal danger. And it is. The problem is to ask why? I believe the European Commission set off on a program without taking the concrete situation into account. A private manager takes the global situation into account, and that is why we are now in a situation where, globally, we cannot produce like China, we have higher costs and inputs, obviously for energy as well, and infrastructure is lacking, the charging system throughout the European Union space, and let us also think about the middle class, Commissioner: do you think it can? The car is not a luxury, only the ones that go to races.

Cars are now a necessity for mobility, and then we must think about building an automotive system that no longer lays off workers, but brings them to Europe. And it is very good that you came with this proposal. Yes, I would like "Made in Europe" to be taken into account in the entire value chain of car manufacturing and let us think about adapting the program for the electric car system as we go along.

Lefteris NIKOLAOU-ALAVANOS

Madam President, you admitted that 600,000 jobs will be lost, 100,000 in the Volkswagen group alone. The European Union's sorrow is to support conglomerates in fierce competition with China and the US in a series of sectors —batteries, electromobility—, but above all with a shift towards a war economy as an outlet for profitability through the production of vehicles, tanks, and dual-use goods. You are further relaxing green standards for businesses to boost their profitability and, conversely, working-class households are saddled with new burdens for old houses, vehicles, oil boilers.

With the Recovery Fund, the dismantling of collective agreements was subsidized, energy poverty, high costs, and inflation escalated. The capitalist mode of production advertised by the European Union, governments, and its parties in growth and crisis skyrockets the exploitation of workers for the profits of capital.

We support the magnificent labor mobilizations in Germany, so that no job is lost, and workers' income is supported with collective agreements and substantial wage increases. Conclusion and necessity: production must be organized based on modern needs and not profits and war.

András LÁSZLÓ

Madam President, Mercedes is decreasing wages by 20 %, Volkswagen is shutting down factories and firing tens of thousands of workers, Stellantis has achieved a net loss of EUR 20 billion last year, and the European Commission estimates that 600 000 jobs in the auto industry are at risk. And the Commissioner is also saying that the automotive sector is in mortal danger.

But only ten years ago, we had in Europe the best auto industry in the world. The Commission now points the finger at China and wants new regulations. But the crisis facing the European car industry is purely of our own making. It is the result of foolish, ideologically driven policymaking at European level.

Restrictive measures have stifled innovation and competition to instead impose a single technology, chosen not by the consumer, but by politicians. We should have never given in to the Dieselgate blackmail either.

We need to re-industrialise Europe. Only a coalition of patriots – ECR, ECN and EPP – can do that. Keeping the cordon sanitaire is industrial suicide.

Ana MIRANDA PAZ

Madam President, Commissioner, the automotive sector is vital for Galiza, for my country, where there are thousands of direct and indirect jobs—as you know—in the sector and, moreover, where we are demanding an industrial plan that cannot be a blank check to give subsidies to the automotive industry while employment is destroyed and made precarious.

Payment is made for relocation, as we have seen in recent years, to lose jobs. It cannot be, Commissioner, that the same treatment is given to vehicles manufactured in Europe as to vehicles manufactured outside. It cannot be that the crisis continues to be paid for by workers. If there is unfair competition, Europe must act: manufacture in Europe, create jobs with decent wages, because a lot of aid has been given to the sector, but the transition, even though it must be fair, must also be for the people, for the local economies.

Therefore, I ask you: more aid for whom? For the multinationals of the automobile sector or to create decent and quality employment?

Özlem DEMIREL

Madam President! Let us be honest: the current crisis is not a crisis of profits, but a crisis of jobs. Hundreds of thousands of jobs have been cut in recent years, and hundreds of thousands more remain on the chopping block. Colleagues at VW, Mercedes, Bosch, in industry in Germany, and across Europe are currently on strike, fighting for their jobs and better wages, and our solidarity belongs to them.

The truth is, this crisis is not a sudden shock; it is a crisis with forewarning. The transformation was delayed and the last drop was squeezed out for profit. The Commission's only industrial policy consisted of expanding the arms industry, which is economic bullshit. Your entry into the exit, your exit from the exit has truly helped no one; the back-and-forth helps no one. Billions in aid have flowed, but no conditions for job retention were dictated – and that is precisely the mistake. The current question is: Whose side are you actually on?

Kateřina KONEČNÁ

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, do you know when the automotive industry stopped being competitive? The moment Ursula von der Leyen and her minions took charge of the Commission, precisely at that moment. We heard the Commissioner here telling us: "We will prevent a deadly cycle, we owe it to our industry." And then he announces to us that he is preparing more legislation, more regulations, that we will define the European car. Please, before we define what a European car is, there will not be a single automotive factory left here. The only thing we should do at this moment, Commissioner, is cut, cancel, immediately stop this huge bureaucracy and support car manufacturers in any way possible, for example in what you have been promising for two years since you have been sitting in the Commission, which is that you will reduce energy prices. You have come up with nothing of the sort, so the only thing that will help the automotive industry is for you to resign, forever.

Nikolina BRNJAC

Madam President, Commissioner, today we are here because the targets set for the European automotive industry were too ambitious, too rigid and insufficiently aligned with the actual capabilities of our manufacturers.

The European industry, which employs nearly 14 million people, has faced high costs, job losses and too little technological flexibility, all due to the insistence of the radical left and the greens.

At the same time, Chinese manufacturers have been strengthening thanks to state subsidies, low costs and control over batteries and key raw materials, and in the first six months of this year they reached a record market share in Europe of 7.3 percent.

That is why I welcome the automotive package and the more ambitious draft report by colleague Salini. They maintain the direction towards climate neutrality, but also give our industry more time, flexibility and technological opportunities.

Europe must not make political decisions that sound good on paper while in practice weakening our industry, investments and jobs.

Malika SOREL

Madam President, dear colleagues, Commissioner, three priorities to preserve quality jobs in the European automotive industry: firstly, to invest massively in skills; secondly, to relocate high value-added segments (batteries, software, power electronics, semiconductors, recycling); thirdly, to strengthen the attractiveness of industrial professions (working conditions, career prospects, partnerships between companies, universities and research centres).

The European Union has set itself ambitious climate objectives, but one question arises: have we evaluated with the same rigour the consequences of these decisions on our capacity to produce, invest, and create sustainable quality jobs? The answer is unfortunately no. The ecological and digital transition creates new opportunities, but requires significant investments in skills, innovation and support for employees.

I propose that, in the future, any major legislative initiative be subject to two complementary evaluations: its impact on our industrial competitiveness and its impact on quality employment in the European Union.

Matej TONIN

Madam President! The future of the automotive industry may indeed be electric, but I am not entirely sure that we are ready for an electric future today. Are the grids ready for this, is electricity production ready for this? Do we have the minerals needed for electric batteries? The answer is no. And therefore, of course, we need a reasonable transitional period where we will ensure technological neutrality.

Europe is the world champion in the production of the cleanest internal combustion engines, and we would truly have to be crazy to give this up and completely subject ourselves to a new dependency, that is, dependency on Chinese electric vehicles. Therefore, the only right path is technological neutrality, to give a chance to both traditional vehicles and electric vehicles.

Ondřej DOSTÁL

Madam President, dear Commissioner, the most important thing is fading from the debate about cars – the interest of customers, ordinary motorists who need a cheap and good car. Not nonsense that makes cars expensive, bad, and full of planned obsolescence. If it were not for EU regulations, a modern, simple car could cost EUR 6,000 and a quality family car perhaps EUR 10,000 or 12,000. It is possible in the world. But our people pay three times as much or drive used cars with an average age of 16 years because they cannot afford new ones. Let us therefore slash regulations, because cars do not run on paperwork, as motorists say. Let people buy the cars they really want, not the ones you prescribe for them. And companies, let them not manufacture according to regulations, but according to customer wishes as they did years ago when our automotive industry was still young and successful. And whoever cannot manufacture a good and cheap car, let them go bankrupt and make room for better ones.

Seán KELLY

A Uachtaráin, I think there is nothing more depressing than to see a traditional industry like the automotive industry basically going down the tubes, especially because of unfair competition from China.

So that's up to us to ensure that competition is stopped and that we give a fair advantage to our own industries. But also, I think, we can move forward and be a little more creative.

I agree with EVs. They suit certain people, they don't suit other people, they are growing in sales, but they have to be European. 'Made in Europe' has to be the key.

But also, hybrid cars. I have a hybrid car, plug-in hybrid. It says it will do 100 km. I have never done more than 50 or 55, driving even as slow as possible. So, if the hybrid cars could cover a longer distance under the electric part of it, then I think that would be a win-win for Europe.

And we have to look at these creative measures to ensure that the automotive industry stays in Europe, is made in Europe and bought in Europe.

Sabine VERHEYEN (Chair)

The debate is closed.

The sitting will be suspended briefly. It will resume in a few minutes with the presentation of the work programme of the Irish Presidency.

András GYÜRK

The European automotive industry is struggling with serious problems. Ever since the green policy announced by Ursula von der Leyen and its accompanying, unrealistic regulations appeared, the global market share of European car manufacturing has been steadily declining. And this has now also appeared in the daily lives of European families – in 2024, one hundred thousand European automotive jobs were lost. According to industry estimates, the livelihoods of an additional four hundred thousand directly and more than one million indirectly living off the automotive industry families may be in danger.

The stakes are huge, so we must act immediately. First, instead of the strict regulations and penalties currently proposed by the Commission, flexibility and positive incentive measures are needed. Instead of new administrative burdens, incentives are needed to give a future to the automotive industry.

Second, the European automotive industry is asking for technological neutrality. And it is right. In order to preserve jobs, the industry must be freed and citizens and businesses must be given the opportunity to choose the most suitable vehicle for them from the numerous available technologies.

Third, energy prices must be slashed. Today, a European automotive company pays four to five times the price for energy compared to its global competitors. This is unacceptable.

We are in the past last minute, which is why the European Parliament's resolution regarding the automotive proposals before the House has special weight. If we decide poorly, mass unemployment could come. Therefore, we have no other option, we must decide well.

Eszter LAKOS

The competitiveness of the European automotive industry poses a fundamental challenge for all member states, but especially for Central European countries. The automotive industry means jobs, exports, supply networks, and technological development. Therefore, it is our fundamental interest that Europe does not lose its place in global competition.

However, we must see clearly: the answer cannot be excessive protectionism. European industry needs a certain degree of protection against unfair competition, but that alone will not solve its current challenges. Manufacturers are in at least as much need of innovation, a skilled workforce, cheaper energy, and predictable regulations. Meanwhile, in the current geopolitically risky period, we cannot afford to alienate our reliable trading partners.

In addition, an increasing number of people think that the electric transition can only be successful if battery supply chains are built in Europe. However, Hungarian experience shows that investments are socially and economically acceptable only if they strictly respect environmental and labor protection, water management, and local community aspects as well.

Europe's goal cannot be isolation, but rather the creation of a strong, innovative, and sustainable automotive industry that thrives even in fair competition. Hungary, together with its Central European partners, will continue to stand up for this at the EU level.

Marcin SYPNIEWSKI

The European Commission first chokes the automotive industry with regulations, which provides a living for 13 million Europeans, and now it drops "rescue packages" on our heads. You are pretending to be a firefighter who first set fire to the economy and is now heroically trying to put it out.

Your so-called "automotive package" from December 2025 is nothing else than the continuation of pathological central planning. Instead of letting the market work, you are creating the "Battery Booster" program to distribute 1.5 billion euros in the form of interest-free loans to battery manufacturers from taxpayers' pockets. To make matters worse, since citizens do not want to buy expensive electric cars, you have decided to rescue demand by force—by introducing mandatory, top-down zero-emission car purchase targets for large companies and their corporate fleets.

On the one hand, you promise companies bureaucratic savings of 706 million euros from the so-called "Automotive Omnibus", and on the other hand, you still keep a deadly target at the industry's throat: a 90 percent reduction in exhaust emissions from 2035. You mercifully allow manufacturers to combine emission results from the years 2025, 2026 and 2027 to slightly mitigate the fines imposed on them. But how are they to avoid them in the long run, when customers outright reject this green mandate?

European motoring will not be saved by further multi-billion subsidies or top-down forced purchases. Reject this climate dictate, abolish the absurd standards and finally stop harming the economy!

Discussion transcript

Presentation of the programme of activities of the Irish Presidency

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberta METSOLA (Chair)

Dear colleagues, it is truly a pleasure to welcome the Taoiseach of Ireland, Micheál Martin, to present the Irish Presidency's programme of activities (2026/2756(RSP)). Dear Micheál, welcome, again, to the European Parliament.

For over 50 years, Ireland's spirit of community, cooperation and compromise has driven Europe forward and shaped how we see ourselves as Europeans. And as you embark on this, your eighth presidency so far, I know that you are more than ready to steer Europe to ever greater heights.

We are entering a critical six months for our continent. As the world around us becomes more uncertain, people are calling increasingly loudly for a safer, stronger and more confident Union – one that stands tall on the world stage while acting at home to improve people's lives in real and tangible ways.

That is what we in this House are working for every single day, and I am pleased to see that with your leadership and with your presidency's focus on competitiveness, security and values, we are both pulling in the same direction.

The coming months are an opportunity for us to act together on some transformative files and deliver the progress that people demand of us: bringing our Union closer together, helping businesses to grow and supporting our allies while ramping up our own security. Meanwhile, negotiations on the next multiannual budget will determine how prepared we are for the next seven years.

In all these challenges, Ireland can continue to rely on the goodwill and the backing of this Parliament. And as always, the Irish put it best: ní neart go cur le chéile. Strength with unity. That is our European way, and it must continue to guide us all in the months to come.

Dear Taoiseach, I know we are all looking forward to hearing you speak. So without further ado, the floor is yours.

Micheál Martin

President Metsola, Members of the Parliament, distinguished guests, and friends, I am very pleased to be back in Strasbourg – in the heart of Europe – and to speak to this Parliament, which gives a democratic voice to 450 million of our fellow European citizens.

We look forward to working closely with the Members of this Parliament over the next 6 months. And we want the Irish Presidency to be a highly collaborative effort working together.

The motto of the European Union is 'United in Diversity'. It reflects the rich network of cultures, languages, and histories from which our Union has grown, and how we depend on each other, indeed our strength when we work together.

I am here, as a representative of the eighth round of the Irish Presidency of the Council, to tell you that we respect your role and your unique perspective.

And the Irish Presidency is determined to work with this Parliament in good faith, on the basis of collegiality, and with the utmost cooperation to get the work of the people done.

I am here to ask for your help. We can do it together.

And the 2026 Presidency will be Ireland's first Presidency since the Irish language became a fully operational working language of the European Union from January 2022 onwards.

President Metsola, it's an honour to present the policy programme of the Irish Presidency of the Council to the Parliament today, and we have a saying in the Irish language: 'Tús maith leath na hoibre' – a good start is half the work. We have prepared extensively for taking on our responsibilities. Irish ministers and officials have had countless discussions with counterparts across capitals, in Brussels and with this Parliament here in Strasbourg. We have sought to listen and to understand. We are ready to get things done.

Our starting position is rooted in the excellent work of the Cyprus Presidency, who have guided the agenda of the Council very effectively through the first half of this year, and I am determined that we will pass the torch forward in similarly good shape to our friends in Lithuania at the start of 2027. With Greece, we are both part of a proud trio of presidencies that stretches from our rugged Atlantic shores to the Baltic Sea and on to the Mediterranean. Nations each located at the edges of Europe, yet determined to be at its heart.

On each occasion Ireland has held the presidency, we have worked tirelessly to make a positive difference to this unique Union. While the rotating presidency was established soon after the Treaty of Rome, the broader and more permanent Council structure was actually established during Ireland's first presidency in 1975. Time and again we have seen that, when we work together, Europe can achieve incredible things.

When Ireland joined the then European Economic Community, the debate was centred on whether we were just too poor to participate, with our opponents claiming that our economy and culture would rapidly collapse and disappear. The Irish people decided to put their faith in a shared European history. They embraced the idea that in the modern world, we can only secure our sovereignty as states by working with others in strong, rules-bound and permanent cooperation. And we rejected the negative and destructive visions of a Europe of permanent national jealousies and competition, of permanent insecurities and falling international influence.

Since then, we have experienced an economic transformation and growing cultural confidence, and our membership has been an irreplaceable foundation for securing our success and sovereignty. We have also achieved historic progress in overcoming a history of sectarian conflict, an achievement directly enabled by decades of working together in Europe and seeing the values which we share.

In particular, Madam President, I would like, once again, to thank you and the Parliament for the solidarity shown to Ireland when the UK decided to leave the European Union. And thankfully, we avoided many of the worst impacts seen by the UK itself, which the British people themselves increasingly recognise.

And in passing, I wish to pay tribute to the patience, perseverance and no little skill of Commissioner Šefčovič, who represented the EU most ably in those negotiations. Moves over recent years to rebuild a constructive relationship with the UK have made great progress and are a tribute to all involved.

Madam President, working together we have overcome many challenges, including in recent years. We have stood resolutely in the face of Russia's illegal invasion and unrelenting assault on Ukraine. Our Union has acted decisively in the face of the largest global pandemic in a century, saving countless lives. And I commend you, President Metsola, and your colleagues here in the Parliament, for your unwavering support for its people, for your consistent, resolute and vital voice in saying that Ukraine is defending basic democratic values, and we have a moral and political duty to support its cause.

For our presidency, we turn to the old Irish proverb: 'Ní neart go cur le chéile' – strength with unity. And yes, the EU faces challenges, but we are strong in meeting them together. Our priorities have very clearly been laid out. We have highlighted three areas in particular: the competitiveness of Europe's economy, the need to protect the fundamental values on which our European Union is built, at home and abroad, and the security of our citizens.

Economic prosperity is what enables us to achieve our policy ambitions. Without a strong economy, we will not have security, and without upholding our values, we will not have a Union in which our people can flourish and which we are proud to call home.

We share the assessment that Europe urgently needs to improve its competitiveness and productivity. All assessments, including the landmark reports from Mario Draghi and Enrico Letta, show that Europe risks falling behind if we don't act now. We need to be economically competitive in order to sustain the European way of life.

If we are competitive, we can have the prosperity we need to protect the vulnerable in our society. It allows us to provide a robust social safety net. It allows us to live in dignity with decent housing, with meaningful and productive jobs. It helps us educate our children and give skills to our workers. It provides excellence in health care, allowing Europeans to live longer, healthier lives.

Most fundamentally, it allows us to make the investments to keep our people safe in an increasingly dangerous world, and it supports us in making sustainable choices that can ensure a liveable planet for those who come after us. The unprecedented heat of recent weeks has shown us how urgent that task is, and the wildfires across Europe in the last week bring it frighteningly home to all of us.

In April, the three EU institutions agreed on the One Europe, One Market roadmap and that sets the course of our work. The single market is the very foundation of Europe's economy and prosperity, and we will work to further eliminate barriers, tackle unnecessary regulatory burdens and boost internal market trade. We will drive the digital and climate transition and ensure a level playing field for businesses and communities across the EU. We will make it easier for businesses to start up and scale seamlessly across the Union, including through progressing the EU Inc. proposal.

I am convinced it is time to take a decisive step forward on the savings and investments union. Progress has been far too slow. The savings and investments union can unleash the potential for Europe's high savings to be used for the benefit of businesses, communities and families in every part of Europe. Trade is also fundamental to our shared future and prosperity for our citizens. The challenges facing international trade today are formidable and possibly greater than at any time in the last half century. And this requires us to be more driven and adaptive than ever before.

Our presidency will pursue a trade policy agenda with ambition, one that strengthens our trade relationships with reliable global partners. We will seek to build an EU-US trade and investment relationship that benefits both. We will work for a close and constructive partnership with the United Kingdom, a trusted ally and friend with a strong voice on the international stage. We will work to strengthen our trade relationships and diversify our markets further afield, deepening trade with important partners such as India, Australia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates.

High energy prices and global volatility are being felt by families and businesses in every part of our Union and throughout the world, we will prioritise work to enhance Europe's security of supply and the development of sustainable, affordable and secure energy systems. And to this end, we will work constructively with Parliament to conclude the European grids package.

We will support discussions on the benefits and challenges of AI so that we have a model that is based on European values. And to further this, we are convening governments and global stakeholders at an international AI summit to focus on how we can best harness AI in support of Europe's competitiveness.

Our shared values, as detailed in the Treaties we all agreed and based on the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, are the foundation of our Union. They are essential to what makes Europe among the best places on earth to be. Europe believes in respect for human dignity, freedom, democracy, equality, the rule of law and respect for human rights, including the rights of persons belonging to minorities. We must defend and vindicate those values, both within Europe and globally, and this Parliament has a vital role to play.

During Ireland's Presidency in 2004, we had the honour of hosting the Day of Welcomes, celebrating the largest ever accession in the Union's history. And as long as there are Europeans who seek a secure, democratic and prosperous future, as long as there are millions who see our flag of blue and gold as a hope for freedom, we must continue to welcome new members. Enlargement is a win-win. It brings more Europeans under our umbrella of prosperity and security, and it makes us stronger and richer for the contribution and energy of new members.

During our presidency, we will work to bring all those looking to join the Union closer to that goal. We will aim to complete accession negotiations with Montenegro, to make substantial historic progress with Moldova and Ukraine. We will advance the countries of the Western Balkans as far as they are ready to go, consistent with our balanced, merit-based approach. At a time when our democratic values are being systematically questioned, we will promote the rule of law across Member States and candidate countries alike.

We will continue to support European Union efforts towards stability in Lebanon, Syria and the wider Gulf region and to urgently work towards ending a devastating and horrific war in Sudan. Our presidency will also promote active diplomatic engagement to support lasting peace and security in the Middle East, reaffirming the European Union's long-standing commitment to a two-state solution.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire. The situation in the West Bank is deteriorating. The behaviour of the Netanyahu Government is increasingly extreme. There are no democratic or humanitarian values which are flexible enough to justify the scale of death, destruction and displacement we have seen. It is a cause of deep and justified sadness and anger to many that Europe has not done enough to put pressure on Israel in the light of its egregious actions. I fully respect and understand that this is a difficult topic for many countries and is challenging many long-established connections and policies, but we must simply do more.

The need for measures to enhance European security and to build our resilience has never been more evident. We will continue to offer unwavering support to Ukraine, whose people have shown such courage and determination in defending their country. They deserve a just and lasting peace. Political, financial, military and humanitarian support for Ukraine must be coupled with ever increasing pressure on Russia, so that its cruel and morally indefensible war can no longer be sustained. We will work to agree tighter and stronger sanctions.

And Europe must also invest in all dimensions of its own security and rapidly develop its defence capabilities. We will actively take forward work on the proposed new European security strategy to ensure the Union can respond dynamically to today's geostrategic challenges.

To achieve all of these goals, of course, we need a budget that can match our ambitions. One of our Union's greatest weaknesses is that we place such high demands on it, but are unwilling to fund it appropriately. We have too often allowed ourselves to fall into a zero-sum approach, which seeks to take funding from successful programmes in order to provide for urgent ones.

In looking forward to the next budget, there are constraints which are unlikely to disappear, but we certainly have the obligation to show both ambition and urgency. We believe that agreement in the Council can be achieved by the end of this year. There are very different views around the table about how we raise our money and how we spend it, but we will work as an honest broker to try to narrow gaps and to bring people together. Building on the excellent work of the Cyprus Presidency, we will set out our thinking in a new negotiating box in the autumn.

President Metsola, to support our policy agenda, we will host an extensive programme of presidency meetings – more than 270 events, in locations across Ireland. We do so conscious of how important it is to engage our citizens in our conversations around the European Union. Telling the story of the European Union and why it remains so vitally important to peace, prosperity and security across our continent is something we attach great importance to.

We look forward to welcoming colleagues from the EU institutions and from across Europe to counties across Ireland, and this includes the meeting of the European Political Community and the informal meeting of the European Council in November in Dublin. At a moment where so many are promoting division and a return to a failed model of competition between nations, we will clearly, and without any reservation, speak for the vital necessity of the democratic and humanitarian ideals of Europe.

For me, a visit to this Chamber always brings to mind one of the most distinguished former MEPs, and unquestionably one of the greatest figures in modern Irish history, John Hume. He remains the only MEP to have been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize while serving in this Parliament. While he represented Northern Ireland, he spoke for the vast majority on our island, who wanted a future free of the sectarian violence inflicted on our society by an unaccountable few.

He was not just our visionary of peace, he was a passionate advocate for peace and prosperity through a shared European future. And just as the great generation which secured our independence brought us to membership of the European Union, John Hume directed us to its values and the opportunities for reconciliation and breaking the historic cycle of distrust and conflict.

So for 25 years, he both led the largest nationalist party in Northern Ireland and he came here as an MEP to work with others to define and build a new future for his community, our island, and the people of Europe. Just outside this Hemicycle, there is a bust of John, as a fitting memorial to how important the Parliament's work can be.

In his Nobel lecture, John spoke about how inspired he was by this place and the European Union. He spoke of his first visit to Strasbourg, and standing with a sense of wonder in the middle of the bridge from Strasbourg to Kehl. He was moved by the almost inconceivable success of leaving behind a tradition of savage conflict between nations, and replacing it with a new era of cooperation.

To honour his legacy, later this year, we will be establishing and funding a new annual prize in his name, and this will be awarded to a European who has contributed to the values which John advocated for, and to the further development of our Union.

John had the vision to see the narrative of Ireland's path to peace and prosperity in the wider narrative of Europe. As he saw it, the road to lasting progress is built in shedding our sweat together rather than our blood. It is a vision that is as relevant today as when he graced this parliamentary Chamber.

Thank you again, President Metsola, for your welcome here today and for your tolerance. On behalf of the Irish Presidency, I look forward to working with you and the Parliament across the next six months, and we will approach this with a spirit of cooperation and ambition to ensure that our shared Union delivers for the people that we all serve.

Maroš Šefčovič

Madam President, dear Taoiseach, dear Minister, honourable Members, my dear colleague Commissioner McGrath, first, I would like to start by welcoming the Irish Presidency and wishing you the best of luck in this very demanding six months because you just ran through the programme, which is very extensive, and we really rely on always competent and delivering Irish Presidency to make success on all the points you mentioned. I also would like to highlight how happy we are in the European Commission that Ireland's priorities for the presidency are very much in line with the Commission's agenda and it starts with the closely interlinked and mutually reinforcing core elements of competitiveness, values and security.

To consider them in turn, Europe must act urgently to enhance its competitiveness and productivity in order to deliver a secure economic future, which meets the needs and expectations of its people. To this end, the Irish Presidency will play a central role in delivering on the One Europe, One Market roadmap, which the three institutions signed in April. We are also on our way to fulfil our commitment to complete the single market by the end of the next year, but it is clear we must move faster. During the Irish Presidency, we expect to come forward with important initiatives, including the public procurement act and the circular economy act, but we also need to close existing files, including the savings and investments union, the industrial accelerator act and EU Inc. regulation.

When it comes to simplification, we need to close the four remaining omnibus proposals, namely digital, environmental, automotive, and food and feed. In addition, last month, we presented two more omnibuses on energy and taxation, with another on citizens to follow still this year. We now count on the co‑legislators to take the work on open files forward swiftly.

Another key element on competitiveness is energy prices, where Europeans and European businesses alike expect action. We need to maintain our momentum if we are to meet the target of reaching political agreement on the European grids package – put forward by the Commission last December – by the third quarter of this year. Looking ahead, next week, we will present the energy package with the proposal on grid charges and an electrification plan, as well as an ETS review and a proposal on benchmarks.

I also welcome that our ambitious trade policy agenda will continue to gather pace under the Irish Presidency and thank you very much, dear Taoiseach, for highlighting this priority. We look forward to furthering our joint work with the presidency and with you, honourable Members, on issues including the implementation of the EU‑US trade and investment agenda, but also on the ongoing trade negotiations with Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and the United Arab Emirates. I am also counting on the Council to approve the signing of agreements with India and Indonesia, and for the Parliament to proceed with its swift consent so that they can enter into force, allowing for the full benefits to be enjoyed as quickly as possible.

Dear Taoiseach, honourable Members, as I informed you last week in Cork at our coordination session, we work in a constructive way with our UK partners to further strengthen our relationship and as I assured you there, I will reassure you here: we will always keep Ireland and Northern Ireland on our minds.

Turning to the second overarching priority: values. Our values remain the cornerstone of European project and we very much welcome that the Irish Presidency has placed them at the heart of its programme. Over the next six months, there will be a great deal of work to deliver on the European Democracy Shield, defend the rule of law and advance citizens' rights, including online, especially when it comes to children. My dear colleague, Commissioner Michael McGrath, who is here with me, is doing outstanding job on all these files and I am sure that together with the Irish Presidency, there will be clear progress achieved very, very soon.

As we all agree, our values are also part of what makes joining the European Union so attractive. The prospect of enlargement is, once again, very much on the table. I will never forget the day in May 2004, when the EU took the historic step of admitting 10 new Member States, including my own, Slovakia, among them. Nor will I ever forget that it was in Phoenix Park in Dublin, with Ireland holding the presidency of the Council, when these 10 Members were officially welcomed into the Union. It was very memorable and it was very emotional for all of us. So, we count on the experience, expertise and know‑how of the current Irish Presidency to advance negotiations with today's candidate countries and, further afield, to contribute to our efforts on the global stage, including in our work to help secure just and lasting peace in the Middle East.

Third, security and defence. The Irish Presidency will lead our continued support for Ukraine. This is also an investment in our own security and we must maintain our support to Ukraine across all fronts: militarily, economically and politically. At the same time, we continue to put pressure on Russia and I welcome the work of the presidency on the 21st sanctions package, including the commitment to reach an agreement by next week. On security and defence more widely, we count on the Irish Presidency to steer work on key files in this area, including our defence industry, military mobility and drones. On migration, this is a European challenge which must be met with a European response. We should now focus our efforts on the prompt implementation of the Pact on Migration and Asylum as the priority.

So, honourable Members, dear Taoiseach, Madam President, lastly, I want to briefly mention the future multiannual financial framework. Our aim is to find an agreement by the end of the year. While this is a complex and challenging topic, I am glad that the Irish Presidency has received a strong mandate from the European Council to continue the work on this. So once again, best of luck to the Irish Presidency. Thank you very much, dear Taoiseach, for coming to share your priorities with us. I would like to thank Madam President and you, honourable Members, for your attention and I believe that we are looking forward to the debate.

Manfred WEBER

Madam President, dear Commissioners, a very warm welcome to the Irish Presidency. Taoiseach Martin, welcome, together with your coalition partner, with Simon Harris, that you are here and also presenting the ideas for the future of Europe from an Irish point of view, having this huge responsibility now on your shoulders.

I want to underline that you are setting the right priorities: competitiveness, security, values. I can assure you the full support of the biggest group here in this House, the EPP family, and your message of 'let things get done' in a way is exactly what Europe needs in this moment of time: delivering, delivering, delivering.

I want to focus in my contribution on one very specific, probably symbolic, issue, because you correctly underline security and the Europe that protects. And Ireland already in a way showed this Europe that protects in one specific issue, and that is when it is about the protection of children, especially children online.

Let me start with an Irish woman, Jackie Fox. Jackie lost her daughter, Nicole – Coco – bullied online and offline for three years, and Nicole took her own life at 21. Jackie brought the evidence to the police and they told her there was no crime for this, nothing. Jackie talked to every political leader in Ireland. She built up a movement. And today, because of her, cyberbullying is a crime in Ireland. It protects thousands of children.

Colleagues, what happened to Nicole is not an isolated tragedy, it is a daily reality for children across Europe. 1 in 3 kids has been bullied online; 1 in 3 of these children will never report it out of fear or of shame. That is a reality, and that's why, dear colleagues – to broaden the perspective next to cyberbullying – online sexual abuse material is today on our agenda, and we are facing a legal gap on this. That's why we have to be clear that this protection of children is a priority for this House.

The facts are shocking. Sexual abuse online is a kind of epidemic in our social media world. In 2010, it was 1 million reports; today we have 20 million reports, and the number of artificial intelligence-based new material increased in only one single year by 1 000 %. It's a shocking number. And by the way, with 60 % of online material, Europe is the hotspot of this material on the global stage – on our servers, on our continent, in our neighbourhood.

Today we have a vote on this, and that's why I thank the European Council for putting this important legislation on CSAM on the agenda. 26 countries supported this. I thank the Commission for the initiative, again, to show the will from all parties based in the Commission's side for supporting this legislation. And now it's up to us as the European Parliament. The EPP will today support the fast-track procedure and also support the content.

The Irish Presidency in a way gives us, with Coco's Law, already one concrete initiative in this, and we want to fight for having Coco's Law at European level as well – that we are protecting our children online. Today is an important day to deliver on children's protection. We have to close the legal gap.

Iratxe GARCÍA PÉREZ

Madam President, thank you, Taoiseach Micheál Martin, welcome to the European Parliament.

Just two weeks ago I walked through the streets of Dublin. Today, I stand here with those streets still in my mind.

Ireland begins its presidency at a defining moment for Europe. Your priorities are competitiveness, security and our values. But after what I saw in Dublin, I want to ask you one simple question: what kind of Europe are we really building?

At Ozanam House, Geraldine, Bishop Amos and other local community workers told me about families who have done everything right but still cannot afford a home. On Gardiner Street, where 10 % of Ireland’s homeless people are living in emergency accommodation, parents are raising children in a single room. I heard about families whose children do their homework sitting on the fire escape because there is nowhere else to study, and a full-time Dublin bus driver with three children whose salary is still not enough to pay the rent for him and his family.

This week, Katherina is here with us in Strasbourg. She received three eviction notices in five years, all while fighting cancer. Taoiseach, these are not only Irish stories. They are European stories. And this is not the Europe we can accept.

That is why your presidency must help deliver a strong affordable housing act, regulate short-term rentals and give local authorities the tools they need to build social and affordable homes. Because without decent housing, there is no dignity, no opportunity and no real competitiveness.

At Liberty Hall, I also met trade unions who reminded us that Europe’s strength has always been its social model. The quality jobs package must strengthen workers’ rights. And the 28th regime must never become a shortcut to weaken labour law, collective bargaining or workers’ participation. Europe’s competitiveness will never come from lowering standards. It will come from investing in people.

And please, do not allow the fight against poverty to disappear from Europe’s agenda.

The same values must also guide Europe’s action beyond our borders. Ireland has often shown moral leadership on international law. Today Europe needs that leadership again. We must suspend the Association Agreement with Israel in full because of Netanyahu’s genocide in Gaza.

Taoiseach, Europe’s future depends on delivering social progress together with economic prosperity. During your presidency, you can count on the S&D Group to turn that vision into reality. If we carry with us the families of Ozanam House, the workers of Liberty Hall and people like Katherina, then we can build a Europe that offers security, opportunity and dignity for everyone.

Go raibh maith agat and ádh mór.

Kinga GÁL

Madam President, Commissioners! We, Patriots, expect the Irish Presidency to keep the real interests of European citizens in mind: their security and prosperity. To guarantee their security, illegal migration must be stopped, not managed. Europe must regain control over its external borders. The effective application of the Return Directive will be a key issue.

Regaining our competitiveness is essential for European prosperity. This requires lower energy prices and less bureaucracy. In the next EU budget, we oppose the reduction of agricultural and cohesion funds. We reject further centralization, the increase of bureaucratic spending, and the ideologically based conditionality mechanism, because it has now been proven that the rule of law conditions are applied on an ideological basis.

The profound silence we see regarding the democracy-destroying constitutional amendments of the new Hungarian government well illustrates the double standards applied by the Commission. The removal of the President of the Republic and the members of the Constitutional Court, and the restriction of the eligibility of members of parliament, are unprecedented steps in Europe that go against every existing democratic and rule of law principle. After years of unfounded harassment of the previous patriotic, sovereignty-loving government, it seems that democracy and the rule of law are only selectively important to this House and the Commission.

There is no room for double standards and ideology in the matter of enlargement either. It cannot be ignored that Ukraine is at war, and its accession will have serious consequences for European agriculture, labor markets, cohesion policy, and our security. We, Patriots, expect more common sense and less ideology from the Irish Presidency.

Beata SZYDŁO

Madam President! Dear Prime Minister! First of all, I want to thank the Prime Minister very warmly for presenting the vision of the Irish Presidency. Indeed, there are very many important challenges, and we keep our fingers crossed that these goals will be achieved. Security is undoubtedly the most important issue today for the European Union and for all of us.

However, I wanted to focus my speech on issues concerning what seems to be the most difficult task facing the Irish Presidency and all of us as well, namely the European Union budget for the coming years, the financial framework for the next financial perspective. This is a huge challenge, but also many question marks. Above all, I think we all take the position, at least in my political group, that there can be absolutely no question of imposing new tax burdens on entrepreneurs and Europeans.

You talk about the need to increase the budget. We also do not want spending to be cut in the most essential, most important projects for the European Union, but this cannot be done at the expense of Europeans. It cannot happen at the expense of the competitiveness of European industry. And this is another task to which I wanted to draw attention.

We are all waiting with impatience for the proposal to revise the ETS system. It will depend on this – this is crucial – whether the European economy will finally be able to spread its wings and become competitive, rather than simply being crushed as before by solutions that, unfortunately, the European Union itself prepared. I keep my fingers crossed, Prime Minister, for your presidency, and I hope that it will be, as we all expect, extremely important, essential and constructive for all of us.

Valérie HAYER

Madam President, Commissioner, dear Taoiseach – dear Micheál –, first of all, a big thank you for this presentation and for your priorities, which are resolutely ambitious for Europe. Now, it is no secret to anyone: we are used to working together. You are a prominent member of the Renew family, and you will not be surprised, therefore, to hear me say that the priorities of your presidency – competitiveness, values, security – well, that is also the roadmap of our political group, Renew Europe.

Now, dear Taoiseach, yes, you are right: let us move forward on our competitiveness, finally complete our single market, invest more in innovation, simplify our rules, give our businesses the means to grow in Europe rather than going to succeed elsewhere, let us move forward on the next European budget! The multiannual financial framework will be a test of truth: if we want a powerful Europe, we must give it the means to match its ambitions. Let us finally move forward on our geopolitical influence: by continuing our support for Ukraine, by preparing the enlargement of our Union and by defending, without ever compromising, the rule of law and the values that underpin our European project!

I would like to say a word on a more specific file, because your presidency will be an opportunity to demonstrate that Europe knows how to protect without abandoning its principles. That is the exact meaning of the regulation on the protection of children online, which you are making an absolute priority, and I would like to thank you for it. It has been four years – four years! – that we have been waiting for this text. There is no time to lose, and we are counting on your presidency to conclude negotiations on the long-term regulation as quickly as possible. You can count on the absolute support of my political group on this issue, which is fundamental.

These reforms, dear Taoiseach, are no longer an option: they are a requirement for European citizens, because your presidency begins in troubled times. The world has become brutal again, force wants to replace law, powers are clashing, democracies are being challenged, and, in this world, Europe can no longer be passive. Faced with this brutality, our response must be the assertion of European power, but of a power that resembles us: a democratic power, a power founded on our values, on our freedoms and on the rule of law. These values are in no way an obstacle to European power – and I know that we share this – on the contrary, they are its condition, because Europe does not want to be brutal – that is not our model – but, obviously, it does not want to disappear either – and for that, we must deliberately embrace the balance of power. We in no way renounce who we are.

So, dear Micheál, as you know, you can count on Renew for the success of your presidency, and since Ireland is in the spotlight today, please allow me to quote one of your greatest writers, Oscar Wilde: “Progress is the realization of utopias.” So let us ensure that, during these six months, our European utopias become very real progress!

Terry REINTKE

You are very welcome, Taoiseach.

You are very welcome in this House, Taoiseach. I said this to you in Dublin and I really mean it, so I think I have to repeat it now also in this House: Europe loves Ireland. I think you are not going to find one colleague in this House that doesn't have a soft spot for Ireland. So we are all looking forward to the Irish Presidency.

But what we need from you is action, action, action. Heat waves are torturing Europe – forest fires, temperature records. The Green Deal is more important than ever. Strong commitment to green targets, especially when we speak about money. The budget and continuing the Green Deal will be your responsibility in the next six months, Taoiseach. And we trust on your commitment here.

Yet – and I have to say it – what we have seen also in Ireland in the recent months has cast some doubt over whether you will be ambitious enough on climate action in Europe. Dismantling parts of the Climate Act in Ireland, delaying climate action plans – Taoiseach, how will you make sure that in Europe we will not experience the Irish Presidency as climate laggards, or even worse, climate quitters. Because with unprecedented heat waves, but also with our still-immense dependency on fossil autocrats around the world, the pressure is on. We have to see action on this.

And – you said this – our values are under attack. We can clearly see it with Russian disinformation campaigns. Ireland can play a crucial role here. A lot of the US tech giants are actually sitting in Ireland, so you have a key role in regulating their business models. Rest assured, this Parliament across the board stands behind you if you are going to take action on enforcing, for example, the Digital Services Act.

We all know that if Ireland wants to, you can, because Ireland has consistently shown over the past decades how the EU is a powerful stage also for smaller and medium-sized countries. Instead of having never-ending pointless debates about how the EU is a barrier to national sovereignty, Ireland has consistently punched above its weight in Europe and gained more sovereignty through European cooperation.

This is what we want to see in the next six months from you. All the best to your presidency.

Lynn BOYLAN

President, Taoiseach, Ireland's Presidency of the Council is an opportunity to be a voice for peace. A voice for human rights and international law. A time to promote our core values.

Unfortunately, though, the Irish Government's approach continues to be: 'We will be principled, but only when it costs us nothing'. Ireland is a country with a proud record on peacebuilding, disarmament and international law. That legacy is entirely missing from the government's programme. Instead, Taoiseach, we see you embracing the militarisation agenda against the wishes of the Irish people and launching a full-scale attack on our neutrality.

Ireland should use its presidency to deliver EU action to end Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine (word changed at the request of the Member) and its apartheid regime. In your speech, you spoke of Netanyahu's government as if it is a rogue government, when the reality is that Israel has expanded its settlements under every single Israeli Government. It is a rogue state.

And as heat waves burn, your programme talks of leading the EU at international environmental negotiations. But you embrace the deregulation agenda, giving billionaires more freedom to destroy our planet.

I also have concerns that the state that hosts so much of big tech can truly lead on data protection. Enforcement remains slow, weak and shaped by the companies that it is meant to regulate.

And while discussion on enlargement is welcome, where is the ambition to end partition of our island? Taoiseach, you talk of a shared island, but Irish citizens in the North do not share the benefits of the EU. Concrete measures, like observer MEPs and participation in civil society platforms, would help to address the democratic deficit. Across our island, the conversation for unity is gaining momentum. Yet the Taoiseach is a spectator.

But on one thing we can agree, Taoiseach: without values, nothing matters. That is why we cannot allow Ursula von der Leyen to run roughshod over our values and act beyond her mandate. Now is the time for moral leadership, not equivocation.

Stanislav STOYANOV

Madam President, the European Union is slowly but surely losing its positions in the global economy. Restoring competitiveness is no longer a matter of choice, but of survival. A more favorable environment for investment, entrepreneurship, and industrial development is needed. Businesses need simplified rules and affordable energy, rather than new regulations.

Europe's chance lies in the abundance of talent on our continent. The courage of the entrepreneurs who press on despite the ill-conceived notions of the Green Deal. And they deserve support. Deindustrialization does not simply weaken the economic power of European states, it damages the dignity of the professional left without a job, limits opportunities for younger generations, and the survival of entire regions is at risk. Strengthening defense capabilities is necessary, but lasting security also requires active diplomacy, because sustainable solutions and peace are achieved through dialogue. We must not forget that managing migration flows is also at the heart of security.

Therefore, I welcome the commitment of the Irish Presidency to reducing administrative burdens for the development of the single market and building a more secure and affordable energy system. Ireland itself shows how a favorable environment for investment, entrepreneurship, and innovation turns into sustainable economic success. It is precisely along this path that Europe can restore its competitiveness and its place in the global economy.

Seán KELLY

President, Taoiseach, Commissioner, congratulations, Taoiseach, on the fine speech you gave us. As you said, you have made a good start and keep up the good work.

The competitiveness, values and security theme of the Irish Presidency – I think most people can see that's good, and it captures the essentials for this mandate. I think Mario Draghi outlined in 2024 the need for competitiveness. This is the fifth presidency in this mandate, and I think we have outlined and identified key reports which need to be either finalised or progressed. But as Commissioner Šefčovič referred to the grids package, I think we can finalise that, hopefully, but also make rapid progress in the electrification action plan, Industrial Accelerator Act and EU Competitiveness Fund. Also, in relation to the omnibuses, these are integral to addressing competitiveness. Six are completed – I think we can hopefully complete another four. That will be massive.

You spoke at length to us last night, a Thaoisigh, of your work to try and complete the savings and investments union. That is going to be absolutely vital if we are to research, innovate, scale up and manufacture in Europe. Your point about enlargement is huge – particularly Montenegro being out in front, but also for the others, but it must be merit based. And finally, a bugbear of my own is to try and end daylight saving. Changing the clock twice a year is nonsensical, and 85 % of citizens don't want it, so let's get rid of it. The EPP will be fully behind you in your work because we are partners with you in government.

Aodhán Ó RÍORDÁIN
