2026-07-07Plenary debate50 speechesEU-Mexico (joint debate)

Discussion transcript

EU-Mexico (joint debate)

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Esteban GONZÁLEZ PONS (Chair)

The next item is the joint debate on:

– the recommendation by Javi López and Borja Giménez Larraz, on behalf of the Committee on Foreign Affairs and the Committee on International Trade, on EU–Mexico Political, Economic and Cooperation Strategic Partnership Agreement (12463/2025COM(2025)0810 - C10-0128/2026 - 2025/0810(NLE)) (A10-0181/2026);

– the report by Javi López and Borja Giménez Larraz, on behalf of the Committee on Foreign Affairs and the Committee on International Trade, on EU–Mexico Political, Economic and Cooperation Strategic Partnership Agreement (Interim report) (2025/0810R(NLE)) (A10-0182/2026);

– the recommendation by Borja Giménez Larraz, on behalf of the Committee on International Trade, on the EU–Mexico Interim Agreement on Trade (12421/2025COM(2025)0812 - C10-0126/2026 - 2025/0271(NLE)) (A10-0198/2026).

I would like to remind speakers that, given the test measures currently in place and the fixed end time of the debate, strict observance of speaking times will be required.

Javi LÓPEZ

Mr President, the debate is not solely about a trade agreement.

Today we are deciding what place Europe wants to occupy in a world increasingly dominated by confrontation, protectionism, and power politics. After more than a decade of negotiations, the European Union and Mexico are concluding a first-rate geopolitical decision: to modernize our Global Agreement.

This Agreement is much more than the elimination of tariffs or the opening of markets. It is a political response to those who believe that the 21st century should be organized through threats, trade wars, economic coercion, or spheres of influence.

We defend a different logic with this Global Agreement: we defend rules over force, cooperation over confrontation, and international law over unilateralism. At a time when some are raising walls, using tariffs as weapons, and questioning decades of multilateral construction, Europe and Mexico are sending a different message to the world: more cooperation, more institutions, more international law, and more predictable trade with high environmental, social, and labor standards.

The alternative to multilateralism is not more sovereignty; it is the law of the jungle. In this context, Europe needs reliable partners, democratic partners, partners capable of providing institutional stability, industrial capacity, legal certainty, and a commitment to a rules-based international order.

There are few in the world that combine all these elements the way Mexico does. Mexico is an economic, industrial, technological, and diplomatic power of the highest order. It is a member of the G20 and one of the European Union's most important strategic partners. But not only that: it is a society with a strong, deep, and millennial identity of its own; a nation heir to deep, rich, diverse, and vibrant cultural roots.

Mexico is a country that has known how to turn its diversity, miscegenation, and plurality into a source of national strength. Europe does not look at Mexico solely as a market. Europe looks at Mexico with respect, never from reductionism, paternalism, or ignorance, because we share essential principles: the defense of the United Nations Charter or the commitment to the sovereignty of States. We share the conviction that no power has the right to impose its will on others through economic coercion or force. We share the certainty that the great challenges we face—the fight against inequalities, climate change, or the energy or digital transition—must be addressed through cooperation, not by belittling others or through confrontation.

I want to highlight here today that the determination of President Von der Leyen and President Costa has allowed us to get here. It has also been made possible by the strategic decision of President Claudia Sheinbaum, for her serene, calm, and firm leadership on the international stage.

We are opening a new stage of shared opportunities for shared prosperity.

Today, as we speak about relations between the European Union and Mexico, I want to emphasize that when Europe went through dark times during the 20th century, Mexico opened its doors to those fleeing war and political persecution; it offered refuge, dignity, and hope. And some of us—especially in Spain, due to the reception of the Spanish republican exile—have a feeling of duty and gratitude toward Mexico that remains.

Therefore, today we are doing something more than approving an Agreement. We are defending an idea of the world. The idea that cooperation is more powerful than conflict, that rules are preferable to arbitrariness, that openness is smarter than retreat, and that in the face of economic nationalism, protectionism, and power politics, Europe must respond by building alliances with those who believe in democracy, international law, and multilateralism.

With this Agreement, it is about defending an idea of the international order, an order based on rules and not on threats, on cooperation and not on coercion, on relations between partners and not vassals. That is the true meaning of this Agreement. And that is why it must be supported with conviction.

Borja GIMÉNEZ LARRAZ

Mr. President, the Global Agreement with Mexico is going to be a reality. It is a turning point in a reality that began 25 years ago. Since then, trade has grown by 148%. Today it exceeds 82 billion euros. It is not an abstract figure: it is industry, it is business, it is investment, it is competitiveness, but the world changes fast. We are in a context of global fragmentation, with trade tensions, with recurring threats of new tariffs. Europe cannot fall behind. We need to diversify, more partners, more strategic autonomy. The more trade, the freer the Union. 25 years after the modernization of our trade relations, this is more necessary than ever.

The economic benefits are clear. The Union and Mexico bring together more than 580 million consumers. It is a huge market. European exports can grow by up to 75%. More than 45,000 European companies will benefit —the majority of them SMEs— and the GDP of the European Union can increase by 1.8 billion euros just from the signing of the Agreement. It is also good news for our agri-food sector. We must not be afraid: sectors such as pork or cheese win, tariffs are eliminated and 568 geographical indications are protected.

Furthermore, it is the first agreement that incorporates an anti-corruption clause. This is key if we want transparent investments and legal certainty. The incorporation of a permanent investment court system is also fundamental.

Mexico and the European Union share a lot: centuries of history. A complex, deep history that has given rise to human ties, traditions, culture, language. All of this is part of our identity.

Today we decide to seal a common destiny; today we take another step in our relationship. This Agreement is based on trust —mutual trust— between two friendly peoples who appreciate and respect each other. Such a relationship demands honesty, the same as between good friends. And that honesty demands sincerity, that we speak clearly to each other, about what we like and what we do not like so much. And there are issues that concern us, sincerely. The reform of the judicial system: the popular election of all judges generates serious doubts, it weakens the separation of powers. Without institutional stability there is no trust, without trust there is no growth. Security concerns us: 90 homicides a day, 94% impunity, the country with the most murdered journalists, organized crime that we know has permeated society and the economy. We cannot look the other way, fundamentally because it is a huge human drama, but also an economic one. And we deeply regret, from a commercial perspective, that the energy chapter has been left out of the Agreement. This will lead to regulatory gaps and disincentivizes investment. We trust that this issue can be resolved soon.

We are friends, we are partners and this Agreement lays the foundations to reaffirm our relationship. An ambitious trade relationship, a deep political relationship, but also a relationship based on the Rule of Law, judicial independence, legal certainty and respect for democratic values. Because trade thrives when strong institutions exist. Investment arrives when there is trust.

Honorable members, let us say yes to a fundamental Agreement for Europe: let us reinforce our global position, improve competitiveness, broaden alliances. The more trade, the freer the Union will be.

Maroš Šefčovič

Mr President, honourable Members, dear rapporteurs, trade is fundamental to the European Union economy, and we just heard an eloquent statement in this regard by the Taoiseach, who is heading the Irish Presidency, in the earlier debate. Why? Because more than 700 000 EU companies export beyond our borders and they support more than 30 million jobs across the Union, contributing in one way or another to almost half of our European GDP, not least thanks to our 45 free trade agreements with 81 countries covering more than half of our trade.

Yet the context for the EU trade policy has become increasingly unpredictable and volatile. We are witnessing deliberate disruptions of global trade and the weaponisation of dependencies. In such turbulent times, we need to work even more closely with our partners in key markets open, as well as new markets, for our exports, and diversify sources of imports for the European Union producers.

During this Commission's mandate, we have struck landmark deals with Mexico, Mercosur, Indonesia, India, Australia and Eastern and Southern African – so-called ESA – countries. We are also continuing to negotiate with the Philippines, Thailand, Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates. Against this background, let me turn now to the subject of today's debate: EU-Mexico trade relations.

The commercial ties between the EU and Mexico are already strong. We have been trading on preferential terms since the year 2000, when the trade pillar of the EU-Mexico Global Agreement entered into force. That has seen the bilateral trade in goods increase by 330 % in the last 25 years, while the trade in services has also expanded significantly, and the EU has become the second most important investor in Mexico.

But in the past two decades, the world has changed, which is why we needed a modernised agreement that takes EU-Mexico relations to a new level, establishing a modern and ambitious framework for bilateral trade and investment. It will make almost all EU-Mexico trade in goods tariff free. And this is especially important for the EU agri-food exporters as duties will be removed on nearly all key products.

While Europe's flagship food and drink products are protected under 569 geographical indications, the agreement will also support growth in EU services exports in sectors such as financial services, transport and e-commerce. It will reduce non-tariff barriers and help ensure a level playing field, including through stronger provisions on intellectual property rights.

It will strengthen cooperation on critical raw materials and support the competitiveness of the European industry. It will promote the digital transition on both sides through the dedicated chapter on digital trade, and it will make it easier for small and medium-sized enterprises to trade and invest. It will expand opportunities for EU firms in Mexico's public procurement market and it will help address practical difficulties faced by our investors in Mexico.

As you have underlined in the interim report accompanying this debate, the EU and Mexico are like-minded, long-standing partners. This agreement will deepen that partnership and strengthen our ability to work together on global challenges.

It also underlines our commitment to fair trade, shared prosperity, sustainability and rules-based cooperation, and it promotes sustainable development through legally binding commitments on labour rights, environmental protection, climate change and responsible business conduct in the TSD chapter, as well as on trade and gender equality and women's economic empowerment.

With the modernised agreement, we are better equipped to seize new opportunities and address common challenges, both bilaterally and at the multilateral level. So, honourable Members, this debate is an opportunity to send a clear message to Europeans and to our partners that Europe believes in fair trade, strong alliances and strategic openness, and that, when it comes to Mexico, we choose partnership and mutual benefit.

So I would kindly ask for your support to back this agreement, and I would conclude by thanking all of you for attending this debate and our two rapporteurs for great cooperation.

Ana Miguel PEDRO

Mr President, the European Union-Mexico Agreement is much more than a trade agreement. It is a strategic choice.

Mexico is the European Union's second largest trading partner in Latin America. More than 45,000 European companies export to Mexico, many of them small and medium-sized enterprises that will benefit from clearer rules, greater predictability and new investment opportunities.

In an increasingly fragmented world, this partnership is essential for a broader transatlantic relationship based on common interests and shared values. But, precisely because this agreement is strategic, this Parliament does not separate its progress from the political and institutional reality on the ground.

Mexico faces profound challenges: organized crime violence, disappearances, attacks and murders of journalists, corruption, pressures on judicial independence and difficulties in the normal functioning of democratic institutions. These challenges are not external to the agreement; they are part of the conditions that determine whether the agreement will be credible, effective and sustainable.

Permanent economic predictability and confidence for businesses do not exist without solid institutions. This Parliament recognizes and supports the agreement, but demands clear and verifiable commitments regarding the rule of law.

The European Union gains by strengthening its presence alongside a key partner in Latin America. It gains weight, it gains influence. But it would lose moral authority and political coherence if it strengthened this partnership while pretending not to see the institutional fragilities that persist, because the more strategic a partnership is, the greater our democratic demand must be.

Hana JALLOUL MURO

Mr President, Commissioner, this Parliament is about to give its consent to an Agreement that has taken almost ten years to negotiate. An Agreement that arrives at a time when global trade can no longer be understood solely in economic terms.

Today, the European Union is more aware than ever that trade policy is a fundamental pillar for our economic security and strategic autonomy. We are aware of the need to diversify our trade relations and strengthen alliances with partners who share our commitment to multilateralism and rules-based global trade.

Mexico is, without a doubt, one of the best examples of that kind of strategic ally. Therefore, the signature of the Modernized Global Agreement between the European Union and Mexico is fantastic news that this Parliament must accompany. It is a decisive step to adapt our trade ties to the realities of the 20th century. And it is because it eliminates almost all of the tariffs we had until now and because it updates investment protection mechanisms by giving more certainty to European and Mexican operators.

These are key elements that will facilitate the operations of the more than 45 000 European companies —many of them SMEs— that export to Mexico.

It is also a relevant Agreement for access to critical minerals such as fluorite or copper, an area where we must ensure that the extractivist dynamics of the past are not repeated.

But the importance of this Agreement does not only lie in the technical details. The new framework includes binding obligations regarding environmental, labour and social matters. The Agreement guarantees respect for the Paris Agreement and, furthermore, Mexico ratifies new conventions of the International Labour Organization, a commitment that must be included as an essential part of the Agreement during the next review.

Along this path, this Agreement must be an instrument that helps guide investment towards high value-added sectors in Mexico, that diversifies European investment in the country and that manages to benefit those who so often are left behind, that becomes a framework in which the voice of civil society and Mexican indigenous communities is heard and that ensures their priorities are not sidelined.

In short, by giving the green light to this Agreement, the European Parliament makes it clear that Europe is committed to cooperation with such relevant partners as Mexico hand in hand and without paternalism.

It is important that this Parliament projects determination in cooperation with leadership, with a Europe that must not lag behind, that is committed to its strategic autonomy, and in a context where others raise barriers.

Daniele POLATO

Mr President, honourable colleagues, the agreement we are going to vote on is a winning one because it will help Europe and Mexico.

Political and commercial cooperation is strengthened with a friendly country, close to our values and culture.

There are several positive elements. Firstly, it will make it possible to strengthen cooperation for the green and digital transition. Furthermore, the agreement will offer better access to Mexican public procurement and new opportunities in strategic sectors, such as the financial, digital, transport and critical raw materials sectors.

Finally, the benefits for European agriculture. Mexico is an important net importer of food products: with the new agreement, Mexico will protect 232 spirit drinks and another 336 European geographical indications including wine, beer and food.

This aspect is also fundamental for Italian agriculture, because it truly defends the made in Europe.

Urmas PAET

Dear President of the sitting! Dear colleagues! Mexico, with a population of one hundred and thirty-three million, is a strategic partner of the European Union and its second largest trading partner in Latin America. Therefore, relations between the European Union and Mexico have already been very important. At the same time, there is still untapped potential. Therefore, the approval of the agreements deepening EU-Mexico relations before Parliament is important both in our bilateral relations and globally. Given that the international legal order is under severe pressure, a new agreement based on and strengthening international law is very necessary, and the European Union has an important role to play in this. Relations between states must not be determined by the unilateral power politics of some regime, but by agreements based on international law. The agreements before you create additional opportunities for European businesses and the economy as a whole. Customs restrictions and tariffs will be further reduced, and markets will open up more mutually. European Union companies will get much better access to the Mexican market.

Attention to the observance of human rights and the rule of law is also important in our relations. Thus, a dialogue between the European Union and Mexico is provided for to improve the safety of journalists and human rights defenders. Joint activities are planned to combat corruption, money laundering and organized crime. It is also extremely important that the European Union is active and continues to conclude such agreements with other countries that are potentially close to us, in order to increase the positive impact of the European Union on global developments.

Anna CAVAZZINI

Mr President, dear Commissioner, dear colleagues! Tomorrow we will vote on the modernisation of the Mexico trade agreement. I will vote in favour, but nevertheless have criticism of the agreement.

Yes, in a world where Donald Trump in the White House pursues erratic trade policy and China plays with unfair rules, we need partners. And yes, Mexico under President Sheinbaum is such a reliable partner – a government that champions multilateralism, democracy, social justice and decisive climate protection, values that are more important at present than ever before.

I explicitly welcome closer cooperation with Mexico. I also support the improvements that the modernisation brings in the areas of sustainability, anti-corruption, gender, etc.

But the truth also includes the fact that this agreement is far away from a perfect agreement. There is no enforceable sustainability chapter like with New Zealand, which unfortunately makes climate, environmental and labour standards toothless in the end.

And even worse: in terms of investment protection, this agreement does not meet the demands of this Parliament. The outdated clauses grant investors disproportionately great power and the ability to proceed before international arbitration tribunals against any democratic decision, be it in climate protection or also the supply of medicines, on all sorts of issues. There are such glaring cases where investors sue states, and I do not understand that the European Union is still continuing this mechanism further.

In the middle of the climate crisis, after a heatwave in Europe has just cost thousands of people their lives, the Commission still does not manage to think trade policy and climate protection together. That finally has to change!

I expect the Commission to use the time, during the review mechanism that is already due in a year, to finally strengthen environmental, labour and climate rights and finally adapt investment protection to our democratic values.

Pernando BARRENA ARZA

Mr President, I will start by saying that we stand alongside The Left's historical criticism of the trade agreements that the European Union and some other international actors or states have entered into.

Most of the time, these agreements are driven by Eurocentrism and extractivism, and negotiations are not held on equal terms. Huge harm on our first sector and better conditions for industrial production offshoring have been commonplace so far as regards to this trade agreement.

This time, the modernisation of the EU-Mexico trade agreement comes with some considerations that will bring my delegation not to take a stand against it. First of all, we as a Basque political force are very aware of our country's presence in Mexico and therefore protection of the employment in the Basque Country is linked to that.

Secondly, unlike in the case of Mercosur, the impact of Mexican exporters on our economy will not be a significant one as tariffs are not changing this time.

A third point for us is geopolitical solidarity with Mexico. Mexican exports are largely dependent on the USA – over 83 % of the Mexican exports' destiny is the northern neighbour, and Europe should help Mexico in reducing those figures and, by the way, fighting the impact of European corporate activity in the direction against human and environmental rights as well.

Acting this way, we are helping Mexico counteract the effects of Trump's geopolitical greed on the country. And this time, we can show that international solidarity goes beyond speeches.

Alexander SELL

Mr President! You talk a lot here about the problems in other parts of the world, but you don't like talking about the problems in Europe quite as much. Today it is about the partnership with Mexico: we generally think it is important – an important trading partner.

Only, unfortunately, the report is not limited to trade policy. EPP and Socialists express concern about the state of democracy in Mexico. They admonish the Mexicans that it is important to maintain a pluralistic, democratic environment through adequate public funding of political parties. But what you want to dictate to the Americans, you do not apply to us Europeans.

Only a few minutes ago, you passed a motion for a ban against our party here. You want to cut our funds, while you explain to the Mexicans that public financing of parties is necessary, otherwise democracy is in danger. What a double standard!

Then you are also pleased that the poverty rate has fallen in Mexico and pensions have risen. That's nice, but in Germany it is the other way around; there the poverty rate is rising, and the pension level is falling. Every fifth German is at risk of poverty, 7 million pensioners receive less than 1,000 EUR a month.

Instead of praising the Mexican government for its success in fighting poverty, we should criticise the German government, which is plunging more and more people into poverty. And that is exactly what we are doing; that is why we are successful. Our party, Alternative for Germany, is by far the strongest force in Germany. You can cut our funds here, but we will still win because we represent the interests of our citizens and do not want to lecture the rest of the world.

KATARINA BARLEY:Vizepräsiden

VORSITZ: KATARINA BARLEY

Vizepräsidentin

Antonio LÓPEZ-ISTÚRIZ WHITE

Madam President, the European Union needs to strengthen its alliances with strategic partners. And Mexico, of course, is one. Not only because of the weight of our economic relationship, but because we share a history, common interests, and a responsibility to defend a rules-based international order.

But precisely because we aspire to a lasting alliance, we cannot be content with talking solely about trade. Strategic alliances are not sustained solely on economic exchanges, they are sustained on shared values. If we want this Agreement to stand the test of time, we must be able to demand from each other what both of us have decided to defend: legal certainty, the rule of law, solid institutions, judicial independence, the protection of freedoms, and full respect for democratic principles.

Trust between partners is not born of silence; it is born of sincerity and reciprocal demand. And that is what we have seen with Mexico. Governments negotiate agreements, but it is Parliaments that provide democratic legitimacy and guarantee their continuity when majorities change. Therefore, as Chair of the EU-Mexico Joint Parliamentary Committee, I want to thank the two rapporteurs—Javi López and Borja Jiménez Larraz—for the magnificent work on the reports, the Mexican Ambassador—Rogelio Granguillhome—, and the European Ambassador—Francisco André—, because they have helped ensure that the European Parliament is also represented for the first time in the signing of an agreement. Thank you very much for that as well to their bosses in the Commission and the Council—important.

Bernd LANGE

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, dear colleagues! Globally, we are living in turbulent economic times; the waters are rough. And Mexico is naturally experiencing this very, very strongly too. Last year, Mr Trump negatively influenced Mexico's economy eight times with various tariff threats and measures. There was a dispute over water distribution. How can one do that nowadays? There were other pressure tactics, so that the economy in Mexico is stagnating.

With the agreement, we expect a significant recovery of the economy in Mexico, of up to 35%. That is, I believe, exactly what we need at the moment - solidarity in the economic relationship and in investment policy, so that people on the ground have the prospect of a good life.

That is why it is good that we are advancing this agreement; that is a sign of our solidarity with Mexico. Let's build bridges over troubled water.

Maroš Šefčovič

Madam President, if you allow me just a short intervention, just to react on the first round of speakers. I think Mr Lange just reminded us what kind of turbulent times we are living in right now and why in these times, especially in this period, we need close partnerships with our like-minded partners and also strong solidarity. I think this agreement is a kind of reflection and embodiment of these key ingredients, which have been part and parcel of our negotiations. Ms Pedro already highlighted that already today we have 45 000 European companies that are exporting to Mexico. And what is also very important is the fact that, as she said, and I confirm the figure, more than 80 % of these companies are SMEs. So for small and medium-sized enterprises to trade with a distant partner, it requires simplicity, it has to be smooth, you have to have a good legal and trade framework in place. And I believe that with the modernisation of this agreement, we are clearly delivering on this goal and therefore I believe that we will have more SMEs and more companies investing and cooperating with Mexico.

Ms Jalloul Muro was highlighting that this agreement goes beyond traditional trade issues. She was underscoring the importance of economic security, strategic economy, strategic autonomy, but also the diversification opportunity this agreement offers to Mexico, but also to the European Union. And I think that once we enter into this new partnership with Mexico, it would help us to also address the issues that have been mentioned by Ms Pedro and Ms Cavazzini as true partners who are ready to cooperate together very closely on all issues.

Mr Polato and Mr Barrena Arza, thank you very much for highlighting the complementarity of our economies because especially the topics which are very often passionately discussed also in this chamber, linked to agriculture and the agrifood business, in this particular case, what we have focused on is making sure that our agrifood exports to Mexico will be done with zero duties. And all this would apply to almost all of the EU's key export interests, either at entry into force or within 7 to 10 years. And I have to underscore that this agreement will remove 99 % of the currently very high Mexican tariffs, like 100 % on poultry, 45 % on cheese, 45 % on pork, 20 % on chocolate and pasta, for example. Despite these tariffs, already in 2025, EU agrifood exports are worth EUR 2.3 billion. So I believe that when it comes to the reduction of tariffs, as I just described only for the agrifood business, we are reducing tariffs for European exporters by more than EUR 100 million. So I am absolutely convinced that, also in this sector, it would be extremely beneficial for our agrifood sectors to have such valuable partners as Mexico.

Enikő GYŐRI

Madam President! The EU-Mexico Global Agreement undoubtedly opens up new opportunities for both parties: hopefully, new jobs and export markets - improving our competitiveness. For the sake of clarity, however, two things. First: I ask the Commission to urgently update its 24 impact assessment on agriculture regarding the combined effect of all free trade agreements, so that we can see exactly what our farmers are facing. Please pay special attention to the honey market. And this time, please do not leave out the impact of Ukrainian imports from the calculation.

The other: This agreement undeniably has a political dimension, and the interim report is swarming with principled concessions made to the left. Yet the author knows full well: what is happening with Mexican the rule of law is unacceptable. Brussels always turns a blind eye to the sins of the left's ideological fellow fighters. Scheinbaum in Mexico, Péter Magyar in Hungary are smashing the democratic order, and the Commission remains deeply silent. With this double standard, you are not only making the Union impossible, but you are destroying it, mutual trust, and cooperation.

Waldemar BUDA

Madam President! Commissioner! Have you not yet learned to draw conclusions from history? What happened in cooperation with China should show which direction to take. Many years ago, exactly the same hopes were placed in trade with China as today with Mercosur, with India, and now with Mexico. It has not led to anything good. Today we live in times when we should build resilience and independence, because geopolitics today is such that a minor conflict anywhere in the world causes dramatic consequences.

And we are constantly continuing the process of becoming dependent on foreign trade with countries very distant from the European Union. This is the wrong direction. COVID and other wars in the Middle East have shown that this is a very wrong direction, but we are not drawing any conclusions from it. The problem is that when Germany made stupid decisions, they harmed themselves and destroyed their own economy precisely through gas trade with Russia, through the elimination of nuclear energy, and through trade with China. That was their business. And today the problem is that they have an influence on the entire European Union and they force all members to apply and participate in these foolish actions. And this is the biggest problem of today's situation.

João COTRIM DE FIGUEIREDO

Madam President, Commissioner Šefčovič, at a time when it seems easier to launch tariffs, which are a sort of walls, it is particularly pleasing to speak here about trade agreements, which are a sort of bridges. And this modernization of the global agreement with Mexico and the interim trade agreement are a fine bridge.

It is not only the 99% of tariffs that disappear, which in agri-food alone represent more than 100 billion EUR in savings for European exporters, but it is also all the other impacts that this market will have, notably the fact that it opens up 130 million Mexican consumers to us, and will make our trade grow rapidly, surpassing 100 billion EUR very quickly.

It also clarifies the rules for access to the digital market and makes it easier for Europeans to access critical raw materials.

We would like this bridge to have one more section. Yes, we would like it to have the energy chapter and it is our responsibility to do so before the end of the first review period of this agreement.

But it also has perfectly new sections: access to public procurement by European companies, notably in state-level public procurement, and the innovative clause to combat and prevent corruption, because there is no free trade without free and transparent institutions, relying on what is truly the first step in combating corruption, which is also combating bureaucracy.

Therefore, we ask, dear colleagues, that you approve this agreement when it comes to a vote, because we believe in the strength of free trade, we believe because free trade has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of misery in recent decades and we believe that fighting for freer trade is fighting for a stronger Europe.

Diana RIBA I GINER

Madam President, Commissioner, the European Union must seek new alliances of all kinds: commercial, political, and surely even in defense. The old world we knew is dying, and the European Union must carve out a place for itself in the new world that is being born. Alliances with sister countries like Mexico are key. They are a first-rate geopolitical opportunity. Here, we all agree; what we perhaps no longer all agree on is with what tools we build these alliances.

For us, a type of agreement that does contemplate binding sanctioning measures in the event of non-compliance with the trade agreement, but only proposes mere recommendations when human rights or environmental rights are violated, does not help build the world we want.

But what is more, in the commercial sphere, these are agreements that do not respond to all the interests we need in Europe. Look, for example, at the automotive industry. In recent months, we have seen how Audi definitively closed its plant in Brussels and destroyed 3,000 direct jobs. Meanwhile, the transfer of the production of historic models such as the Volkswagen Golf to the Puebla plant in Mexico is consolidated, which leaves assembly lines empty in Germany. Is this a good agreement? For the profit and loss statement of multinationals, yes, but for working families, evidently no. And this is just the tip of the iceberg.

The question is not whether we want an alliance with Mexico: we want it. The question is whether we are willing to build it on these foundations. For us, it is clear: Europe's progress is not defended by destroying its industry or its precarization, employment here or there. Therefore, for coherence and social justice, we will vote against.

Manon AUBRY

Madam President, Commissioner, giving all the power to multinationals, that is what you are preparing to do with this new free trade agreement with Mexico. And we are supposed to be here applauding with both hands! Companies are certainly not fooled. Attracted by cheap labor and zeroed-out customs duties, they are already taking advantage of this to massively relocate, like the Volkswagen group which, at the same time as it relocates the assembly of its Audi and Golf cars to Mexico, is cutting at least 50,000 jobs in Europe.

But the scandal of this agreement does not stop there. Tomorrow, companies will be able to sue the Mexican State or European States before a private international court and claim several hundred million euros if a public policy does not suit them, for example to keep public control over energy or preserve the environment. This is exactly the same scandalous mechanism that was present in TAFTA, in CETA, in the Energy Charter Treaty, which Europeans have already said loud and clear that they do not want.

So, left-wing, socialist, and environmentalist colleagues who are preparing to vote for this agreement, how can you accept this completely unfair agreement that will accelerate deindustrialization, further erode our food sovereignty, and promote limitless raw material extraction? In football, that is called an own goal. Commissioner, if you will allow me, your "free trade at all costs" policy deserves a red card. That is why our Left group will continue to mobilize against this "free trade at all costs" policy at the European level.

Elena YONCHEVA

Madam President, before us is an agreement that will open European markets to duty-free imports of honey from Mexico in an amount comparable to the honey production of three Bulgarians. First, the quota is increased to 35,000 tons. After the seventh year, all restrictions are lifted. This is happening at a time when European institutions themselves are warning about the risk of adulterated honey. Research from the hives of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre shows that in 22 tests of honey samples originating from Mexico, more than a quarter are suspected of adulteration. We are talking about fake honey, honey, colleagues.

Even more inexplicably, Mexico is not even fully using its current duty-free quota. Why then are we offering even greater liberalization? We cannot sacrifice European beekeepers in exchange for trade concessions in other sectors, because when we destroy our own production, it is not only the beekeepers who lose, but also European consumers, who have the right to real, quality, and free [unadulterated] honey.

David MCALLISTER

Madam President, Commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the modernised global agreement is more than just a trade agreement; it is a comprehensive and strategic renewal of the relationship between Mexico and the European Union. As such, I am sure it will provide an updated framework for political dialogue, economic cooperation and sectoral engagement across a wide range of policy areas.

Against the backdrop of growing geopolitical uncertainty and increasing pressure on the rules-based international order, the agreements with Mexico highlight the European Union's commitment to strengthening cooperation with like-minded partners.

Most of today's challenges are transnational and therefore they require international cooperation. Be it security, migration, digitalisation, energy or climate change, we all know that none of these complex issues can be addressed by any country alone. Consequently, our relations with strategic partners no longer focus solely on trade, but also address the multifaceted concerns of an increasingly connected world. The modernised global agreement is a prime example of exactly this approach; in particular, I welcome the strong and timely political signal it sends in support of openness, fairness and international cooperation with our partners in Latin America and beyond.

Brando BENIFEI

Madam President, honourable colleagues, while the United States is questioning the agreement linking the United States, Canada and Mexico, which for thirty years has been the pillar of North American economic integration, Europe is making the opposite choice and strengthening its alliances.

The agreement with Mexico is a fundamental geopolitical choice: in a fragmented world, diversifying markets strengthens our strategic autonomy.

Together with Canada, the Mercosur countries, Australia and other partners, we are working to build a space of middle powers that believe in open trade and rules, reducing dependence on third actors. And the European Union, as a space that can be a great democratic power, can aim to lead this change.

A strategy of global importance that also has very immediate benefits for our regions. I am thinking of businesses in our regions, in Italy, with protected geographical indications such as those for cheeses or wines. We have products that are protected and that will be able to reach Mexican consumers more easily.

This too is an important part of our strategy for the future of our Union's economy.

Elisabeth DIERINGER

Madam President, ladies and gentlemen! This House is presented with a fait accompli today. The Commission has deliberately split this agreement. The interim trade agreement will enter into force as soon as this Parliament and the Mexican Senate approve it. The national parliaments, including the Austrian National Council, may only ratify it afterwards, when a fait accompli has long been created. This is not trade policy; this is premeditated circumvention of democracy.

And while we are being told about growth and diversification, under the guise of free trade, Green Deal ideology and sustainability goals bureaucracy are cheerfully smuggled into a trade agreement that should actually serve our farmers and our small and medium-sized enterprises, not Brussels' pet projects. We cannot place our trust in this procedurally questionable approach.

At the same time, we are aware of the legitimate interests of those domestic businesses that depend on fair and reliable market opportunities. The Commission does not resolve this contradiction with its approach; it has created it itself.

Kris VAN DIJCK

Mr President, Commissioner, this modernized agreement with Mexico comes at a crucial moment, for several reasons.

From a geopolitical perspective, we are strengthening our position in Latin America and building a reliable partnership in a region where other players are also trying to increase their influence.

From an economic perspective, this agreement also opens up new opportunities for our companies, including through better access to public procurement and fewer administrative burdens.

It confirms our belief in free, rules-based trade in these difficult times of deglobalization and fragmentation. Moreover, it takes clear steps forward in improving working conditions and sustainability standards.

Finally, Commissioner, I call on you to consistently pursue this ambitious trade agenda. The EU must continue to choose strong trade agreements that further strengthen prosperity, resilience, and open strategic autonomy.

Svenja HAHN

Madam President! Every time we talk about free trade here, our colleagues on the left expose their economic ignorance. That is why I am happy to say it again very clearly: economic dependence drives us into political dependence. We saw this with Russian gas; we see it with critical raw materials from China. The solution cannot be isolation. It is more trade with more partners, even if the left does not want to accept that.

The modernized agreement with Mexico is an important success for our prosperity and for Europe's strategic independence. Prosperity is not created behind tariff walls; prosperity is created when people trade with one another. With this agreement, our exports to Mexico can increase by up to 75%. European companies can save up to 100 million euros in tariffs. And we secure access to critical raw materials, create new opportunities from small and medium-sized enterprises to agriculture and industry. This is how strategic independence works, and this is how European strength works, dear colleagues!

Rudi KENNES

Mr President, colleagues, this policy of the European Commission is completely incomprehensible. Yesterday we were still debating our automotive industry, which has left Europe and sees thousands of jobs lost every year. And what does this Commission do? It is concluding another neoliberal trade agreement, an agreement that undermines our industrial capacity and will play workers off against each other worldwide.

European car producers will be able to move their assembly to Mexico even more cheaply. Consequence: thousands of jobs gone again. The agreement also gives large corporations the right to sue governments if they even dare to pursue social policies that might mortgage their profit margins.

I thought the European Union was going to do industrial policy, but what do we see instead? Once again the same neoliberal recipes that have plunged us into this crisis. What we need is a fair deal that creates prosperity for the EU and for Mexico, and not just for multinationals. So vote this agreement down.

Davor Ivo STIER

Madam President, Mexico is a strategic partner of the European Union and—consequently—in these times of international order fragmentation, it is necessary to reinforce our ties through the modernization of the Global Agreement and the approval of the Interim Trade Agreement.

In this way, we will increase trade by further reducing tariffs, covering more sectors, and better protecting producers. But it is also necessary to deepen political dialogue, opening up topics such as judicial independence and the Rule of Law. And we cannot ignore the serious problem of the disappeared. When we were with EuroLat in Mexico, the official number was 130,000 people, but that number continues to increase.

I share Amnesty International's concern regarding the operations in Mexico City over the repression during demonstrations by relatives of the disappeared. Therefore, we must not remain silent. We must support the Modernized Global Agreement, but also denounce authoritarian drifts because our commitment and friendship is not with a Government, but with the brotherly and beloved Mexican people.

Leire PAJÍN

Madam President, Commissioner, with our support, Europe and Mexico will not only seal a strategic agreement, but a shared way of understanding the world. It is an alliance between two democracies that, in the face of those who use their power to impose their will and their own benefit, defend dialogue, cooperation, and clear, agreed-upon rules to build peace, prosperity, and collective sustainable development.

We support it because it reinforces political dialogue with a strategic partner, because it is based on cooperation and benefits health, education, and research, as well as disaster preparedness, because it respects people and natural resources, and because it is based on commitment and human rights, the Paris Agreement, labor rights, trade, equality, and the environment. Because, furthermore, it opens new opportunities for our SMEs and especially protects sectors such as nougat or citrus fruits.

But, above all, we support it because, in the current geopolitical chessboard, an agreement with a country like Mexico is the best compass. From mutual respect, from the recognition of our own history, our diversity, and from cooperation.

Sebastian KRUIS

Mr President, the Party for Freedom chooses trade that makes the Netherlands stronger and therefore we support this strategic partnership agreement.

With 130 million inhabitants, Mexico is one of the largest economies in the world and an important growth market for our entrepreneurs. European export of goods and services can increase by 75% and European companies will save up to 100 million EUR in customs duties annually. This agreement lowers trade barriers, gives our companies better access to Mexican public procurement and offers enormous opportunities for Dutch high-tech machine building and logistics. Our farmers also benefit, because high import tariffs on cheese, chicken and pork, among other things, will disappear.

But although we are in favor of the agreement, we are against the resolution of Parliament. Because once again the left is abusing a trade agreement to push through its climate hysteria, gender agenda and NGO obsession. Strategic partnerships are about trade and mutual benefit. "Woke" is not an export product.

Jessika VAN LEEUWEN

Madam President, Commissioner Šefčovič, finally, we have a trade deal in front of us that does not jeopardise the position of European farmers or our European food security. The trade deal with Mexico offers ample opportunities for farmers and the EU industry: lower tariffs on agricultural products to Mexico, protection of geographical indications and easier access to Mexican products.

Nevertheless, I do have one concern because we cannot import what we cannot produce, meaning Mexico needs to comply with all EU standards if they want to export to the European Union. As the use of antibiotics as growth promoters through veterinary prescription in feed is still common practice in Mexico, I urge the Commission to implement sufficient audits on the ground to make sure there is compliance with our standards.

The Farmer‑Citizens Movement of the Netherlands welcomes this deal as a necessary diversification in a conflicted world where the EU cannot afford to bet on a single horse.

Oihane AGIRREGOITIA MARTÍNEZ

Madam President, we live in a complex context full of uncertainties where we know that — furthermore — tariffs are being used as continuous threats.

In this context, trade agreements with allies that are stable and trustworthy and that give us guarantees that shared values and the rules of the game we establish will be respected seem more important than ever.

It seems that this year 2026 is a year of new opportunities for new markets and for the reduction of dependencies. It is about Mercosur, India, Australia, and Mexico, which is what we have to discuss today.

What are we going to say: Mexico is a strategic international ally for European companies and for Basque companies.

We highlight three things that we expect from the deployment of this Agreement. First, that it serves to reduce the levels of violence that exist in the country and solve the complaints that exist in this regard. Second, that trade is deployed respecting the rights of local and indigenous communities in their entirety. And third, that we are able, of course, to accompany our companies and industries to get the maximum benefit from this Agreement with relations that are beneficial for both parties in a balanced way.

Jörgen WARBORN

Madam President, Commissioner, I would like to start to congratulate you and the Commission for bringing this agreement forward. I will fully support it and I am actually very impressed by the Commission and the pace with which you now deliver new free trade agreements. It is important to mention also that the trade policy of the European Union is not only about new free trade agreements, it is also about modernising the ones we have.

The modernised agreement with Mexico has been in play for 26 years, I think, and now, the update of it will bring new possibilities for European businesses, new opportunities for European farmers. It will strengthen the cooperation on critical raw materials. It will simplify the rules for SMEs and it will improve the access for public procurement and provide stronger protection for intellectual properties.

So, I call on the Commission to continue to modernise other existing trade agreements. We need to ensure that European companies can benefit from the growth taking place beyond our borders.

Marco TARQUINIO

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, honourable colleagues, we live in a time of vertical challenges, where force is proclaimed to be worth more than rules.

Global actors aim for supremacy over neighbors and distant lands, brandish blackmail, impose tariffs, raise walls, wage war.

The European Union knows and can pursue the opposite path: encounter, negotiation, construction and custody of shared rules, a winning partnership, the only real victory.

The renewed global agreement with Mexico comes at a crucial moment, goes in the right direction, strengthens political dialogue with a strategic partner in Latin America, opens concrete opportunities for businesses – especially SMEs and agri-food – and specifies binding commitments on human and workers' rights and climate issues.

All this must be implemented and monitored in an open dialogue with civil society. Today more than ever, Europe must demonstrate that another way of being in the world is possible and bears fruit.

Gilles PENNELLE

Madam President, while all the major powers are protecting their economies from foreign competition, the European Commission is embarked on an endless race for free trade agreements. With which country have we not yet signed a free trade agreement? The list is short.

With Mexico, we are told that all our guarantees have been taken, and that it will be very favorable. But I note nevertheless that health and phytosanitary controls have been completely abandoned. And secondly, we are still going to import numerous agricultural products - beef, honey, fruit - which worry our farmers. So each time, we are told: "Yes, but these are small volumes."

Yes, but: small volumes + small volumes = large volumes. Because, at the same time, we have free trade agreements with Ukraine, Malaysia, Mercosur, Australia.

Our farmers live in a very tense context regarding their incomes. They can no longer bear these free trade agreements. It is time to stop this headlong rush.

Mariateresa VIVALDINI

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, honourable colleagues, Europe's strength is not measured by the number of agreements it signs, but by its ability to build partnerships that protect its interests and promote common values, including the rule of law and fundamental rights.

As Vice-Chair of the Delegation for relations with Mexico, I am proud of the signing of the modernized Global Agreement. It is a foreign, industrial and strategic policy choice; it means diversifying our economic relations, strengthening value chains, protecting our geographical indications and eliminating tariffs for our businesses in an increasingly competitive international context.

But no partnership can be solid without an indispensable principle: mutual respect, respect for rules, commitments made and our businesses, and truly fair competition conditions.

On these bases, cooperation becomes a factor of growth, security and shared prosperity, because a truly leading Europe is not the one that signs the most agreements, but the one that knows how to enforce them, that defends its own interests and that turns every partnership into an advantage for its citizens and its businesses.

Juan Ignacio ZOIDO ÁLVAREZ

Madam President, Commissioner, Europeans and Mexicans know well that our prosperity is greater when it is shared and, in a world where trust is scarce and the list of reliable partners is getting shorter, Mexico reaffirms itself with this Agreement as a strategic trade partner for Spain and for Europe.

This Agreement will open up new opportunities for our exporters and our companies and will encourage many European companies—already present on the other side of the Atlantic—to continue investing, growing and creating prosperity together with Mexico.

Precisely for this reason, because we believe that this is a solid and future-oriented relationship, we regret that an ambitious chapter on energy was not included. We therefore ask the Commission to continue demanding from the Government of Mexico the necessary legal certainty for the investments of our energy companies. Only in this way will we guarantee that this agreement is not just a circumstantial trade opportunity, but a true strategic alliance between Europe and Mexico.

César LUENA

Madam President, Commissioner, I believe this is precisely what we need: honest, proportional relations, based on principles and democratic, tolerant values.

Congratulations to the rapporteurs; more so to rapporteur López than to rapporteur Larraz, because I noticed he "Ayused" a little bit and I am not sure if that was necessary.

I find the agreed standards on labor, health, and environmental protection to be especially positive. By the way, speaking of the environment, the report mentions the Paris Agreement and the Convention on Biological Diversity. Very well, gentlemen of the EPP. Since you have caught that streak with Mexico, do it here as well. Let it not be that you defend the European Green Deal in the agreements and then fail to do so within the European Union.

By the way, regarding the agri-food sector: I believe it will bring benefits concerning the elimination of Mexican tariffs on our products. For those of us who come from wine-growing lands, it is very good news that these tariffs are removed. Therefore, this is the way: proportional, tolerant, democratic relations. This is the way.

Reinhold LOPATKA

Madam President, dear colleagues, for Europe to thrive in a multi-polar world, economic and political agreements are essential, especially with reliable and like-minded countries like Mexico. This is why the modernised strategic partnership agreement is so important. It is not only a trade agreement, it is a strategic investment in our common future.

This partnership opens new opportunities for European agri-food exports, improves access for EU companies to public procurement and services in Mexico, and supports small and medium-sized enterprises through simpler rules and procedures.

It enables us also to strengthen Europe's global competitiveness by diversifying supply chains and deepening cooperation with a key partner in Latin America. While we are separated geographically, we are united by shared values and by a clear mutual interest in strengthening our partnership.

Sakis ARNAOUTOGLOU

Madam President, Commissioner, the Strategic Partnership Agreement between the European Union and Mexico is certainly an important step towards stronger, more democratic, and resilient cooperation in a period of major geopolitical upheavals. However, it is not enough to speak only of increased trade. Trade must be accompanied by strong guarantees for human rights, environmental protection, workers' rights, and the fight against corruption.

For us in Greece and across Europe, the agreement can create new opportunities for the exports of quality agri-food products and for our small and medium-sized enterprises. However, it is crucial to ensure the effective protection of European geographical indications and the maintenance of a level playing field, so that European producers do not face unfair practices.

Europe needs reliable partners. This must be the compass of our European trade policy.

Francisco José MILLÁN MON

Madam President, I also welcome the modernization of the Agreement with Mexico, a country with which we share deep ties and one of the European Union's two strategic partners in Latin America.

I hope that this modernization will also strengthen our political dialogue and our coordination in the face of common challenges. I am thinking, for example, of the fight against organized crime and drug trafficking, and the deterioration of the rule of law.

The Agreement is good news in general, but I regret that, ultimately, a specific chapter on energy was not included: it would have been advisable to provide legal certainty for European investment in this sector of such importance in Mexico. I hope that the three-year review includes regulation on this matter.

I am concerned—Mr Commissioner, you know this—about the complete liberalization of Mexican exports of canned tuna starting from the seventh year. It is a very sensitive product for certain regions of the Union and Mexico has great export potential. The Commission must monitor the evolution of the volume of these imports. The European canned fish sector is very concerned about the cumulative effect of these concessions on canned tuna in trade agreements: now it is Mexico, tomorrow it will be Southeast Asian countries, major producers. The Commission must be careful in these negotiations.

Alexandra MEHNERT

Madam President! Today we are talking about an agreement that we have worked towards for a long and patient time: our new partnership with Mexico. Almost ten years of negotiations, and since May 22nd the signed result has been before us. This is more than a technical agreement; it is a strong signal of partnership. I am thinking of the many small and medium-sized enterprises in Europe that need exactly such agreements as a signal - fewer tariffs and practical hurdles in everyday business life, less waiting time at the border and more reliability when exporting.

We live in a time when supply chains can break and trading partners are no longer reliable as a matter of course. All the more important that we have a partner in Mexico with whom we have enjoyed good cooperation for over 25 years. Over 45,000 companies, most of them small and medium-sized, will benefit from this agreement through simpler customs procedures, clear investment rules, protected designations of origin. And we are opening our markets without compromising our standards - binding commitments to workers' rights and environmental protection, high requirements for food safety.

But, this must also be considered: trust in the rule of law and institutions in Mexico can be improved. We must point that out. Nevertheless, I am glad that we are voting on the agreement and therefore ask for your approval.

Lukas MANDL

Madam President, Mr Commissioner, dear colleagues! On the agenda now is EU-Mexico - that sounds like a football match in days like these, but it is not this time. After all, the EU is still in the running with many teams, including the team from Belgium, the home country of our European capital.

This time it is about cooperation, and that is what I advocate time and time again. In a world full of confrontation, where many also try to achieve their goals through more and more confrontation, we must seek cooperation, not least because that is the lesson of European history and also because it will serve our prosperity and the prosperity of future generations all the more.

Mexico shares a lot with us: the values of our civilisation; Mexico is a reliable partner, and on a continental level Europe is clearly the most reliable partner in today's world. Therefore, it is good for both sides that we make prosperity possible, make growth possible and modernise the agreement with Mexico.

Sebastian TYNKKYNEN

Madam President, I support free trade with democratic partners. Strengthening our relationship with Mexico makes strategic sense, especially when it comes to critical raw materials and reducing our dependence on China. But this Parliament's report on the EU‑Mexico agreement is such a disgrace to read.

While Mexico struggles with cartel violence, corruption, organised crime and border security, this House chooses to devote almost manic attention to gender ideology, identity politics, and climate activism. Instead of these leftist slogans, I have conservative guidelines for the EU when it negotiates new trade deals: defend our strategic interests, support trade where it benefits Europeans, protect our farmers and leave ideological activism out of our trade policy.

Kateřina KONEČNÁ

Madam President, dear Commissioner, dear colleagues, the modernization of the global agreement between the EU and Mexico is another in a series of trade liberalizations between the EU and the other side. And just like previous liberalizations, this one is primarily aimed at the detriment of our workers. Is it really not enough that we are destroying jobs in the automotive industry through the green transition? Do we now have to try to make it easier to relocate our production to Mexico, where, by the way, such strong environmental measures do not apply? What is the reason for this? Who is this supposed to help, apart from a few of the richest? Certainly not the people who work in car factories here in Europe, and it will only harm the environment for the sake of which we are destroying this industry here.

But I consider it a real audacity to once again attempt to bypass member states and their parliaments by placing the trade part of the agreement in an interim agreement, meaning this part can effectively apply despite the possible disagreement of any democratically elected body. For the mantra of free trade, you are allowing the local industry, the environment, and the democratic principles and sovereignty of member states to be destroyed. This logic should truly come to an end.

Maroš Šefčovič

Madam President, I would like to thank all honourable Members for their intervention and, very telegraphically, I would like to reassure honourable members that, if it comes to the concerns concerning tuna, honey or SPA standards, we have been really carefully negotiating all these categories. I can assure you that everything will be okay, under control, and this agreement will bring huge benefits to European economic operators and, as I mentioned earlier, especially to the agrifood sector.

On the energy sector, what I would like to say is that we made also big progress in this regard, because we have been able to assess with certainty the domestic energy policy, which was related to the now finalised Mexican constitutional reforms in the economic sphere, and the agreement we reached on energy issues ensures consistency of the modernisation with the Mexican reforms in the energy sector, while ensuring the overall balance of the negotiated outcome is rebalanced and that now we are in a much better situation than before.

On top of it, we got the guarantee that EU investors will be treated on equal footing with investors from other important third countries. Also, you rightly pointed out that we have agreed on a review clause in order to discuss in the medium term the changes, recalibration or removal of some of the energy commitments that have been agreed in in the agreement, and we will definitely use those opportunities.

If you allow me, the last point concerns the issue which was raised by Mr Warborn and this is linked with the pace of our free trade agreement negotiations. We accelerated it because the economic situation in the world and in Europe clearly demands it. We simply need to diversify our trade. We need to diversify the opportunities for our economic operators. We'll simply have to look for new markets beyond the traditional export destinations. And, of course, if you want to be strategically autonomous, we have to have new access to the critical raw minerals, to the sensitive technologies, and therefore we are actually expanding the horizon and possibility for the European economy to thrive.

Let's not forget that almost half of our GDP depends on how well we trade. Despite what is happening right now, we are the biggest trader in the world if we take together goods and services. So I think what we should focus on is how we can consolidate the position in the future. And with the pace of negotiation comes my request.

Madam President, I would like to kindly ask this House and great colleagues from the INTA and other committees to support us in a smooth consent vote, organisation and procedures. Today, we discuss Mexico. Earlier with the Taoiseach, I was putting the accent on our agreements with India and Indonesia, which should get the consent of this House this year, so we can really benefit from these agreements as of 1 January next year. And, of course, we have on the table also the agreement with Australia. So I would just highlight these agreements where we need to coordinate very well between Parliament, the Council and the Commission, so we can really use these opportunities as soon as possible.

Javi LÓPEZ

Madam President, first of all, as rapporteur, the first thing I would like to do is acknowledge the fantastic cooperation between the Committee on Foreign Affairs and the Committee on International Trade, especially with Borja Jiménez Larraz, who has been its rapporteur, and with co-rapporteurs from different groups, but who have worked with visions toward a common goal—even with nuances—the strengthening of relations between the European Union and Mexico. We have not only worked with Borja Jiménez Larraz, but also with all the shadow rapporteurs who have contributed to a better resolution and to doing a good job in Parliament.

I would highlight three political messages. One: the diversification of our economy is a geopolitical insurance policy. With this, we are taking a step forward for our economic diversification. Mexico is also doing so, betting on its diversification. Furthermore, thanks to the good work and the fantastic cooperation that Commissioner Šefčovič and Parliament always have, today we have a battery of association agreements underway—some of them important—with the region. These are agreements that will bet on this diversification. It is strategically important for the European Union.

Two: we have spoken about the challenges and some problems that Mexico has. Not only does Mexico have them, we also have some of them. And furthermore, many of them have not appeared now or in recent years, but have been there for a long time. The important thing for Parliament and for Europe is to send the message that the Modernized Global Agreement is going to help us jointly address common challenges and cooperate to be more effective. Among the challenges, obviously, are organized crime, strengthening security, the ecological transition, the digital transition, having true shared prosperity... What we do not do is evaluate the laws decided by another Parliament, since it is another Parliament that has to decide the results in a plural and diverse way based on elections. I say this because the Mexican people have also made quite clear what their opinion is regarding the decisions made by their authorities.

Lastly, we all agree that Mexico is a reliable partner with whom we share values and, for that reason, tomorrow it will have very majority support in this House during the vote, just as it had unanimity in the European Council, with a plurality of governments and political colors.

Borja GIMÉNEZ LARRAZ

Madam President, first of all, I would also like to thank the Commissioner for this eagerness and this objective that he has set himself to diversify trade relations, which I believe is something fundamental, and, of course, for the collaboration with the rapporteur—Javi López—during these last months.

This Agreement is, in essence, a commitment to openness, to cooperation and to rules-based trade. Mexico and the Union share much more than economic interests. We share strong ties: history, traditions, culture, language. This is an Agreement that also reinforces our global position, which improves our competitiveness. It is also a clear message: Europe continues to bet on rules-based trade, in the face of protectionism and market closure.

This is, moreover, an opportunity to consolidate a strategic relationship in Latin America, but I also want to insist that this new level of relationship demands honesty and sincerity—speaking clearly to one another. And there are issues there that can be improved, that is what we have been expressing throughout this debate: without a strong Rule of Law there is no investment, without legal certainty there is no trust.

Mexico and the European Union share history. Today we have the opportunity to build a future together, in a world in which more and more actors relate to one another through the imposition of the law of the strongest, in which cooperation and multilateralism are despised.

This Agreement is born from the conviction and determination of those who know that we are on the right path. The path of two peoples who understand each other, who dialogue and who know that cooperation is the best way to generate prosperity. Two peoples who believe that a rules-based international order is the best investment. And this Agreement is also based on a basic conception: an open Europe is a freer Europe.

Katarina BARLEY (Chair)

The joint debate is closed.

The vote will take place tomorrow, Wednesday, 8 July 2026.

Tomasz FROELICH

Mexico is an important partner. It is in our interest to deepen relations with Mexico - in terms of our trade, our investments, and the geopolitical diversification that makes us more independent and strengthens our strategic autonomy. This requires open markets, reliable partnerships, and better framework conditions for our companies. It also requires mutual respect - but that is the weak point of this report, which ideally would have been limited to trade policy, but unfortunately reveals the value-imperialist hubris and bigotry of the EU: Brussels worries about democracy in Mexico, while at the European level the ESN party is to be banned and in EU member states repression against patriotic parties is the order of the day. Whoever demands democratic standards from the rest of the world that they themselves constantly violate lacks credibility. And this lack of credibility weakens us internationally. The Eurocrats are not in a position to morally lecture a proud people like the Mexicans and treat them condescendingly. In our relations with Mexico, we should focus on common interests, above all on mutual trade. Arrogant lectures must be refrained from.
