2026-07-07Plenary debate13 speechesThe impact of the 1974 Turkish invasion on Cypriot women and girls, and the crimes committed by Turkish forces and consequences on gender equality

Discussion transcript

The impact of the 1974 Turkish invasion on Cypriot women and girls, and the crimes committed by Turkish forces and consequences on gender equality

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Katarina BARLEY (Chair)

The next item on the agenda is the debate on statements by Parliament on the consequences of the 1974 Turkish invasion for Cypriot women and girls, the crimes committed by the Turkish armed forces and the consequences for gender equality (2026/2617(RSP)). I would like to point out to Members that for this debate there will be only one round of speeches by political groups. Therefore, neither catch-the-eye interventions nor blue cards will be accepted.

Eleonora MELETI

Madam President, dear colleagues, it is not only the resolution on Cyprus that I am asking you to support. It is the story behind the resolution. It is the women, the girls, those who left, those who are still here, those we met a year ago on our mission, those who recounted to us the darkest events of violence, despair, humiliation, and abuse; those who in 1974 were still underage girls, pregnant women, newlywed daughters, mothers, grandmothers, and were tortured, raped, and abused by the Turkish invaders.

The women we met last year broke their silence for the first time 51 years later. Many of them saw us secretly from their husbands and children. They admitted that they had never spoken, either out of fear or shame, because their rape did not end back then. It continued through stigma, isolation, marginalization, rejection, and loneliness. The women we met spoke for all those who will remain forever condemned to silence. We, on the other hand, could not say much. The words would not come out. It was the sobs that dominated and the tears that united us in those hours.

Before leaving Cyprus, we made a promise: that we will make the cries of these women heard everywhere and loudly; that we will give our all so that they and all women, both then and now, are recognized as victims of war crimes. So that someone finally cares, even late, for these open wounds. So that rape is recognized as a weapon in conflict zones. So that Turkey pays reparations for the victims and we send a strong message that everything it did cannot be forgotten because it belongs to the past.

We made a promise that the pain of these women, the collective trauma of the Cypriots, will remain neither silent nor invisible. Therefore, it is not the resolution I am calling you to support, dear colleagues. It is the story that has already been written. It is the soul, the need for vindication of the victims, the promise we gave, the women of Cyprus that I ask you to support.

Cecilia STRADA

Madam President, honourable colleagues, 1974 was a year of unprecedented violence for the population of Cyprus.

The Turkish invasion turned the island into a theatre of massacres and horrors against the civilian population, with unprecedented ferocity. Rape was used on a large scale as an instrument of war, and the women and girls of the island paid the price.

Turkish forces systematically conducted gang rapes and violence against Greek-Cypriot women aged 12 to 70. The fascist parliamentary forces of EOKA-B raped and massacred the female population of entire Turkish-Cypriot villages.

As in many, too many war scenarios, those responsible have remained unpunished and the victims, in most cases, have not had access to adequate healthcare and psychological support.

1974 in Cyprus is not an isolated event: it fits into the historical furrow of the use of rape as a weapon of war, an abomination that even today some try to treat as "isolated cases", "collateral damage". But it is not so. Gender-based violence in armed conflicts is a systematic and deliberate horror, which can and must be fought by pursuing two paths: bringing the executioners to justice and offering real support for the victims.

Even today, from Ukraine to Sudan, to Palestine, victims of rape ask us for justice and ask us for assistance. Even today, in Europe, we have a duty to guarantee victims of gender-based violence, including refugee women and girls, full free access to reproductive health services, including abortion and the treatment of venereal diseases. We have the duty to bring war criminals prosecutable under universal jurisdiction and those wanted by the International Criminal Court in The Hague to court.

It is not only out of respect for the law: it is the only way to respect the dignity of victims around the world, those of the past and those of the future. Because the impunity of rape fuels the culture of rape and, instead, we demand justice for what happened in 1974 in Cyprus, for what happens today, we demand justice because we no longer want to mourn the victims of tomorrow.

Afroditi LATINOPOULOU

Madam President, "The dead smelled from a mile away. It was a merciless last summer. It pierced the shadows of the trees, the roofs of the houses. A dreadful summer for the people. They brought the dead through the back door at St. John; they said the coffins couldn't hold them. And the little boy, blood soaked through his clothes, was digging pits, the sun beating mercilessly on his temples, deep in memory into the future. You knew the Cypriot sun differently, Aunt Marina, at dawn with the doves on your shoulders." Lefkios Zafiriou.

And yet, on July 20, 2026, a full 52 years will have passed since the soul of Hellenism was blackened forever by the seizure of half of Cyprus. Families were uprooted, women were raped, men were cowardly murdered by the Turkish invading conqueror. Thousands are the missing persons who leave behind mothers, wives, sisters, and daughters who are still waiting for their remains to be given to them. Women, mothers, and girls were raped and tortured by Turkish soldiers in a bestial manner.

And you here want to put these cowardly murderers, who continue to this day to threaten Greece, our Cyprus, and Israel, into the European Union, and you have no shame. About the Russian invader we know how to speak and do the right thing; about the Turkish invader, however, we only know how to turn a blind eye. And our Cyprus, Famagusta, Kyrenia, Karpasia, Morphou, Karavas, Rizokarpasso? Still there, our lands sanctified with blood, under the Turkish invader. And you, only silence, stuffed with the dirty money of the conqueror. Shame on you!

Geadis GEADI

Madam President, today we bring back to everyone's memory a forgotten war crime: the rapes and sexual violence suffered by the women and girls of Cyprus during the 1974 Turkish invasion. We remind everyone that in a member state of the Union, 52 years later, the pain remains indelible, the drama unvindicated, the memory unquenched, the occupation ongoing.

While we should be talking about the obvious, we are here to restore common sense. It is a shame that senior European Union officials, Ms. Kallas and Ms. Kos, chose a few days ago to present Turkey as a key strategic partner, talking about deepening cooperation. Their stance is an insult to the women we declare we are defending today. An insult to the very values of the European Union. The women of Cyprus are proud and do not beg. They demand justice and accountability. Not oblivion and hypocrisy.

Jana TOOM

Madam President, colleagues, the suffering of the women of Cyprus following the Turkish invasion in 1974 and the enduring consequences must not be forgotten. These women were attacked for the simple fact that they were women. They were put for these terrible sufferings as a way to demoralise the population and achieve a military goal. It is despicable.

We have to recognise publicly the harm that the women of Cyprus went through. We have to ask for a better support system that can help women deal with the trauma. And we have to continue advocating for a permanent solution for Cyprus.

Just as importantly, we have to learn from these devastating events because we see that conflict-related sexual violence continues to be a tool used in war in other conflicts, even today. I am afraid to say that its use might even be increasing. And that is because we are turning a blind eye to so many examples across the world.

We cannot normalise sexual violence and allow for impunity. We need the EU to speak out against any form of sexual violence, no matter where it happens and no matter who is committing it.

Isabella LÖVIN

Madam President, everything we know about war, we know with a man's voice. Belarusian Nobel Prize laureate Svetlana Alexievich wrote that about women's often forgotten testimonies and experiences of war. Three decades later, those words remain tragically relevant.

Sexual violence is among the most devastating weapons of war. They can destroy people's lives, but also destroy entire communities. The widespread stigma means that women and girls are often left isolated, untreated and silenced, carrying these traumas for decades. What makes me most furious about this is that we know. We don't only know what happened in Cyprus, but we know that today over half a billion women and girls live in conflict zones where they are not only victims of fighting, but their bodies are actively used as targets.

With increasing wars and conflicts, sexual violence is tragically on the rise, from Congo to Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan. This is the security threat that requires special attention. We know this, we know the devastating consequences and we know what is needed to prevent it and to help survivors. The EU must make the prevention of conflict‑related sexual violence and comprehensive support for survivors a top priority in its external action. We must also break this silence.

Giorgos GEORGIOU

Madam President, the gendered consequences of war—one of its most chilling aspects—are often concealed. The Turkish armed forces in 1974 in Cyprus, systematically and in an organized manner, committed sexual violence against Greek Cypriot women and men of all ages. Yet another heinous crime by Turkey that remains unpunished.

However, we must be honest. Barbarities were also committed by Greek Cypriot paramilitary groups against Turkish Cypriot women. Rape has no color, race, or religion. Wounds heal with difficulty. Now that they are timidly being confessed, let them be redeeming. Cyprus and the European Union have an obligation to ensure the rights, dignity, and historical memory of all women in Cyprus. May the shared pain become a driving force for bicommunal cooperation and peace on our island.

Irmhild BOẞDORF

Madam President! The Cyprus conflict is one of the topics at today's NATO summit. Tomorrow, the President of the European Council, the President of the Commission, and Turkish Head of State Erdoğan will meet regarding this; a solution to the Cyprus conflict is not to be expected. While Turkey demands the two-state solution as the basis for further negotiations, the EU prefers a rapprochement with a confederation model. Especially we Germans know how difficult it is, decades after the outbreak of a conflict, to reconcile, to speak with one another again, and to be able to forgive each other. With our Polish neighbors, we have succeeded in doing this to a good extent: meanwhile, we are fighting together in the European Parliament for a Europe of sovereign nations.

All the more incomprehensible is why the FEMM Committee of the European Parliament comes up today of all days with a resolution on the abuses by the Turkish armed forces against Cypriot women and girls from the year 1974. No one wants to relativize or even play down the suffering and crimes from that time, but here an attempt is being made once again to link an ongoing geopolitical conflict with EU guidelines on gender mainstreaming.

A hearing involving gender-sensitive NGOs to formally recognize past testimonies within the institutional framework of the EU, a retroactive justification of abortions to elevate pregnancy termination into an international law context, financial and technical support from the EU for gender-sensitive counseling are not the most urgent problems between Turkey and Greece.

Once again, the FEMM Committee is exceeding its competences and wants this conflict to be read in a gender-sensitive way. What an assumption! Let us instead work on better cooperation between these two NATO partners.

Katarina BARLEY (Chair)

At the end of the debate, a motion for a resolution has been tabled pursuant to Rule 167(2) of the Rules of Procedure.

The debate is closed.

The vote will take place tomorrow, Wednesday, 8 July 2026.

The sitting is suspended. It will resume in a few minutes with a control sitting: Commission statement – Explanation of the action plan on cybersecurity and AI.

There is a point of order – then I must reopen the sitting for that.

Costas MAVRIDES

Madam President, thank you for allowing me to raise a point of order. I think that the wording being used by some of my colleagues, and also, perhaps in good faith, by the translation, was wrong. In Cyprus, there is no conflict between Greece and Türkiye. It is an invasion by Türkiye against the Republic of Cyprus. And I wanted to make sure that there is no such conflict in Cyprus between the two communities. It is a Turkish invasion, a continued occupation of EU territory by Türkiye in Cyprus.

Katarina BARLEY (Chair)

The session is now definitively suspended and will resume in a few minutes.

Λουκάς Φουρλάς

- Dear colleagues, today's discussion concerns Europe's very credibility toward the victims of war and its commitment not to allow silence to cover up crimes.

I am proud that today, even fifty-two years after the Turkish invasion of 1974, the European Parliament has taken this historic step. For the first time, it clearly recognizes that rapes and systematic abuses of Greek Cypriot women by the Turkish army constituted war crimes and that sexual violence was used as a weapon of war.

Behind every testimony is a woman who carried for decades a burden that did not belong to her. The shame was never theirs. The responsibility lies exclusively with the perpetrators and those who allowed silence to prevail.

This recognition constitutes a moral vindication for the survivors, as well as a strong message that the truth does not statute-bar. The naming of Turkey and the demand for accountability and reparations are essential steps toward justice.

Europe must defend human rights consistently, without discounts and without double standards. The memory of the victims obliges us to continue fighting for truth, justice, and a solution to the Cyprus problem that will be fully grounded in international law, United Nations resolutions, and the European acquis.

2026-07-07Plenary debate77 speechesPresentation of the Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI

Discussion transcript

Presentation of the Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Roberts ZĪLE (Chair)

The next item on the order of business is the check session.

Statement by the Commission – Presentation of the action plan on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence (2026/2795(RSP)).

I would like to remind speakers that, given the test regime measures currently in place and the set end time of the debate, speaking time will be strictly enforced.

Henna Virkkunen

Mr President, honourable Members, today, the Commission has adopted a new action plan on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. It follows a commitment I made to this House in May, in light of the unprecedented cyber security capabilities of the latest models. Such models can be used not only for defensive, but also for offensive objectives in cyberspace. Their new capabilities are marking a strategic shift for the Union's security. Most importantly, these models fundamentally now change the economics of malicious actors, whether cyber criminals or national states. These advanced AI models can now build cyber exploits in minutes or hours at a fraction of the cost of vulnerability discovery by trained humans. Once weaponised, these vulnerabilities endanger the security of our infrastructure and society, so we must be prepared for these new capabilities being available widely, including to malicious actors, especially as other capabilities, (inaudible), for instance, are also growing.

The Commission's response has been immediate. We engaged with the entire AI and cybersecurity ecosystem, with you, with Member States, with our AI providers, with industry, and with our international partners. The action plan is not starting from scratch, as we know. The EU already has very robust legal and policy foundations. We are now turning them into action: capability and resilience along three priorities.

So first, AI models with high cyber capabilities deployed in Europe must be safe and our European players must have access to use them. The AI Act provides us with the world's most advanced framework to protect us against the risks of AI. And in less than one month, our AI office will also have the enforcement powers to ensure that providers also establish appropriate safeguards against misuse, including in the cyber domain. Assessing models before release is a cornerstone of risk mitigation. Europe must build excellence in this area. We will launch a call to step up Europe's evaluation capacity of AI models, including in cybersecurity, by 2027. The EU agency for cybersecurity, ENISA, will play an important role in making this action plan operational and together with ENISA, the Commission will also develop a European blueprint for structural access to advanced AI models with a focus on cybersecurity. We need common, clear and also transparent conditions for accessing these models, which also serves as a basis for cooperation and alignment with our international partners. And we must also strengthen our know-how on how to deploy these technologies for our cybersecurity. And this is why already by the end of this year, the Commission will also set up a secure platform to test how these models can be used safely for cybersecurity in critical sectors such as finance, energy, health, transport or public administration.

Second, we must protect ourselves against malicious attacks exploiting such models. Our immediate priority is now to identify and fix the most critical vulnerabilities, faster. The first step is the full and effective implementation of our cybersecurity legislation, so the NIS2 Directive, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act. Not tomorrow, now. And to fix these vulnerabilities where exposure is the highest for our critical infrastructure, this is open source software. So we will launch a critical open source resilience campaign. In parallel, we will also support our critical sectors and our SMEs in understanding and also deploying existing AI tools, including those openly available to enhance their cyber resilience.

Third, we must build Europe's own AI powered cyber capabilities. We cannot rely only on non-European solutions for capabilities that are becoming critical for our security. So Europe has everything it takes to be competitive in this area. We have talent, a solid cybersecurity and AI ecosystem, and with AI factories and in the future also AI gigafactories, we have also the infrastructure. But we must get serious about financing. Frontier AI requires very large-scale investment, as we know. Far beyond what public funding alone can provide. We need to mobilise private capital especially equity. The new European tech equity capacity announced in the tech sovereignty package can be a game-changer here. Some will say that the cost of building European frontier capabilities is too high. In today's world, the cost of not building them will be much higher and it will grow every year. So our action plan now addresses the pressing challenges that frontier AI models present to cybersecurity, and we are building capacities for a stronger Europe in this domain.

Aura SALLA

Mr President, cybersecurity is a matter of national security. Yet even here, Europe remains heavily dependent on US vendors for cloud security, threat intelligence, identity management and endpoint protection. The same is true for AI. We must reduce the risk of supply chain attacks by expanding trusted partners worldwide, while gradually building more of our own tech stack.

Our dependency is not primarily about AI models, it is about the infrastructure they rely on. Europe has strong AI research, but too few companies operating at this frontier. That is why we must speed up EU‑level regulatory sandboxes, market harmonisation, and make sure our public sector chooses European tech first.

Right now, Europe is rightly pushing for computing capacity. However, quantum and giga factories don't help us if we don't have European businesses who use this capacity so that quantum can be commercialised. Investments in data centres and European cloud must go hand in hand with policies that help to create demand here at home. Data centres will not bring high‑tech jobs to Europe.

We also need to be realistic. We unfortunately cannot switch off from the US vendors any time soon. Europe relies so heavily on US cloud, software and hardware solutions that we will shoot ourselves in the foot if we speed up without extended supply chains and domestic solutions. The answer is not more regulation. It is smarter enforcement, strategic public procurement and an industrial policy that strengthens security, supports emerging technologies and reduces critical dependencies.

A shift from digital regulation towards tech sovereignty does not have to happen overnight. It will require a tremendous focus on details and pushing for overall mind change. But the worst we can do now is do nothing.

Alex AGIUS SALIBA

Mr President, the more we digitise our lives, the more vulnerable our society is to cyber attacks. Where previously hackers were only human individuals, today we are facing bots and artificial intelligence models. These can further expose our vulnerabilities. We have seen what Anthropic's Mythos can do and in the future we will see AI-based hacking tools that are much more powerful. This is not a matter to be taken lightly. Situations like these can leave devastating repercussions: power outages, disruption to airport operations or worse, in hospitals or other essential services when they are targeted.

Europe must anticipate, prepare and strengthen its defences against AI-powered hacking. Let us use the most advanced models proactively, identify the weaknesses of these attacks, while strengthening our digital defences. But in this digital reality we can no longer rely solely on foreign technology to keep us safe. Let us direct the right resources and European technological talent in the right direction. Let us invest in European capabilities.

Jaroslav BŽOCH

Mr President, Commissioner, ensuring the security of our citizens is one of the highest priorities, but also challenges, that we currently face in the European Union. And the issue of cybersecurity is becoming increasingly pressing in today's world. The advent of artificial intelligence is making cyberattacks faster, more sophisticated and more dangerous than ever before. Therefore, I welcome the European Commission's action plan for cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. Europe must be prepared to protect its citizens, its businesses and its critical infrastructure.

At the same time, however, we must admit one uncomfortable reality. In recent years, Europe has adopted one regulation after another. Instead of creating an environment for innovation, we have become a world leader in rule-writing. And the result is an environment that has forced many startups and innovative companies to move their development outside the European Union. And that is really not a success. That is rather a warning to all of us. If we really want to be a leader in the field of cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, we cannot just regulate technologies that are developed elsewhere. We must create conditions such that these technologies are created right in Europe, and therefore I would have a few specific questions for the Commission:

How will this action plan prevent the further outflow of innovation from the European Union? How will it ensure that strengthening cybersecurity does not mean an additional administrative burden for European businesses, and especially for small and medium-sized enterprises? And where is an equally ambitious plan to support European developers, startups and technology companies? Because without them, Europe will never be technologically self-sufficient, but will only regulate technologies developed somewhere else. How will the Commission ensure that sensitive security data remain under European control and do not leave the European Union? And in conclusion. According to what criteria and indicators will the Commission measure the success of this action plan?

When discussing new cybersecurity rules, we have the opportunity to learn from the past. We need solutions that will increase security, but at the same time support European innovation, investment and research. Security and competitiveness are not opposites and one cannot exist without the other. Because without European innovation, Europe will not be safe and sovereign.

Tobiasz BOCHEŃSKI

Mr President! This debate is not about cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. This debate is proof of the European Union's failure over the last 20-30 years.

Europe was once a continent where the greatest technical discoveries were made. It was a continent where the industrial revolution took place. It was a continent that dictated the development of practically the entire world.

Today we are a community that subsidizes a bureaucracy with its taxes, which brings nothing innovative or modern. We are riding in a second-class carriage. Right before our eyes, an absolute revolution is taking place, comparable to the introduction of computers. It will affect the economy, societies, and every aspect of our lives. And we are sitting in second class because bureaucracy, regulations, and a lack of innovation are the motto of today's European bureaucracy.

Bart GROOTHUIS

Mr President, I call on all business leaders in Europe to take good note of today's recommendations on AI and cybersecurity, released by the European Commission and ENISA.

It is not business as usual anymore. Your software and IT systems will be tested by hackers. Aided by the latest AI models, hackers will operate at the speed of light, and will try to put you out of business. So, today's recommendations will help you to defend at the speed of light, and with the help of the best talent and the best capabilities Europe has to offer.

Currently, there are some 3 000 large language models in the world, only 30 of which are European. Zero are compliant with EU laws and regulations. The only condition is that European funds also reach the east of the Union.

Member states must remain the main actors in national security and, last but not least, the fight against cybercrime cannot become a pretext for the generalized surveillance of citizens.

Svenja HAHN

Mr President, dear colleagues! From major banks to small and medium-sized enterprises and critical infrastructure - Europe's security depends on whether AI technology is created and can scale here. Therefore, the Cybersecurity and AI Action Plan must do one thing above all: cut red tape, enable investment, and bring new technologies into application faster.

While new AI models are emerging at breakneck speed in the US and China, Europe is still primarily writing rules. But cyberattacks and technological dependency are not fought with reporting obligations, but with a technological edge. Europe becomes safer when the best technologies come from here. For this, we need less bureaucracy, more capital, cheaper energy, and a genuine European single market so that our brightest minds can simply get things done. Because digital sovereignty does not grow out of isolation, and cybersecurity does not emerge in legal texts, but through innovation.

Let us stop wanting to regulate the world! Let us finally show the world again that Europe can change it!

Jutta PAULUS

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues! A quiz question: How many resources does one minute of AI-generated video require? 200 kilowatt hours. That is the electricity consumption of an average family in two days. Seven liters of water, clean drinking water that is no longer available to our citizens and also to our agriculture. Tech corporations not only have an extreme hunger for data, but also an extreme thirst for water.

Therefore: Yes, the EU must become more independent in the digital sector, but it cannot be that scarce resources are sacrificed for the profits of a few, especially when these on top of that do not create jobs, but rather destroy them. Wise people learn from their mistakes; wise people learn from the mistakes of others. The growing resistance to data centers in the USA because of rising electricity prices, because of the water issue, because of air pollution - we must learn from that.

Therefore: We need data centers - yes, with clear rules -, efficient technology, renewable energies, waste heat utilization, transparency, public participation: Then something will come of it.

Per CLAUSEN

Mr President! I think it is a pity that the Commission does not present its proposals in good time so that we have the opportunity to read them before we discuss them. I think that is particularly a pity because in this proposal there are actually also positive things about the development of open source and a strategy for it.

But if we really take the EU's cybersecurity seriously, why wouldn't we start by closing completely obvious gaps? Why don't we quickly transition the EU away from programs like Outlook, Webex and Teams and fill them with European-anchored open source programs that secure our data and digital sovereignty? And I must also say, we also hear warnings that the cyber resilience act and artificial intelligence act risk ending up as a continuous American dependency act. And surely we agree that continued dependence on the USA in this area is a serious problem for our cybersecurity.

Paulius SAUDARGAS

Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, the action plan on cybersecurity and AI is a welcome step in supporting our Member States and companies to navigate the digital transition. But regulation alone will not solve our innovation deficit or mitigate the threats we face.

In 2024, the United States produced 40 notable AI models, China produced 15, while Europe produced only three. We are heavily dependent on foreign cloud and other digital technologies. To bridge this gap, we need aggressive public‑private investment in European computing capacity, critical digital infrastructure, cloud computing, data centres and advanced connectivity. We have built a robust regulatory foundation with the Digital Markets Act, Cyber Resilience Act, etc. Now, we must ensure these frameworks are enforced effectively, and our own tech gets adequate financing. We should become creators, not only regulators.

Cybersecurity and AI are our security issue too. Last year, Europe recorded thousands of major cyber incidents, largely traced back to actors in Russia and China. In my home country, Lithuania, we recorded nearly 4 000 incidents, averaging 10 attacks every single day. Advanced AI is now making these threats exponentially more dangerous.

So let me stress this: Europe's security and competitiveness are only as strong as the technology we control.

Kristian VIGENIN

Mr President, Commissioner, we cannot protect our hospitals, energy grids, public administrations and elections with tools that can disappear because of a decision taken in Washington or somewhere else outside the EU. Of course, we should cooperate with the United States, with companies and with other partners, but cooperation should never mean dependency.

I hope the action plan could answer three concrete questions. First, what does guarantee that the case with the ENISA and Anthropic will not happen again? Second, what is the timeline for building real European AI capability for cybersecurity, including for EU and national authorities, municipalities and companies? And third, where is the money?

So, Member States speak every day about security, defence and geopolitical threats, but then want to limit the EU budget when Europe needs the capacity to act. That is undermining our security while pretending to be sovereign. Digital sovereignty means public investment, democratic control and accountability, not simply subsidising a few private companies to build data centres in Europe.

We need an action plan with deadlines, funding and enforcement, not another strategy that sounds strong in Brussels, but leaving Europe vulnerable when the next surprises come.

Mélanie DISDIER

Mr President, dear colleagues, every contribution to technological innovation, every human advance has always been accompanied by its share of risks and new vulnerabilities. Artificial intelligence will be no exception.

Motivated by centuries of experience with technological risks, we would be well advised to ensure that AI does not become a new source of dependence for our nations. Europe, the cradle of the industrial revolution, was at the forefront of the major discoveries that shaped the modern world. Today, however, we have missed the digital turn, overtaken by the new giants that are the United States and China, and we will not catch up without rediscovering that European spirit which was once our engine. Yet we all know here the European Commission's formidable capacity to innovate in a single field: that of generating ever more standards, which stifle this European creative spirit.

So yes, caution is required, but not at any price. It will be of no use to impose binding standards on companies that we will never have managed to develop. It will be of no use to talk about resilience if we still depend on third countries in the fields of new technologies. We will therefore remain vigilant to ensure that the Commission does not use cybersecurity to justify its inaction, especially since, by risking stifling our entrepreneurs, the Commission could also crush European cybersecurity innovations.

Helmut BRANDSTÄTTER

Mr President, dear Commissioner, dear colleagues, always in those difficult times, I talk about good news. So, it's good news that there is an action plan for cybersecurity and AI. The good news is that we had a very interesting debate here. And the next good news is that I think most of us have understood it is not true that it's always the Americans who invent and we who have regulation. But yes, we have too much regulation. So please, less regulation, that's important.

The next thing we really have to do, and you said it also Commissioner, this capital investments union, we have understood it, everybody. So, please tell us: are there any states who don't want it? So, let's blame them and then let's talk about here why we still do not have that. That is necessary, especially for AI and for investments.

One more thing, of course, we rely too long on the United States. But finally, in this football or soccer game, now we understood that they don't play fair. So, we can't trust them and we can't trust the Chinese, that's also true.

But one more thing: this technology independence is basic for our democracy. People have to understand that. Also, we only have a common European policy together. It has nothing to do with centralism. It has to do that only as Europe together we can make it.

Damian BOESELAGER

Mr President, Executive Vice-President, colleagues, Europe is becoming a colony of the US and China. That is the clear message of the Europe 2031 simulation and similar ones looking into our immediate future.

They claim that all companies and governments will have to use frontier models to stay competitive and safe; that all labour is replaceable by the mix of AI and robotics, meaning that a significant part of our people will lose their jobs; that all the savings from the firings will be extradited to the US‑based models and Chinese robotics; that the US government will at some point soon redistribute AI gains to the workers that have been laid off in the US; and that Europe, without access to this redistribution, will fall into bankruptcy, poverty and despair before becoming fully bought by the US or China.

So my question to you, Commissioner, is, first, on a scale from 0 to 10, how likely do you think that this scenario is true? Second, how come we only spend EUR 50 billion of the ECF of a seven‑year industrial programme on AI? And third, what will we do to develop frontier models or these very good copycats here in Europe?

Regina DOHERTY

Mr President, Commissioner, for the first time, human activity has become the minority on the internet. More than half all of web traffic is now generated by bots, with almost 40 % of that traffic coming from malicious bots designed to scam, steal, manipulate or attack.

Maybe the dead internet theory is no longer so far-fetched. AI-powered bots are mimicking human behaviour, spreading disinformation, stealing personal data, carrying out sophisticated cyberattacks and generating explicit sexual material which is endangering our children.

Because behind every fake account and every AI-powered scam, we have to remember there is a real person, a real victim, being exploited. We also must stop AI being weaponised against our systems, and that includes Mythos' AI systems, which now risks becoming a global security threat.

We also must accept that if Europe does not develop its own AI capabilities, we're always going to be at the mercy of other countries that can shut off our access to AI software in a moment, as we have recently seen. But we must remember that strong cybersecurity systems do not mean centralising bureaucracy, and it is not about who gets to use what software and when in a supply chain framework.

We must detect and remove malicious bots. We require clear labelling of AI-generated content. And we can't allow platforms, when automated networks are involved, to operate unchecked.

Because if people can no longer tell what's real online, the internet becomes the perfect place and perfect weapon for criminals, hostile states and scammers, and Europe can't afford to let that happen.

Elena SANCHO MURILLO

Mr President, Madam Vice-President, thank you for presenting this action plan at a time when events surrounding the Mythos model once again demonstrate the degree of dependence of the European Union on external access to critical AI systems.

Given that we see it is not only Anthropic that decides whether to grant or deny access to advanced models because the Commission now directly stops asking the White House what political strategy to follow—it seems crazy, doesn't it?—I would like to know what the conclusion of the G7 discussions on artificial intelligence has been and what exactly the European Union has contributed in terms of cooperation to define common rules on artificial intelligence and new frontier models.

Bearing in mind that there are no international rules today, how does this affect the implementation of the Artificial Intelligence Act—whose application has already been delayed—in high-risk cases? AI governance must be developed with international collaboration, but without replacing and prioritizing our capacity to guarantee access, independent evaluation and legal certainty... (The President cuts off the speaker's microphone).

Fabienne KELLER

Mr President – dear Roberts Zīle –, Madam Vice-President – dear Henna Virkkunen –, the recent blocking of access to the most advanced artificial intelligence models has been a wake-up call for Europe. In a few hours, we discovered the extent to which our security, our administrations, our businesses depended on technologies that we do not control.

The European cybersecurity action plan, which we are delighted to discover – but I do not have artificial intelligence to read it, I have not yet been able to read everything –, must therefore integrate a genuine sovereignty strategy. This means: investing in European capabilities, supporting trusted models, guaranteeing secure access to the most advanced technologies, and strengthening our computing infrastructure. This means there is a need to answer an essential question: how can the Union face the risk that a third country could, overnight, restrict Europe's access to essential AI technologies?

Our goal is not to isolate ourselves, but to ensure that the protection of our citizens, their data, and their fundamental rights never depends on decisions made outside the Union.

Sven SIMON

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, ladies and gentlemen! Today we are talking about artificial intelligence, but in truth we are talking about Europe's future, and this future is currently being created elsewhere. Europe has only around 5% of global AI computing capacity; the United States of America is at almost 75%. American tech corporations are investing hundreds of billions in data centers, chips, networks, and energy. What is Europe doing? We are vetting, we are regulating, we are delaying.

AI needs more than good intentions; AI needs electricity, land, fiber optics, permits, and speed, and that is precisely where we are failing. And we have also heard in the debate that this is partly intended by political competitors. The AI Act, I think, stands for this European disease: first come the regulations, then perhaps value creation at some point.

This is not how Europe will become sovereign. We need disruptive decisions, the consistent dismantling of those vested interests that we have poured into laws over years and that today block almost every investment in the future.

Brando BENIFEI

Mr President, honourable colleagues, the "kill switch" is no longer a hypothesis: it has been pressed. In June, with a single signature, Donald Trump cut off access to the world's most powerful artificial intelligence model, even for the European Cybersecurity Agency, which had just obtained it.

Our rules decide how we can use artificial intelligence safely; today, others decide whether we can use it: this is dependence.

Therefore, the cybersecurity plan is good, but without funds and binding deadlines, it risks remaining a list of intentions. Resources are needed for the European Artificial Intelligence Office, which will have increasing responsibilities, a truly ambitious cloud and AI law, and European public capacity, not subsidies to the giants we already depend on.

And let no one dare think of buying access to American models by secretly easing the enforcement of our laws. European digital security must no longer be rented out to anyone; it must be built, with openness, but with determination, to defend our interests.

Engin EROGLU

Mr President! Dear Commissioner, I explicitly thank you for your report on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, because cybersecurity is changing massively through the use of artificial intelligence. And of course, the security authorities have their task there, just as in the public space, and of course politics must shape the framework so that security authorities can work.

Regarding what you did not say, however, Commissioner: You said nothing about quantum computers. What is the European Union's strategy on quantum computers? How do we protect our infrastructure in quantum computer technology that is coming towards us?

You also said nothing about the fact that, alongside the many criminals who operate as entrepreneurs to defraud other entrepreneurs, third countries also specifically deploy hackers to attack the European Union and its member states, specifically the Federal Government of Germany: Government authorities are attacked daily with 800 cyberattacks. There, we must not only repair, but also act; we must counter-attack cyberattacks from third countries. And my question is: What are you doing there? Have you held discussions with Mr Kubilius?

Nicola ZINGARETTI

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, honourable colleagues, the action plan that the Commission has just presented represents a non-definitive, but certainly important step on the path towards European technological sovereignty.

Autonomy is not autarky, of course, but it is leadership, because the Union cannot continue to depend on opaque processes and unilateral decisions by third countries.

And recent episodes linked precisely to restrictions on access to frontier models demonstrate how this vulnerability is today a security issue, even before being a competitiveness issue.

Europe, therefore, must build its own autonomous technological capacity in frontier artificial intelligence, and this requires a clear political choice.

Beyond the measures, however, that are finally being adopted, adequate investments, both public and private, are needed, capable of bridging the gap with the United States and China.

For this reason, the choice that governments made regarding a forward-looking budget for Europe is a mistake: it is timid, it is wrong, and in part in contradiction with the right choices we are making.

Without concrete resources, you do not get anywhere.

Sophia KIRCHER

Mr President, esteemed Executive Vice-President of the Commission, dear colleagues! AI and quantum computing will determine whether we are economically successful. Cybersecurity will determine whether we will still be able to act at all in the future. Therefore, we urgently need to set the course for the future.

It is positive that the Commission has now presented this action plan, but now it is all about implementation. And one thing is clear: our SMEs need more digital security, rapid assistance in emergencies and, above all, no new bureaucratic burdens. Europe must become digital, sovereign and competitive – with European cloud solutions, its own digital infrastructure and excellence in quantum computing. Because whoever develops the key technologies secures prosperity, competitiveness, jobs and also sets the rules of the game for our future.

And cyber skills must also find their way into our classrooms. They must be taught there as naturally as reading, writing and arithmetic, because the most important firewall sits in front of the screens.

The message is clear: digital sovereignty and security are not a technical question; they are the basis of our competitiveness, our security and our freedom.

Maria GUZENINA

Mr President, dear Commissioner, in Europe, in cybersecurity, our biggest vulnerability is believing that we are protected and that we have time, which we are not and which we do not have.

As the rapporteur for IMCO on the Cybersecurity Act 2, I welcome the action plan Commissioner Virkkunen has presented today. European society needs to be defended from all angles. Our cyber ecosystem needs to be protected urgently, but my worry is that the funding is not adequate.

Experts speak already of 'Q-Day': the day quantum computing becomes powerful enough to break the encryption that protects our banking system, critical infrastructure, weapon systems, communications and data. Hostile actors are already collecting our encrypted data, hoping to decrypt it as soon as possible.

So cybersecurity is not a matter just of national security. It's about economic resilience and, finally, democracy...

(The President cut off the speaker)

Sofie ERIKSSON

Mr President, things are going so fast. A lot of people feel like we are losing control, and billionaire oligarchs act like there is no choice. But to me, they sound like: 'We are the Borg. You will be assimilated. Resistance is futile.'

This endless race: catch up, keep up, don't fall behind. But the only question worth asking cannot be how fast we can plug ourselves into someone else's system. Our hospitals, our power grids, our most sensitive government data are dependent on systems we do not own and do not control.

The line must be drawn here. We welcome the action plan. We need our own public, accountable, democratically controlled capability, even if it's harder – because, unlike the humanoids assimilated by the Borg, we still get to choose our way forward: with technology, with democracy, with humanity.

José CEPEDA

Mr President, Mrs Virkkunen, I share this plan and, fundamentally, its three objectives, which speak of promoting, encouraging and fostering, but while these verbs are used in that plan, the reality is that the threat is already being carried out in real time.

Therefore, I would like to tell you that I believe it is very important to implement the NIS 2 Directive across the entire European system. We must demand, finance and also penalize, why not say so.

ENISA, which is the great pillar on which you base yourself, has a major deficit and that is that it proposes 341 million over seven years and, unfortunately, in practice in a year or a year and a half quantum computing is going to be here and that is going to be a major threat.

Look, I believe that apart from talking about critical infrastructure, we also have to talk about people. For example, the example given yesterday by the Government of Spain —with my dear friend Óscar López— by implementing a major coalition with France and Kenya, together with the United Nations, goes in that direction, precisely to also protect our minors from AI, which is a very important challenge for the future.

Salvatore DE MEO

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, honourable colleagues, the European action plan on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence represents a strategic choice to strengthen the Union's security, competitiveness and resilience.

Because protecting networks, critical infrastructure and our data means safeguarding our businesses and ensuring the continuity of essential services to citizens.

Artificial intelligence is a decisive lever for innovation, strategic autonomy and our security. At the same time, if used by hostile actors, it can turn into a tool capable of striking our systems, our economies and even our democracies.

For this reason, Europe must govern this process and not wait for its evolution. As authoritatively recalled by the encyclical letter "Magnifica Humanitas" by Pope Leo XIV, technological progress acquires its full value only when it is at the service of the human person and preserves their dignity.

For this reason, artificial intelligence must remain a tool in human hands and never a substitute for human judgment and responsibility. Only in this way will Europe be able to win the challenges of cybersecurity, building a stronger, protected and deeply free future.

Henna Virkkunen

Mr President, honourable Members, thank you for your interventions and very valuable comments. I think it is important to underline that, really, this action plan is not the end of our discussion, because this is now the real beginning of European efforts to ensure that AI becomes a strategic asset for our security, not a systematic vulnerability. And this is the European way for AI and cybersecurity: built on trust, transparency and safety. These are the conditions for ensuring that the most advanced AI models can be deployed in Europe safely, used for cybersecurity responsibly, and also turned into instruments of our security rather than weapons against our societies.

Many of you were underlining very much the importance of tech sovereignty and its crucial pillar in our action plan, really to scale and boost our own capabilities in this area. But, as you said, also, and I underlined, massive investments are really needed now and urgently in this area.

Also, the second priority in our action plan and an important pillar is, of course, to prepare our cybersecurity environment and also be able to fix the vulnerabilities fast. Here we will work very closely with our industries and Member States.

The third pillar is about evaluating, testing and having access to these capable models, and there we are also working with the blueprint. So we will need to move quickly. It is important to underline that now we have nine key actions identified here and seven of them we will implement now already during the autumn. We will work very closely with our Member States, with this House, with our industry, with the open‑source community, and with our international partners, of course, because this is a challenge that Europe cannot afford to face alone or too late.

Sunčana GLAVAK

Mr President, Commissioner, digital sovereignty is not a question of protectionism, but of resilience. The goal is not to replace one dependency with another, but to reduce strategic dependency and increase European competitiveness.

Therefore, I welcome the Commission's action plan because artificial intelligence is no longer just a driver of innovation, but also a new factor in European security. Today, more than 80 percent of phishing campaigns already use elements of generative artificial intelligence, and cyber threats are developing, unfortunately, faster than our defense systems.

Key questions lie ahead of us: will we invest enough, do we have the experts for coordination and for the protection of critical infrastructure, and are we ready for the transition to post-quantum cryptography before quantum computers threaten today's encryption systems, and are we finally doing enough to protect children and our personal data.

Juan Fernando LÓPEZ AGUILAR

Mr President, OpenAI, Mythos, Anthropos, frontier artificial intelligence... Why are they rebelling against the regulatory power of the European Union? Because they fear it.

Therefore, a cybersecurity strategy in artificial intelligence that is purely European must focus on what distinguishes it and precisely on what the mastodons fear: its transparency, its accountability, its subjection to fundamental rights. And it must also be explained that we do not do this out of panic of an unstoppable technological revolution, but because we care about human supervision, which is what makes them consistent with our standard of fundamental rights.

We are willing—of course we are—to reconvert our labor market knowing that artificial intelligence will have a tremendous impact on many jobs that now exist and will not exist the day after tomorrow. But what we are not willing to do is to have an algorithm impose a guilty verdict in justice. That is what differentiates the European model and what distinctively European artificial intelligence cybersecurity must preserve.

Sebastian TYNKKYNEN

Mr President, I will present a few statistics on artificial intelligence. In Finland, the proportion of companies using artificial intelligence has risen to almost 38 percent. Compared to the EU average, that is almost twice as much.

But what is actually stifling Europe's artificial intelligence development? The figures provide the answer. At the EU level, the usage percentage of large companies reaches up to 55 percent. Then comes the catch: at the EU level, only 30 percent of medium-sized and only 17 percent of small companies use artificial intelligence.

Complying with EU artificial intelligence regulations requires large resources that smaller companies simply do not have. Europe's role on the future international stage depends on how well we utilize the latest technology. This role begins to take shape when we stop being a superpower of regulation.

Lukas SIEPER

Mr President,

(Speaking into a smartphone)

Hey Mistral, what do you think about the action plan on cybersecurity and AI?

One second please.

(Reading from the smartphone)

'The European Commission's action plan on cybersecurity and AI, unveiled today, tackles AI's dual role, both as a cyberthreat and a defence tool. By Q4 2026, it will deliver a European blueprint for structured access to advanced AI models and a secure testing platform with ENISA, practical guidelines for AI-based threat protection and the EU Grand Challenge for home-grown solutions. Strengths: proactive, holistic, collaborative. Risks: uncertain access to US frontier models, ENISA's capacity to execute. With the AI Act's cybersecurity rules starting on 2 August, this plan is Europe's practical playbook. Verdict: the necessary execution speed will decide if Europe can lead on safe AI cybersecurity.'

Well, now, of course, everything in that is true except for the fact that this was pre-prepared, because European AI is way too slow to deliver this result within 10 seconds.

Petras GRAŽULIS

Mr President, ladies and gentlemen, you must still admit that Europe is regulated by the United States and China invests. We are unable to invest, we do not produce computers, we do not produce phones, we do not produce software, but when it comes to regulation, we regulate the best. Today, two regulations. Putin reminds me of the situation in Russia. Putin's dictatorship bans TikTok, and we regulate TikTok, WhatsApp, Telegram. It poses a danger to him. TikTok, artificial intelligence poses a danger to you. So how are you different from Russia? Nothing at all. Except that your regulation is democratic, and Putin's is dictatorial. Today you banned, having started the procedure, one of the parties that does not suit you. And Putin has long ago closed the parties that do not agree with his policy. Well, how are you different? You are no different. Also today you adopted another decision...

(The Chairman of the meeting takes the floor away from the speaker)

Ondřej DOSTÁL

Mr President, dear Commissioner, in the ASEAN Delegation of the European Parliament, we discussed the issue of cyber scamming in Myanmar. There are non-state actors, mafias, who run basically slave factories on cyber scams, targeting people all around the world, including in Europe.

So I spoke to diplomats from the region and received very positive replies from China, Cambodia and Myanmar itself, which now has a stable government, and they are genuinely willing to work on this issue with us. But the Commission told us we will not cooperate, we will not even speak to Myanmar because they are not a democratically elected government.

So I ask you, is it better to do virtue signalling and let a grand mass in Europe get scammed? Or is it better to work together on resolving this important problem?

Michał SZCZERBA

Mr. President! AI, artificial intelligence, is on the one hand a tool strengthening cybersecurity, but it is also a source of new challenges. What is important is, above all, cooperation, exchange of information, joint response mechanisms and coordination of actions. Mr. President Zīle, we can say together today: our task has been accomplished. We have the position of the European Parliament on an important regulation, which is military mobility, and next week we will jointly start interinstitutional negotiations.

But what I am particularly pleased with and what I would like to boast about before this High House is, above all, the fact that we included the issue of systems security along with communications security issues in our regulation. This is a very important basis for joint, further actions.

Roberts ZĪLE (Chair)

That concludes the item.

Laura BALLARÍN CEREZA

We socialists have stressed that Europe must strengthen its technological sovereignty in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. Twenty-first-century security also depends on the control of data, algorithms, and digital technologies, which is why Europe cannot depend on capabilities developed outside its borders. Although the European Commission's action plan on cybersecurity and artificial intelligence is valued, the S&D Group has pointed out that regulation is not enough: it is necessary to increase public investment, support European companies, and apply effective measures to guarantee security, which includes compliance with regulations such as the NIS 2 Directive. We have also warned about new threats, such as quantum computing, and stressed the importance of protecting not only critical infrastructure, but also citizens—especially minors—from the risks of artificial intelligence.

Vasile DÎNCU

Cybersecurity and artificial intelligence influence each other and must be conceived as part of the same European security strategy. The action plan can be strengthened through a few very concrete measures.

All artificial intelligence systems used in public administration and critical infrastructure should be subject to independent audits before deployment and periodic evaluations after commissioning.

Europe needs a common alert and rapid information exchange mechanism regarding cyber incidents and AI vulnerabilities, because time is often more important than resources.

Another priority is investment in people. The shortage of cybersecurity specialists is becoming a strategic vulnerability. We need European training programs, joint exercises, and better circulation of expertise between member states.

We cannot ignore the impact on democracy either. AI makes possible the industrial-scale production of manipulative content, informational attacks, and disinformation campaigns. Democratic resilience must be part of European cybersecurity policy.

Technological autonomy is not a slogan. If Europe's digital infrastructure depends on technologies we do not control, our vulnerability remains structural. This is why investment in European capabilities must become a strategic priority.

Commission report on Ukraine

Nicolae ȘTEFĂNUȚĂ (Chair)

Good afternoon, colleagues. It is my honour to chair the next point.

The next item on the agenda is the report by Mr Michael Gahler, on behalf of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, on the Commission's 2025 Report on Ukraine (2025/2259(INI)) (A10-0172/2026). I would like to remind speakers that, given the testing measures, strict compliance with the speaking time will be required.

Michael GAHLER

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues! Ukraine and the Ukrainians are on their way into the European Union. This path is irrevocable because the Ukrainians want it and because we want it too. It is in our mutual interest that this European nation finds its place in the community of free peoples of Europe. Imperialist Russia, led by a man who, after Hitler and Stalin, is committing the third-largest crimes of modern European history against Ukrainians and his own people, will not prevent this. Russia will fail historically when Ukraine is on the path to the EU.

The first cluster of negotiation chapters is open. I think it would be a good signal to ideally open the others at the next European Council as well. That does not cut corners; it does not replace the necessity to fulfill the prerequisites for accession in terms of content. However, it would be another clear signal to Ukrainians, EU citizens, and the aggressor Russia that there is no way back into the Soviet Gulag, but rather forward into a shared European future.

In this report, which is supported essentially by five political groups and a number of other Members beyond that, we make clear where Ukraine stands on its way to the EU. To this end, we have used a multitude of sources, but above all we have practiced dialogue with those politically responsible in Kyiv, in the regions down to the municipal level, and of course with our own representatives on the ground and in Brussels, and with the strong and impressively competent Ukrainian civil society.

This paints a clear picture of what needs to be done. All institutions relevant to the rule of law must be strengthened or reformed. That means anti-corruption agencies must be able to carry out their work independently. The supreme courts must be staffed following a transparent selection process. University graduates who have qualified for judicial office must renew the judiciary from the bottom up. The Prosecutor General's Office does not have the task of issuing instructions to the anti-corruption agencies. The secret service must fight enemies of the state. Anti-corruption agencies are not enemies of the state, but rather fight those who have a false understanding of the state; it can therefore not be the task of the secret service to spy on anti-corruption agencies. A State Bureau of Investigation should not appeal to a district court to prevent the publication of the result of an investigative journalistic report concerning the director's brother. Elected politicians are not public employees; civil service law does not apply to them; they therefore cannot be sanctioned with civil service law measures; the free exercise of a mandate is a high good even in times of war.

Since for all parties in the Verkhovna Rada, alongside the EU accession process, fighting the aggressor Russia is the top priority, I advise concentrating domestic political disputes or tactical games on the time after the end of hostilities and the preparation for elections, and instead standing together against the aggressor.

And here the accession process comes into play once again: we must realize that alongside the traditional merit-based approach—that is, progress in accordance with the fulfillment of the acquis—a geopolitical dimension is being added, and this is increasingly in our interest as well. It is Ukraine that is buying us the time to become capable of defending ourselves against the threat posed by the aggressor Russia. The Ukrainians are currently the only ones who can stop Russia.

This results in an overall perspective that brings the Ukrainians and us together in the interest of jointly shaping both processes after the end of the state of war—EU accession and a mutual security guarantee that we will stand up for each other even before EU or NATO membership. Not a direct, but a corresponding application of Article 42 Paragraph 7, which applies not only from us toward Ukraine, but also from Ukraine toward us. Only together are we strong enough. Slawa Europa! Slawa Ukrajini!

Marta Kos

Mr President, honourable Members, thank you, dear rapporteur, Michael Gahler, for your report and for your engagement on Ukraine at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks against Ukraine. As it struggles to achieve its objectives on the battlefield, it is important to remember what this war is ultimately about. This is not only a war over territory. It is a war about Ukraine's right to choose its own future – a sovereign nation that has chosen democracy, has chosen Europe, and has chosen the path towards membership of the European Union. That is a choice Moscow does not accept. Ukraine's European future is about the security, stability and prosperity of our entire continent.

Just two weeks ago, at the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Gdańsk, I met with Ukrainian defence companies. I saw first‑hand an industry that is producing some of the world's most advanced drones at remarkable speed and with an extraordinary capacity for innovation. This is why we are deepening cooperation between the European and Ukrainian defence industries. Ukraine is already facilitating exports of military technologies to the European Union, and this cooperation will continue to expand.

For example, through the Ukraine investment framework, we have also started promoting joint projects with Member States by providing guarantees that support dual‑use production, helping to integrate our industrial bases and strengthen Europe's defence readiness. Ukraine has become a fundamental pillar of Europe's security architecture. The courage of the Ukrainian people and their military innovation are already strengthening Europe's security today, and this brings me to enlargement.

Security and enlargement cannot be seen as two separate agendas. They are two sides of the same coin. A stronger, more secure Europe requires a credible enlargement policy, and a credible enlargement policy strengthens our collective security. We must get this right. That is why the accession process will remain rigorous, fair and firmly merit based. This principle is not negotiable. Over the past years, Ukraine has maintained a consistent reform trajectory and continued aligning with the EU acquis. Across all the negotiating chapters, we have seen no backsliding or stagnation. Good or some progress has been recorded in 27 out of 33 chapters assessed. This reflects sustained political commitment under exceptionally difficult circumstances.

At the same time, further efforts remain necessary. Particularly on the fundamentals, Ukraine must continue strengthening the fight against corruption, as you have said, upholding the rule of law, ensuring the effective functioning of democratic institutions and advancing public administration reform. I have made this clear in all my exchanges with the Ukrainian authorities, Parliament and also civil society. The interim benchmarks for the rule of law for cluster one, together with the roadmaps adopted last year, provide a solid framework to guide these reforms. The Commission will continue to monitor progress closely and provide the support needed to maintain reform momentum.

The opening of the first cluster on 15 June was an important milestone and, for many in the Hall at that time, very emotional. It demonstrated the actual progress is possible when reforms deliver results. Our objective should now be to open the remaining negotiating clusters as soon as possible, building on the extensive preparatory work already undertaken. At the same time, while Ukraine advances on its accession path, we should continue exploring every possible avenue for gradual integration, for instance under the Association Agreement, enabling Ukraine and its citizens to benefit progressively from closer integration with the Union even before accession is completed.

Honourable Members, we should not forget the bigger picture and have it all the time inside. Ukraine's accession is an investment in a stronger, safer and resilient Europe. It is not just about Ukraine: it is also about us. So let us remain united and continue walking this path together with Ukraine. This can only be for the benefit of Ukraine, for the benefit of the EU and for the security of all us Europeans.

Andrzej HALICKI

Mr President! We all want Ukraine to win against Putin. The criminal Russian army attacked Ukraine because Ukrainians want a European future for their country. And we want a European Ukraine. We want and believe that this can happen. Of course, consistent action is needed for this. That is why reforms are so important, why it is so important to base the state on the rule of law, on a real, genuine, consistent fight against corruption, because no euro can be transferred and embezzled.

But it is also necessary to respect common European values, because in the Community one cannot glorify those who based their past, their activity on the fight against minorities, on genocidal actions. If we recall this fact as the European Parliament, we recall it to state one message once again: you choose your future. But if you want to be in the Community, you must respect those values that are described in Article 2 and truly promote what is our common European principle.

There is no room for glorifying criminals. No euro can be spent on those units that bear the name of criminals responsible for genocide. The European future lies in your hands.

Mr President, Ukraine is squeezing the Russian economy. It regains territory, despite dire front-line conditions. Putin is lashing out with deadly strikes on cities where air defence ammunition has run out.

Europe needs four things now more than ever: vigilance, focus, unity and resolve.

Vigilance: we need vigilance because Russia wants to break our support for Ukraine. Further probing, a false flag, stoking bilateral disputes to split our unity – even a minor incursion. Let us signal clearly that the cost of any probe or incursion will be catastrophic, almost non-European, and it will only bring more backing for Ukraine.

Focus: we need focus because Member States must stop ignoring accession non-papers, and start empowering Ukraine's EU membership. That means backing reforms, making accession a truly credible perspective with immediate interim steps, proving there is no turning back, and also a clear trajectory to the finish line. It also includes building a security architecture with Ukraine rooted in our shared future.

Unity: because Europe must act and speak as one – on accession, on defence support, on the shadow fleet, on banning any dual-use exports, on peace talks. Our report calls for a European negotiator to protect our interests and help defend Ukraine and end Russia's war, not to normalise relations. There can be no normalisation without respect for Ukraine's territorial integrity, without justice, accountability and reparations, and without an end to Russia's hybrid war on Europe.

And finally, resolve: as long as our response to Russia killing civilians is broken, allow me to be a broken record. Air defence, deep strike capabilities and jointly operated sky shields – they save Ukrainian lives. Our statements do not. Europe must be unwavering in words and deeds.

Mr. President, Commissioner, I'm speaking Portuguese.

We stand, without hesitation, alongside the Ukrainian people, alongside mothers who have lost sons, a people who saw their land invaded, their cities destroyed, and their future suspended. Russian aggression must be condemned with all clarity, as we would condemn it if it were our own country.

The sovereignty and independence of Ukraine cannot be a bargaining chip, and no peace can be negotiated without Ukraine. But standing with Ukraine also means telling the truth. The best thing for Ukraine is not an endless war. The best thing is a just, secure, and lasting peace, a peace that arrives as soon as possible.

Reconciliation requires truth. Ukraine should unequivocally condemn the UPA ideology that led to mass crimes, and enable full exhumations and a dignified burial of all victims. Historical truth is not an obstacle to reconciliation, nor is it an obstacle on the path to Europe. On the contrary, it is its foundation. Only on the foundation of truth and mutual respect can we build a common European future.

The claim that Ukraine has failed to meet any of the core criteria for joining the European Union is false; the EU granted Ukraine candidate status in 2022, officially opened accession negotiations in 2024, and opened the first negotiating cluster on 'Fundamentals' in June 2026, repeatedly recognizing the country's progress in implementing key reforms.

AI-assisted fact check

The claim that the EU is violating the 2016 legally binding declaration by advancing Ukraine's accession is false; that declaration only clarified that the EU-Ukraine Association Agreement itself did not confer candidate status or commit the EU to future membership, and it did not restrict Ukraine from applying for membership under Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union, which is the legal basis for its current accession process.

The claim that the EU's mutual assistance clause (Article 42.7 TEU) would immediately put the EU at war with Russia if Ukraine accedes is misleading, as the clause does not automatically trigger a state of war or require direct military intervention, instead leaving the specific response to individual capitals and explicitly respecting the security policies of neutral member states.
