However, this process must be based on mutual respect, democratic principles and historical truth. I emphasise: historical truth. Without truth there will be no reconciliation. Without reconciliation there will be no lasting cooperation.

Dear Ukrainians, there are no shortcuts to the European Union. We went down this path earlier and we tell you this with all the responsibility that responsible politicians should play. And those who try to make us believe that Ukraine's security is contrary to Poland's security are repeating a narrative straight from the Kremlin. Anyone who does not understand this is an ignorant person or a fool. Both push us straight into Putin's fire.

André FRANQUEIRA RODRIGUES

Mr President, I was in Kyiv a few days ago. I saw a country at war that does not stop: Parliament meets, institutions reform themselves, civil society monitors. But I bring a warning: beware of managing expectations.

Promising dates that we do not meet undermines trust, and it is this trust that we need to strengthen: that of Ukrainians in us and that of European citizens in this process.

Now, this trust is built on balance - demand in the rule of law reforms, the fight against corruption, judicial independence and unequivocal support, without hesitation, without mince words. Demanding without supporting is abandonment, supporting without demanding is illusion. The Union's credibility lies in this balance.

Ukraine resists and, with it, we must transform words into actions, actions into reforms, reforms into accession.

Tomasz BUCZEK

Mr President! During World War II in Volhynia and Eastern Lesser Poland, UPA gangs committed one of the most cruel genocides in European history. Innocent Poles, civilians, including the elderly, women and children, were murdered in a way that exceeds human imagination. They were burned alive in locked barns and churches, sawed alive, pregnant mothers had their stomachs cut open, tearing out children and sewing cats in their place so that the women would die in unimaginable suffering. Small children were nailed with knives, nails to the doors of houses, victims had their eyes gouged out, their heads scalped, and their bodies torn apart with axes and pitchforks.

Entire Polish villages and families were murdered by their Ukrainian neighbours. Their homes were looted and burned. This was a bestial ethnic cleansing. With animal brutality, Ukrainians, who at that time were Hitler's allies, murdered over 100,000 Poles. To this day, the Ukrainian state does not allow them to be buried.

And today President Zelenskyy honours units of the Ukrainian army by naming them after UPA heroes. And yet they are mere barbarians. This scandalous provocation cannot pass without a condemning voice coming from the European Parliament. Down with the cult of murderers, with Bandera, Shukhevych and the UPA. With the cult of genocide and ethnic cleansing, Ukraine will never be part of...

(The President withdrew the speaker's right to speak)

AI-assisted fact check

Although the historical massacres of Poles by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) are well-documented, the claim that Ukraine does not allow the victims to be buried is false; the Ukrainian government has authorized and actively cooperated with Poland on joint search, exhumation, and reburial efforts, including the dignified reburial of 55 victims in August 2026.

Aurelijus VERYGA

Madam President, dear colleagues. Today, the enlargement of the European Union is not just the expansion of a common economic and political space. It is also a struggle over whose sphere of influence the candidate countries will or will not fall into once the membership process is completed. A warring Ukraine is carrying out reforms that other candidates had the luxury of carrying out in peacetime. Reading the report sometimes gives the impression that Ukraine is being pushed to achieve goals that the European Union itself is beginning to doubt. Agree that in a warring state where the aggressor daily bombards strategic objects and kills civilians, it is very difficult to talk about the green agenda and reducing climate change. Therefore, a sober assessment of the situation is needed. A state that resists the aggressor Russia and manages to make its citizens feel the price of the war caused by their own country is at the same time making huge progress towards European Union membership. Observing the political processes of recent weeks or months, I want to wish all of us a cold mind and political insight so that principledness does not become a gift to Europe's enemies.

Michał KOBOSKO

Madam President! Difficult, most painful historical issues, such as the UPA crime committed against Polish civilians, exist and must not be ignored. Without working through them, we will not go any further. Responsibility for the increase in tension lies on both sides. Both in the actions of President Zelenskyy, who fueled nationalist narrative, and in the actions of President Nawrocki.

A great achievement of trust built between our nations has been put at stake, including Poland's huge contribution to helping Ukraine. I observe with regret that at a moment of historical opportunity, which is Ukraine's future accession to the European Union, we are devoting more and more attention to divisions. Because of this, we are not focusing on the greatest threat, which is Russia, and on the positives that the enlargement of the Community can bring. Together with my colleagues, for two months we have been working on amendments to this report, which concerned the development of investments in roads, railways, energy, also in border states such as Poland.

Today, above all, we need responsibility and the calming of emotions. Poland and Ukraine have a common interest: the security, stability and development of Central and Eastern Europe. This is a real European perspective. Together we will win or together we will lose everything.

Mika AALTOLA

Mr President, Commissioner, time is running out. Russia does not move just one piece at a time. It looks at the whole board, and right now it sees a gap. American support is weakening. Our own joint defence is still in its infancy. Russia is currently thrusting its hands into that gap and testing our readiness.

We have one ally that can decide the game: Ukraine. It is not asking for security, it is providing it. Ukraine already knows what we are still spelling out, and it has paid for its lesson in blood. It has knowledge, skill, and courage that must not be left unutilised.

That is why the German Chancellor's proposal for associate membership is the right move at the right time. It is not watered-down membership, but an intermediate stage. It binds Ukraine more closely into our defence precisely when we need it most. Passivity is a move we hand over to the opponent, and Russia reads every hesitation as weakness.

Giorgio GORI

Madam President, honourable colleagues, Russia is not winning the war in Ukraine; on the contrary, bolstered by its moral resilience, Kyiv has been able to transform its inferiority into a structural capacity for innovation.

For Russia, it was supposed to be a demonstration of power. Instead, it is a carnage from which derives the erosion of the prestige upon which Putin's power rests. It is also the failure of those who continued to write off Ukraine, opposed the sending of military aid, and advocated a pseudo-peace equivalent to submission.

Russia is not winning, but this is no reason to slacken European support. The inability to achieve a victory on the field leads Moscow to intensify its bombings of Ukrainian cities and hybrid actions against the countries of the Union and NATO.

The real stake at the Ankara summit is therefore the cohesion of the alliance and its deterrence capacity. Structural support for Ukraine and the consolidation of a European defense pillar are objectives that are also ours, which we must support with great determination.

Ewa ZAJĄCZKOWSKA-HERNIK

Madam President! Over 360 ways of murdering civilians. Sawing people alive, ripping open the bellies of pregnant women, impaling children on pitchforks – this is how the UPA murdered Poles, Jews, Czechs, Armenians, and Ukrainians themselves. And today Zelenskyy names a military unit after UPA heroes, builds a state pantheon, and declares that Ukraine will choose its own heroes. It is a pity that it chooses them from among Nazis.

If Germany named a unit after SS heroes and erected monuments to Hitler, Himmler, Goebbels, or Eichmann, would you invite them to the Union? No! You would call them neo-Nazis. And rightly so. There is no moral difference between venerating the SS and venerating the UPA. The same cult of force, the same ethnic hatred.

The report on Ukraine is silent on this matter. It is a silence that murders the memory of the victims of the genocide in Volhynia and the Eastern Borderlands for the second time. Ukraine's march to Europe with genocidal killers on its banners is a disgrace. As Poles, we should never agree to Ukraine's entry into Europe. Down with Banderite Nazism!

Małgorzata GOSIEWSKA

of Russian war crimes in Ukraine. I ask, however, what about the crimes of Ukrainian nationalists from the period of World War II? What about the children, women, and old people murdered just because they were Poles? Thrown into nameless pits without a cross, a name, or respect. The genocide committed by the OUN and UPA in the name of a nationalist ideology modeled on German Nazism.

Over 100,000 Poles, but also Jews, Czechs, Belarusians, and Ukrainians saving their neighbors. There were such people. The symbols of these crimes are Bandera and Shukhevych, Zelenskyy's heroes, and in fact the beasts responsible for these crimes.

Today, Ukraine proclaims that these were formations fighting against the Soviets. The facts, however, are more complex. In the years 1944–53, about 3,000 Soviet soldiers and officers lost their lives at the hands of the Ukrainian underground. 8,000 Soviets, and on the other hand over 100,000 Poles. So yes – for aid to Ukraine, but definitely no – for Ukraine's membership in the European Union without the recognition of historical truth and with Bandera on its banners.

Lukas SIEPER

Madam President, dear people of Europe! Last week I was in a bombed-out house in Kyiv. That made me think of a song, and it goes like this:

My friends are Iranians.

My friends are from Gaza.

My friends are Ukrainians, Russians.

And Americans.

My friends say politics ruins this world.

My friends perceive the lust for power as nothing but filth.

Their enemies are the Trumps, Netanyahus and Khameneis.

Their enemies are Hamas, Putins.

All with missiles.

Their enemies have nothing to do with normal people.

Sow hatred upon the earth and spill blood upon it.

My friends scream.

Free Palestine.

Free Iran.

My friends hate war.

Yet they are not radical.

Their enemies are not Jews and Muslims or Christians.

Their enemies are dictators and fascists.

Who incite us against each other, look, we are going round in circles.

How often in history did we pay the same price.

I am sick of it!

Because a human being has emotions.

Yet what they are capable of.

Makes them more like demons!

Slava Ukraini!

Matej TONIN

Madam President, Ukraine is not only writing its history today, it's writing our shared European future. Ukraine has already reached 84 % implementation of the Association Agreement. Yet some still play games with vetoes instead of building a common Europe.

EU enlargement is not a charity. It is a strategic necessity. A bigger Europe is a stronger Europe. But the process is not just one way. We, the existing Member States, must also keep our word. We cannot demand everything from Ukraine while hiding behind vetoes and excuses ourselves.

Promises we do not keep destroy our credibility. The time has come for courage. The time has come for determination. The time has come to say it clearly: Ukraine belongs to the EU.

Heléne FRITZON

Madam President! Russia's brutal war against Ukraine demands our continued and solidary support. At the same time, we must do more to weaken Putin's war machine. EU countries must stop buying Russian gas.

The EU must also put a stop to the Russian shadow fleet that bypasses the sanctions. It is a threat to both safety and the environment in our seas.

We must never, ever forget the war's most innocent victims: the children. Tens of thousands of Ukrainian children have been forcibly deported from their homes, and we demand that Russia immediately and safely return all kidnapped children to their homes.

Finally: Ukraine shows an impressive belief in the future. Despite the war, purposeful work is underway for a green reconstruction and a build-up of renewable energy. The EU must be there. We must support them and welcome them into the European community. Slava Ukraini.

Anna ZALEWSKA

Madam President! 100,000 murdered Polish women and men is not a Polish-Ukrainian issue, moreover a "historical" one. Honoring the murderers of Poles is not a Polish-Ukrainian conflict. It is a provocation.

A provocation not only aimed at Poland, which after all has always been an advocate and supporter of Ukraine. But a provocation against European values, because these are European values enshrined in the treaties. No one can build relations with the European Union on such values. It is as if we allowed Germany to glorify Hitler and his criminals back again.

We want an end to the war, because after all, this is a basic condition to enter the European Union. We want the borders to be settled, because this is another condition to join the European Union. Finally, we want real negotiations. And what are we proposing? Tell Europe this: point 102 – opening borders and free trade. You are talking about the fact that CBAM, i.e. the border tax, has ceased to be important. Throw it in the trash, because products from all over the world through Ukraine will reach Europe without any restrictions...

(The President revoked the speaker's floor)

Ingeborg TER LAAK

Madam President, it is easy to promise Ukraine a future in Europe. The question is: how are we going to fulfill that promise together with Ukraine?

Ukraine is a country at war. Precisely for this reason, the accession process demands urgency. We need Ukraine for our security. At the same time, the accession process must proceed carefully to guarantee the stability of Europe.

Ukraine is not an ordinary candidate member state. The country has an agricultural area larger than that of France. This offers many opportunities for Europe's future bio-economy. At the same time, the gross domestic product per capita is well below the European average.

Ukraine's accession means a modernization of Europe. Otherwise, our promises will remain mere promises, without substance.

Liudas MAŽYLIS

Madam President, Commissioner, colleagues. While facing unprecedented war pressure, Ukraine is successfully strengthening democratic institutions, carrying out judicial reforms, striving to fight corruption and proving that it is capable of responsibly absorbing every euro of support. Meanwhile, the European Union must, it should have already opened the remaining negotiation clusters, continue to provide financial support and further tighten sanctions against Russia, including the fight against sanctions evasion. Today, Ukrainians attacked several more sanctioned shadow Russian tankers, but we are still far from systemic prevention. Russia's shadow fleet still transports two-thirds of Russia's oil exports. We must increase pressure by ensuring the continuous systemic destruction of Russia's economy, their banking system, and the confiscation of frozen assets so that the Russians finally stop their aggression.

Seán KELLY

Mr President, this is a matter of real importance to all of us.

Therefore, our support for Ukraine must continue to be unconditional and unwavering. This support must remain unconditional even where this brings economic or political challenges for all of us. Ukraine is defending all of Europe, and we must take every single measure possible to choke the Russian economy and ensure nothing we do in the EU enhances its ability to maintain this war.

I support the strongest possible sanctions against Russia and we must build on this in the 21st package, and also on our energy independence. Yesterday, we saw more deadly missile and drone attacks in Kyiv – another stark reminder of the horrors that the Ukrainian people must live with.

On Ukraine's accession: reforms are needed. Enlargement is and must remain merit-based. But we should applaud Ukraine for the work it is doing to make reform after reform, whilst under constant bombardment from Russia.

As regards peace, I will quote Warren Buffett: 'you can't do good business with a bad person'.

Be careful, win the war and we will achieve war and lasting peace.

Jan FARSKÝ

Madam President, twelve years ago, Putin attacked Ukraine. He wanted to stop Ukraine from joining the EU. Since then, hundreds of thousands of people have died. Millions of lives are broken. But Putin has not defeated Ukraine. He has made it stronger. With EU and US support, Ukraine is not just resisting, it is growing stronger – in security, in industry, in technology.

Since the war began, the EU has given Ukraine over EUR 200 billion. Ukraine needs this money to defend itself. But the EU needs Ukraine too – to keep Europe safe. If we are not safe, money means nothing.

The question is not 'Who needs who more?' We need each other, and Ukraine should join the EU as soon as possible.

Alice TEODORESCU MÅWE

Madam Speaker, Ukraine has proven that it is possible to strike at the heart of Russia. Through precision attacks against refineries, military bases and other strategic infrastructure, the cost of Putin's war is raised.

Europe has an obligation to give Ukraine more of the long-range missiles and weapon systems that make a difference. Our duty is not only to help Ukraine survive, but to make Russia too weak to be able to continue its war of aggression.

The Gripen cooperation between Sweden and Ukraine shows that individual countries can lead the way. Now political restrictions on attacks against legitimate military targets in Russia must be abolished. At the same time, we must transition from sending equipment to building a joint defense industry with Ukraine, and make Ukrainian companies a natural part of Europe's defense market.

Leadership is not about failing to show the way when others hesitate. It is about acting more forcefully to secure peace in Europe. Slava Ukraini.

Michał SZCZERBA

Madam President! We are adopting a very important report concerning European Union–Ukraine relations. We are evaluating a candidate. The formal process of accession negotiations with Ukraine has begun. It was unblocked after a long period. This decision was unity and it also has our full support.

But the Union is not only a common market, not only Schengen, not only a budget, it is above all values. And this must be stated outright. In the discussion about a common future, one matter has remained unresolved. The European Union is formed by states and societies that have managed to overcome the demons of the past and face evil in truth. And truth has always been the foundation for reconciliation and cooperation.

Ukraine and its elites must resolve this matter. This is not a matter between Poland and Ukraine. This is about European values. There is no consent to referencing individuals and formations responsible for the crimes of genocide. This matter must also resonate in this report.

Juan Fernando LÓPEZ AGUILAR

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, this intense and prolonged debate on Ukraine highlights two pieces of evidence that need to be expressed.

The first is that the connection between supporting Ukraine's defense against Russia's aggression and the negotiations for future accession is so close that it cannot be resolved unless the European Union matures enough and grows enough to be seated at the negotiation table that will decide Ukraine's future and establish a dignified and honorable peace for this neighboring country that aspires to accession.

The second is that this accession cannot simply be resolved as a matter of examining its individual merits in the rule of law and the fight against corruption, but it will be necessary—sooner rather than later—to also bring into the debate the institutional reforms that make it possible to create the space to accommodate all accession candidates and, particularly, a country as huge, with such significant agriculture, and with rule of law and corruption-fighting problems as important as those represented by Ukraine.

Piotr MÜLLER

Madam President! It is obvious that Russia is a huge threat to Europe, including Ukraine, as we see in the military actions that this country is waging against Ukraine. However, we must also realize, when we discuss the report on Ukraine here today, that any steps by Ukraine towards Europe must be preceded by the truth. And I am unfortunately shocked by the decision made by President Zelenskyy, deciding on the step he took, that is, naming one of the Ukrainian units after the UPA, i.e., war criminals who murdered over 100,000 Poles during World War II.

Without a clear declaration by the European Parliament that this was a genocide, without a clear declaration by the European Parliament that there is no consent to honor such persons as Bandera, we cannot talk about the future European integration, deeper with Ukraine. This must resound today. And therefore I appeal to my colleagues from all political groups, also to colleagues from Poland, to support the amendments submitted by the ECR group.

Dainius ŽALIMAS

Madam President, dear colleagues, I would like to address the deplorable tensions between Poland and Ukraine of historical memory; and it echoes today as well.

We must not fall into this trap. I would recall the example set by Lithuania and Poland in their Treaty on friendly relations and good neighbourly cooperation. The Treaty openly acknowledged that our two nations could hold different interpretations of their shared history. Yet it also affirmed that an awareness of both the good and bad chapters of our past should strengthen mutual understanding.

More than 30 years later, this formula continues to guide the relationship between Lithuania and Poland. I also believe it offers the approach we need today: the courage to accept that history may be interpreted differently while choosing reconciliation over resentment. We must not allow Russia to divide us.

Reinier VAN LANSCHOT

Madam President, colleagues, dear Commissioner, the EU is a unique geopolitical force: the only one that doesn't grow through conquest. We grow because countries freely decide to join. Ukraine chooses the EU for its promise of democracy, freedom and dignity.

But sometimes this can create a wrong perception. Just because countries aspire to join our Union doesn't mean that we are the only side with something to offer. Ukraine does not come to the EU empty-handed. On the contrary, since the start of the war, the script has flipped. Ukraine has shown us extraordinary innovation, courage and above all, resilience. Right now, Ukraine has the strongest army in Europe and is the world leader on drone technology. Guess who we ask for help when drones are flying over Europe?

Especially with Ukraine, people mistake a decision of geopolitical survival for charity work. So let's make it clear: both Ukraine and the EU are stronger together.

Luis-Vicențiu LAZARUS

Madam President, dear colleagues, I knew that when a country joins the European Union, it has to meet certain criteria and we must think logically, without any collateral issues: Does Ukraine meet these criteria? For example, does Ukraine respect the rights of minorities? I have heard here from all my colleagues that it does not. I can also tell you about the Romanian minority, and it is the second minority in Ukraine, after the Russian minority, that it has suffered all sorts of misfortunes and that our priests have been beaten, arrested and accused of all the nonsense in the world there.

Not a single one is condemned today for anything, because none of it was true. Does Ukraine respect freedom of expression? There was a colleague here who said it is not true that Zelenskyy closed some television stations in 2021. I am telling you that he did close them and they are called ZIK, NewsOne and 112. They were the opposition television stations at the time, which opposition was very close to coming in first place. Of course, we can say whatever we want, but Ukraine (...)

(The President withdrew the speaker's floor)

AI-assisted fact check

The claim that the Romanian minority is the second largest in Ukraine and that no accused priests have been convicted is false; official census data shows Belarusians are the second-largest minority (with Romanians at 0.3%), and Ukrainian courts have convicted multiple priests of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church—which includes Romanian-speaking parishes—for offenses such as collaboration and justifying Russian aggression.

Vytenis Povilas ANDRIUKAITIS

Madam President, dear Commissioner, colleagues, the European Union proposed clear possible timelines in the Ukrainian accession to the EU. I can tell you: in June 2026, the opening of all six clusters; until the end of 2026, substantial progress in all negotiating chapters; beginning 2027, start of closing all chapters.

And where are we now? Only one cluster was opened. It's a shame on the Council, and today we see certain Member States in the Council finding new reasons to stop the Ukrainian accession. The Council must stop doing this! It is a rotating veto dressed up as a national interest defence. It is our promise to press the Council, to fulfil obligations and to follow the timelines.

Michael GAHLER

Madam President, colleagues, thank you for all the contributions. The message to Ukrainians is clear: the commitment for your country stands firm from a large majority in this House. That is also because Ukraine has already achieved so much on the reform path. There is no comparison to 2014.

I regret that the focus of the debate was partly diverted from the accession-related issues to the designation of a Ukrainian special forces unit as 'Heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army'.

Let me be clear: I think this was a wrong move, a political mistake, as it hurts the feelings of Polish citizens and the descendants of other victims. The fact that these UPA groups were fighting also against Stalin, and in favour of Ukrainian statehood, can by no means balance, neutralise or even justify the atrocities that have been committed.

No person, no organisation, can be selectively judged for what they have done. But what is more important than assessing the tragic past is the shared will to address the common future.

In this regard, I welcome the statement from Prime Minister Tusk from the outset, and also later during the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Gdańsk, and on other occasions, and the meeting of the Foreign Ministers, Sikorski and Sybiha, showing the will to resolve the existing tensions.

Steps in this regard had already been taken earlier, and I call on all concerned to refrain from further verbal or political escalation. Such verbal radicalism from the extreme right only makes Putin happy and serves no constructive purpose. We cannot change the past, but we have to assess it in full, especially each nation's painful periods, and promise ourselves for the future: never again.

It is good to leave the historic assessment to historians, perhaps not only from the two countries concerned, but add experts from third countries who are sometimes more independent in their findings.

Coming from the country that inflicted the most atrocities on other nations in the 20th century, I am grateful that the European Union's purpose and legacy is that those who are inside will never again inflict such horror on each other.

So it is good to be all together for a better future and stand together against our real enemies, which are not inside, but outside.

Pina PICIERNO (Chair)

The debate is closed.

The vote will take place tomorrow, Wednesday, 8 July 2026.

Ľubica KARVAŠOVÁ

The European integration of Ukraine strengthens our entire region and creates space for shared prosperity. From Kyiv, through Košice, to Dublin.

We need a stable, secure, and prosperous Ukraine in our neighborhood, not a destroyed country controlled by Russia. If Ukraine prospers, our regions that directly border it will also prosper. The Prešov and Košice regions can benefit from new investments and business opportunities and better transport connections, as well as profit from cross-border cooperation.

Support for Ukraine is in our best interest. Indeed, it is also support for Slovakia's future. And those who say otherwise are harming not only Ukraine, but also Slovakia and its interests.

Ewa KOPACZ

At least twenty thousand, and perhaps even thirty-five thousand Ukrainian children have been forcibly deported to Russia or detained in occupied territories. They were denied contact with their families, their personal data was changed, and they were subjected to Russification and war propaganda. Some had their identities changed and were put up for adoption. These are not war losses. This is a crime that Russia is committing systematically and deliberately.

Behind every one of these numbers is a real child. Their fear. Home. A family that is waiting and does not know if they will ever see their child again.

Europe cannot pretend it does not see this. Collective responsibility does not end with declarations of solidarity; it begins with concrete actions: documentation, identification, return, and rehabilitation. Every child who does not return is proof that this responsibility has not been fulfilled.

Over four million Ukrainians are currently benefiting from temporary protection in the European Union. Among them are children who are studying in our schools and building their lives here. We do not forget them. We also do not forget those who are not here, those who are waiting on the other side for someone to find them.

It is our duty to ensure their safe return, mental health, and future. Every child deserves this.

Urmas PAET

The opening of the first fundamental cluster of accession negotiations with Ukraine in June 2026 is commendable, although in my opinion it should have happened even earlier. Now, however, I hope that the negotiations will progress rapidly. The EU must strive for the future security of Ukraine and Europe, and when assessing the readiness of candidate countries, it should also take into account their internal situation, including Russia's attempts to incite anti-EU sentiment. Ukraine has made tremendous efforts in strengthening democratic institutions and protecting the separation of powers. Despite the ongoing war, Ukraine has made great progress, including in the areas of judicial reform and the fight against corruption. This work must definitely be continued. A strong rule of law ensures transparency and accountability in the reconstruction of the country and the recovery of the economy, and improves the investment climate and partners' trust. I certainly do not agree with the US administration's demand to hold elections in Ukraine even before the end of the war. Creating the conditions necessary for free and fair elections takes time and must be done when martial law has ended. It is important to support Ukraine's new momentum on the battlefield and increase pressure on the Russian war economy. I also commend the G7 leaders' statement on June 2026 regarding Ukraine and the disbursement of the first installment of 3.2 billion euros of the Ukraine support loan.

Sebastian TYNKKYNEN

Ukraine is turning the tide.

Its campaign of “long-range sanctions” against the Moscow regime's targets is proving wildly effective.

Russia, a country like a gas station, is watching its oil refineries burn across its territory.

Russia’s war is increasingly being felt on its own soil.

And that’s how it should be.

Where international partners failed to deliver, Ukraine developed its own capabilities.

At the same time, the country is preparing for EU membership.

The progress made by Ukraine in these most difficult circumstances deserves recognition.

Despite our political differences, one thing must be clear:

Europe must secure Ukraine’s victory.

Ukraine today is defending Europe against a common enemy.

Discussion transcript

Commission report on Moldova

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Pina PICIERNO (Chair)

The agenda calls for the report by Sven Mikser, on behalf of the Committee on Foreign Affairs, on the Commission's 2025 report on Moldova (2025/2258(INI)) (A10-0164/2026).

Sven MIKSER

Madam President, Commissioner Kos, dear Marta, as tonight's debate precedes the vote on this year's EP report on Moldova, I would like to stress that, while a few of Moldova's fellow travellers among the EU candidate countries may have started the journey earlier and covered more ground by today, Moldova's progress over the past year has definitely been among the most impressive.

Moldova's Government has set for itself an ambitious timeline. In order for it to be met, the pace of reforms must not only be maintained, but further increased in many areas, and the reform effort must continue through all domestic political hiccups.

We, on behalf of the EU, must also live up to our end of the bargain. I welcome the start of formal accession negotiations – the opening of Cluster 1 – and I urge the Council to take a merit-based approach seriously and open the next negotiating clusters without any unnecessary delay.

Colleagues, when assessing Moldova's progress, it is particularly remarkable given the extraordinary geopolitical pressure the country is experiencing. During the parliamentary elections last year, we saw how this pressure manifested itself: the Russians orchestrated an unprecedented campaign of information manipulation and interference in order to destabilise Moldova and derail its European path. Russia weaponised significant resources, spending an estimated equivalent of 2 % of Moldova's GDP on illicit financing, disinformation and other malicious operations. I do believe that EU assistance and advice played an important role in beating back those hideous designs.

Furthermore, we cannot discuss Moldova's current situation without recognising how profoundly the country has been affected by the ongoing Russian war of aggression against Ukraine. Moldova has been hit by the security, economic and social fallout of the war. Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have had a direct impact on Moldova, threatening energy stability and water security, and triggering an environmental emergency.

It is of the utmost importance that the EU and its Member States provide the necessary financial resources, technical assistance and specialised equipment to support Moldova. We must accelerate investments in critical energy infrastructure, such as the recently completed Vulcănești-Chișinău high-voltage power line, in order to eliminate Moldova's reliance on Russian energy sources and reduce vulnerabilities.

Obviously, besides helping to defend the country against external adversaries, Moldova's European integration must deliver concrete, tangible benefits to its citizens. Institutional reforms are at the core of this process. Moldova has made significant strides in reforming its justice sector and fighting corruption, although I must emphasise that these efforts demand sustained, depoliticised commitment to completely dismantle the entrenched oligarchic structures and interests.

Economically, Moldova is deepening its integration into the EU single market. The recent review of the terms of the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area, alongside Moldova's successful inclusion in the Single Euro Payments Area and the EU's 'roam like at home' initiative, are good examples of how our partnership improves livelihoods and stimulates growth. To sustain the momentum and help Moldova meet its target of concluding negotiations by 2028, robust and predictable financial backing by the EU is indispensable. We welcome the timely disbursement of EUR 270 million in pre-financing under the Reform and Growth Facility, as well as the additional EUR 207.9 million delivered following the successful achievement of key reform milestones.

As we provide this support, we must also continue to champion the vital role of civil society and independent media, ensuring they have the tools and protections to hold institutions accountable. We also reiterate our firm commitment to a peaceful, comprehensive resolution of the Transnistrian situation – a solution that will have to be based on Moldova's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

In conclusion, Moldova's goals are ambitious and its European path is not without challenges. But the Moldovan citizens have repeatedly proven their dedication to our European values. Let us stand firmly by their side, providing the guidance and solidarity needed for a secure, vibrant European future for Moldova and, indeed, for our own continent.

Marta Kos

Madam President, honourable Members, thank you to the rapporteur, Sven Mikser, for your report on Moldova and for your work for Moldova. You have painted a picture of a nation transforming itself as it advances on its European path. Moldova's delivery on reforms is seen all over Europe.

Over the past years, we have seen a nation that stood up against foreign interference and hybrid attacks, and made its choice for Europe and its path towards membership of our Union. This sovereign choice deserves our full support. We have seen a country that is moving against corruption and organised crime, putting people in jail that once seemed untouchable.

Moldova has also been delivering on enlargement reforms at record speed. In the 2025 enlargement report, the Commission assessed that Moldova made progress across all negotiating chapters. This includes important advances on the fundamentals, energy alignment and digital transformation. Since then, Moldova has continued moving forward. We have also seen impressive numbers in the implementation of the growth plan reforms: with 93 %, Moldova is ahead of all other EU candidates that have growth plans.

These reforms build trust. Moldova's European future is an investment in the security and stability of our continent as a whole. I was in Chișinău last month, discussing the next steps in the accession process and, once again, I could see a strong determination to deliver reforms, despite the immense pressure they continue to face. In line with our recommendations, it has implemented key reforms, supported by the guidance provided by Member States during the front‑loading exercise in December 2025 and March 2026. Therefore, I share your opinion: we should call on the Council to open all the clusters as soon as possible. I hope that we will reach this goal.

At the same time, Moldova should continue delivering reforms – particularly on justice, the fight against corruption and economic governance. These reforms are essential to meet the interim benchmarks needed to start closing chapters. As you have stressed, Moldova joined the Single Euro Payments Area in October last year and also became part of the 'roam like at home' area. At the same time, we are also advancing together on energy integration, trade liberalisation and connectivity.

Much has been achieved, but the work is not finished. I count on your continued support in accompanying Moldova on its European path. Supporting Moldova is an investment in a stronger, safer and more united Europe.

Andrzej HALICKI

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues, first of all, I would like to thank Sven Mikser and our colleagues for the excellent and very smooth cooperation. It's really a pleasure to work as a team. I would like to confirm, in the name of EPP Group, the four amendments tabled by the rapporteur we support.

Because of the report, I have three messages to our Moldovan friends.

First of all, the EU should open negotiation clusters with Moldova without any delay. My personal perspective, and also in the name of EPP, I can confirm all the clusters should be open because of the number of reforms and the implementation of the reforms. Moldova is ready to continue these negotiations very effectively. So we should do it. This is our obligation not to postpone it.

The second message is a political one because a bigger and more integrated Europe is also a safer Europe. But we have to take into account that we can learn how to fight effectively against disinformation, against Russian activity. Moldova did it. So we should learn from Kyiv how to be effective in the fight against disinformation. We should take into account that issue also.

The third message is about economic progress. This is a huge success and, I think, also personal success of the leadership, Maia Sandu's leadership and the past party, but of course, important is also the European help. It is not a huge one, but very effective. We can mention EUR 1.2 billion in grants – this is last five years – and another EUR 1.7 billion for private sector also during the last five years. But now, very important is the growth plan for Moldova – close to EUR 2 billion in the coming year and also additional EUR 2.5 billion for the private sector.

The fourth – last – message for the Moldovans, in conclusion, we are waiting for you in common Europe.

Marcos ROS SEMPERE

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, in the September elections, the Moldovan people taught a lesson and clearly stated that they want to move forward together with the European Union and towards the European Union. Furthermore, they did so in a difficult context marked by external interference, pressure, disinformation, and a great deal of intoxication.

For this reason, the message sent by the citizens of Moldova has even greater political value. And we, the European Union, have the obligation to respond with responsibility and rigor. Responsibility and rigor imply reforms, independence of the judiciary, the rule of law, and the fight against corruption. But we must also respond with a constructive attitude so that every step forward taken by Moldova is taken into account.

Furthermore, we find ourselves at a time when some are even working from within, from within the European Union, to weaken the Union and its values. At such a time, Moldova is firmly reminding us all why our project—the European Union project—still makes sense, because there are still peoples who see in Europe a promise of freedom, democracy, security, and prosperity as we experience it.

Now is the time to be ambitious and open all negotiation clusters at once, because Moldova needs the European Union, and Europe also needs peoples who continue to believe in the European Union.

Cristian TERHEŞ

Madam President, dear colleagues, Madam Commissioner, a stronger Europe means a Republic of Moldova that is part of the European Union. Integration is a technical and political process. That is why it is important to look at it from a historical perspective: in 20 years, where do we see Moldova and the European Union? When we leave a security vacuum at our borders, that vacuum is filled by instability, and the Republic of Moldova is today on the front line of this reality.

Supporting Moldova is not only an act of solidarity, but also a strategic investment in the security and stability of the entire European Union. Despite external pressures, hybrid attacks and constant attempts at destabilization, the Republic of Moldova has chosen democracy, the rule of law and Western values. However, this choice requires firm and consistent support from us.

A Moldova in the European Union means a safer eastern border, greater resilience against external interference and a clear message that Europe protects its partners who choose freedom and peace. European enlargement has always been one of the EU's most powerful tools to consolidate peace, prosperity and stability in Europe. With each enlargement, all EU countries have become stronger, more prosperous, and Europe more stable.

By supporting the Republic of Moldova, we both consolidate the future of a neighboring state and strengthen the security, unity and credibility of the entire European project. That is precisely why the future of the Republic of Moldova must be in the European Union.

Dan BARNA

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, Mr Rapporteur, the report we are debating today confirms an undeniable reality: the Republic of Moldova is advancing rapidly and resolutely towards its goal of becoming a member state of the European Union.

I want to praise the extraordinary resilience of Moldovan citizens, despite the hybrid threats, disinformation and unprecedented interference orchestrated by the Kremlin. They have defended their democracy and reconfirmed the irreversibility of Moldova's European path.

The technical progress and reforms in Chișinău are remarkable. The fact that we recently opened negotiations on the first cluster, that of fundamental values, is proof of the seriousness of this commitment. Moldova is already part of the European roaming area and is integrating into the single payment area. Also, through the approved 1.9 billion growth plan, we are tangibly and directly supporting the modernization of schools, hospitals and local businesses.

The Republic of Moldova is no longer just a beneficiary, but is already actively contributing to the security of our continent. Our responsibility is to give up formal excuses and pretexts and to stand by Chișinău at every step, because Moldova's natural place is here, in the European family.

Villy SØVNDAL

Madam President! On 28 September 2025, together with other colleagues from here, I was an election observer at the parliamentary elections in Moldova. There was great nervousness leading up to the election due to massive Russian influence with misinformation, bribery, and so on. But fortunately, the pro-European democratic parties won. Therefore, Moldova can continue its path towards EU membership, and we support reforms, but there are still challenges with corruption and organized crime. The biggest challenge is, of course, the breakaway region of Transnistria, but also in general the continued Russian attempts at hybrid warfare, misinformation, and destabilization. It is my hope that Moldova, as Europe's poorest country, will continue the reform process and prepare for EU membership, so that Moldova definitively becomes a part of Europe. We would like to help them as much as we can.

Jonas SJÖSTEDT

Madam President! I would also like to thank the rapporteur Sven Mikser for a good report. Several of the points that were important for us in the Left are included, such as combating poverty in Moldova, continuing the work against corruption, supporting investments in renewable energy and for true energy independence, and protecting the environment. As a whole, it is a good report.

Right now, Moldova is shaken by some turbulence in domestic politics. Important people have resigned. There are accusations of corruption. That is naturally bad, but it would have been even worse if it had not come to light, if irregularities had not been brought into the light.

In a way, it is a good sign that even within the governing party, corruption is exposed. It shows that the work against corruption is taken seriously.

Stanislav STOYANOV

Madam President, Moldova continues to face serious challenges in the fight against corruption, judicial reform, and the strengthening of state institutions. Precisely for this reason, calls for the immediate opening of all negotiating chapters and the acceleration of the accession process are in the interest neither of the citizens of the European Union nor of the citizens of Moldova.

European integration is a powerful tool that must create real economic benefits for business, strengthen competitiveness, and protect traditional national communities such as the Bulgarian one. Hasty movement towards membership, before the necessary reforms are implemented, would put precisely these long-term benefits at risk. The European Union must apply its own criteria equally to all candidate countries. Only in this way will we preserve confidence in the enlargement policy and guarantee that membership is based on real merits rather than political expediency.

Siegfried MUREŞAN

Madam President, dear colleagues, Madam Commissioner, over the past year, the Republic of Moldova is the candidate country for accession to the European Union that has registered the most significant progress on the path of European integration. The citizens of the Republic of Moldova are beginning to feel the concrete benefits of integration into the European Union. Already together, through the effort of the authorities in the Republic of Moldova and through the effort of European institutions, we are succeeding in integrating the Republic of Moldova into more and more European programs, so that the citizens can already feel, before the date of accession, the advantages of European integration.

A few weeks ago we managed to open, also at the political level, at the highest political level, the negotiations on the first cluster of accession negotiations, as a result of the good progress registered at the technical level.

Through the report of the European Parliament, which we will adopt tomorrow. We request three things.

First of all, the opening of negotiations on all negotiation chapters at the political level, as soon as possible, no later than the end of this year. One. Two: the continuation of reforms on the path of European integration and, three, the increase of financial and technical support from the European Union for the Republic of Moldova, because the Russian Federation has tried in recent years to hold the Republic of Moldova back and has failed. But the Russian Federation will continue to try to spread fake news, propaganda, disinformation in the Republic of Moldova, trying to hold the Republic of Moldova back.

We must be stronger, be in solidarity with the people in the Republic of Moldova, so that the Republic of Moldova continues to advance rapidly on the path of European integration. A strong, stable, reformed Republic of Moldova is good for the citizens of the Republic of Moldova, but it is also good news for the European Union as a whole.

Victor NEGRESCU

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues, I would first like to congratulate my Social Democratic colleague, Sven Mikser, for his report. We, the Social Democrats, have always supported the European path of the Republic of Moldova. Because yes, the place of the Republic of Moldova is in the European family. Despite external pressures, hybrid attacks, and repeated attempts at destabilization, its citizens have chosen the European path.

The authorities have the duty to carry out all the reforms necessary for accession in order to meet the ambitious deadline set for the completion of negotiations, the end of 2028, and we are here to support the Republic of Moldova, and to achieve this objective, the consolidation of the rule of law, the independence of the judiciary, the fight against corruption, and the modernization of the administration must remain priorities.

I encourage political actors in Chisinau to efficiently manage the current political context and transform it into an impetus for accelerating European reforms through the participation of the entire population. That is why the European Parliament is sending a clear message today: the Republic of Moldova has made remarkable progress and deserves to continue this path by opening all negotiating chapters with the European Union, and we want this opening to happen immediately, because we cannot afford delays.

Furthermore, the European Union must reward the merit, determination, and concrete results obtained by the Republic of Moldova, and in this sense, we must offer an accelerated accession path, a path of its own, and why not, even additional European funds. In this regard, Republic of Moldova, we are waiting for you here, in the European Union.

Mariusz KAMIŃSKI

Madam President! Opening actual accession negotiations for Moldova with the European Union is a good and well-deserved step on this country's European path. Moldova has the right and the will to break out of the post-Soviet sphere of influence, and we want to help it in this.

Our task is to support our Moldovan partners in building a strong, modern, and democratic state. This means, among other things, a consistent fight against corruption and oligarchy, which are the bane of every post-communist society.

The Union must also support actions for Moldova's territorial integrity. Chisinau regaining control over Transnistria is a key issue. The Union has a leverage tool, as 70% of goods exports from Transnistria go to the European market. A tough sanctions and customs policy must be applied – either loyalty to Moldova or an end to business with Europe.

Commissioner, a major problem concerning the pace of Moldova's integration with the Union is the linking of its candidacy with that of Ukraine. Today, Ukraine is struggling with corruption, oligarchisation, and resuscitated nationalism. Therefore, the principle must be adopted that each state is assessed on the basis of its individual achievements.

Eugen TOMAC

Madam President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues, the report we are discussing today should not be seen as a simple evaluation of the Republic of Moldova's progress in the integration process. The discussion on enlargement has often focused on the cost of accession. Perhaps it is time to stop looking at everything solely in terms of the value of the investment, and instead ask ourselves what the cost would be if we did not bring the Republic of Moldova into the European Union more quickly.

The security of the European Union also depends on the security of the Republic of Moldova, which has been fighting for over 35 years to escape Moscow's malevolent influence, which illegally maintains military troops on its territory. The citizens of the Republic of Moldova have earned the right to receive a clear perspective of accession to the European Union, and this must simply be accelerated.

The Republic of Moldova, despite Russia's aggressive and constant pressure, has managed to start the reforms necessary to be prepared for accession, and this path must be encouraged and supported. That is why I believe it is important for all of us to stand by Chisinau at every moment.

Nicolae ȘTEFĂNUȚĂ

Mr President, Moldova is the sole candidate that has achieved 28 out of 30 accession targets. And this despite hybrid attacks, energy blackmail, the poisoning of the Prut river and many other price hikes generated by war. And I believe it is our turn to rise to their level, and not the Moldovans' turn to rise to ours. They have been doing it for a long time already.

I am Romanian, I know what it means to fight for Europe when others convince you that you do not deserve it, that Romania struggled to prove it had to be in Europe and behold, we are celebrating 20 years. But for these people who struggle from one election to another through hardships, to enter the European Union, and they do it convincingly, with a dedicated government, we must show solidarity.

So I do not want us to stop at all, because Moldova wants it, Europe wants it, Moldova can do it, Europe can do it. And I believe this is a unique moment, a window of opportunity that does not always open. So I truly wish, Ms Kos, that we do that circle dance in which you also danced in Chișinău, with the European Union (...)

Sebastian EVERDING

Mr President! The Republic of Moldova is on its European path – and that is a good thing too, dear colleagues. But this path does not only mean reform on paper; it also means putting European fundamental values into practice in reality.

There are still serious human rights problems. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found violations, including due to inhumane detention conditions, violence and degrading treatment. Human rights apply universally: A punishment may take away freedom, but never humanity.

This responsibility is also evident in the treatment of animals. The situation of stray dogs in Moldova continues to be concerning: reports of poor keeping conditions, cruel treatment and killing practices must be taken seriously.

The way the weakest are treated is a benchmark for the values of a society. Therefore, European standards are also needed in animal welfare: neutering and vaccination programmes, better conditions in animal shelters and support for local actors.

The protection of human rights and animal welfare both follow the same basic idea. A society shows its strength by how it treats the weakest.

Luis-Vicențiu LAZARUS

Mr. President, dear colleagues, I will not join the choir of glorifiers of this matter regarding the accession of Moldova and Ukraine to the European Union, because I knew that always these candidate countries must meet certain criteria. And the corruption criterion, which is among the first, is not respected at all. As you probably know, Moldova no longer has a prime minister. They just resigned.

Why did they resign? In what context did they resign? In the context where Maia Sandu's cousin, the pseudo-president of this pseudo-republic... because, in fact, isn't Moldova ours? It is part of Romania. It strikes me that no one says this thing here, as if a Ribbentrop-Molotov pact, for example, had been normal.

So we woke up finding out that the president's cousin has a salary of 6000, over 6000 euros. Well, we are helping Moldova, we are bringing billions there for reforms and they are giving themselves salaries of 6000. But doesn't it seem to you (...)

(The President withdrew the speaker's floor)

Davor Ivo STIER

Mr President, Moldova is, first of all, an independent state, whether someone wants to recognise it or not. And it is an independent state that, despite strong Russian interference and pressure, has chosen a European future.

When some Western Balkan countries complain about the alleged double standards of the European Union, about delays in opening certain chapters or clusters, then I would recommend them to look at everything Moldova has done, starting, of course, with sanctions against Russian aggression.

I will remind you here that the Municipal Court in Chișinău established the existence of camps, unfortunately, in Serbia and in the entity of Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where people were trained who were later supposed to undermine the pro-European orientation of that country in Moldova.

Of course, Moldova still has a lot of work to do, primarily related to the fight against corruption, but its progress is obvious and therefore the European Parliament must continue to give it strong support.

Kristian VIGENIN

Mr President, Moldova deserves categorical and consistent support from the European Parliament. Despite the war on its borders, despite hybrid attacks and constant external pressure, the country shows resilience and a commitment to its European path.

The European perspective of Moldova must remain a cross-party national priority based on democracy, social justice, the rule of law and real benefits for citizens. When a candidate country fulfills its commitments, the European Union must also fulfill its own. Therefore, I welcome Moldova's progress and call on the Council to give the green light for the next step in preparation and membership negotiations.

But support for Moldova does not mean turning a blind eye to the challenges. On the contrary, European integration requires real results in judicial reform, in the fight against corruption, in the independence of institutions and in the restoration of public trust, especially after the resignation of Prime Minister Munteanu. The next government must quickly restore stability, preserve the European course and show citizens that reforms are not just a requirement of Brussels, but a path to more security, a better life and stronger social protection.

I also want to emphasize something particularly important. Respecting minority rights is a fundamental criterion for any candidate country. This includes the Bulgarian community in Taraclia. Any administrative reform must guarantee the cultural and linguistic diversity of the communities in Moldova and their political representation.

Georgiana TEODORESCU

Mr President, we all agree that Moldova's place is in the European Union. They are our brothers, the brothers of Romanians, they speak the Romanian language, the majority are Orthodox Christians and they share the same past and the same values with Romania, an EU member state. When and how will this accession take place? Here is the true key to this debate.

The first, and at the same time the fastest and most natural solution, would be the German solution, which I and my party colleagues have been talking about. The second option, actual accession, must be done on its own calendar, independent of Ukraine. Moldova has its own path and its own speed for fulfilling the conditions for EU accession. So there is no reason to treat it bundled together with Ukraine.

In addition, Ukraine is, unfortunately, a country still at war with disputed territory, so we cannot talk about effective accession at this stage. And it would be unfair to keep Moldova blocked bundled together with it. Any country that wants to accede to the EU must meet the exact same conditions as its predecessors, and from this point of view we must say it clearly: Moldova is many steps ahead of Ukraine, and therefore many steps closer to the European Union.

Nathalie LOISEAU

Mr President, so accession negotiations are finally opening with Moldova: it was about time! The Moldovan people have said it, said it again and are repeating it: they feel European, they want to join the European Union. They have voted to this effect on several occasions, despite the insane pressure that Russia has exerted on them. Information manipulation, vote-buying, oligarchs at Moscow’s beck and call, criminal gangs, economic pressure: little Moldova has faced it all and resisted it all.

It is sometimes looked down upon with condescension: we would do better to take a leaf out of its book. Because information manipulation, foreign media groups well-disposed towards Vladimir Putin and attempts at intimidation, well, that doesn’t only happen in Moldova.

The Moldovan people want to join the European Union, and its authorities know what they have to do, the reforms they have to carry out to achieve this. But do we know what we want? Are we ready to welcome new members into our Union? I am very much afraid that we have not yet grasped the measure of the world around us.

Enlargement of the European Union can be an opportunity: that of escaping our encirclement. But its success will also depend on us.

Reinhold LOPATKA

Mr President, dear colleagues, Russia's brutal war of aggression has shown that there are no grey zones on our continent, no place for grey zones. We must therefore continue supporting all enlargement countries who are demonstrating willingness to progress on the path of EU integration.

Moldova has shown a strong determination in the implementation of reforms, in the face of challenging circumstances, despite disinformation campaigns and hybrid attacks from Russia.

While there are still some changes necessary, of course, we cannot allow Moscow to undermine Moldova's European cause.

Russia's actions remind us that enlargement is not a bureaucratic exercise, but one of the EU's most important geopolitical instruments to strengthen stability, security and prosperity across our continent.

Candidate countries must deliver on reforms. At the same time, the EU has to remain a reliable partner.

Maria GRAPINI

Madam Commissioner, Mr President, dear colleagues, the ambitious program of the Republic of Moldova to conclude accession by the end of 2028 must be supported. It is to be welcomed, but it will not be able to be implemented if we do not all support it. And I want from the very beginning to thank both the Commissioner and the colleagues who have supported this project.

I am Romanian, I am Moldovan, I know the Republic of Moldova very well, I know the citizens there, the citizens want this and we must encourage them to have confidence in the European Union project, because the administration in Chisinau needs popular support.

Of course, I see no other path and we must also be realistic: the Republic of Moldova is at the border, how difficult it is to resist direct and indirect attacks, fake news and everything that happens there with Russia. The European Union is a project that I, as a Romanian, wanted us to be there with my country. Therefore, Madam Commissioner, the Council, the Parliament must understand that the Republic of Moldova has its place in the European Union and we must support it.

And I also want to add one thing: I strongly believe that what is happening now in Ukraine is also holding back the Republic of Moldova. We must separate them. Romania and Bulgaria experienced the same thing with Schengen. Let us be fair, objective - in Ukraine the deadlines and milestones cannot be respected - and let us give Moldova the green light and, at the end of 2028, the Republic of Moldova should be in the great family.

Şerban Dimitrie STURDZA

Mr President, dear colleagues, I am glad that the Republic of Moldova has opened the first negotiation chapter for accession to the European Union. From now on, our duty is not to turn this European path into an endless waiting room. The Republic of Moldova must be correctly evaluated. It is natural for Romania to support the Republic of Moldova in its EU accession path.

Supporting the Romanians across the Prut is a historical duty and a strategic necessity. All the more so since almost half of them are also citizens of Romania. Its integration into the European Union represents more stability and more security at the eastern border of the Union. However, the Republic of Moldova must continue to break away from its Soviet heritage and the reflexes of the past, and Brussels must prove its openness for a concrete and prompt final result.

If the Romanians from both banks of the Prut could not reunite like the Berliners, then the Republic of Moldova and Romania must reunite at least through their belonging to the European Union.

Krzysztof BREJZA

Mr President! Moldova gives the hope so much needed today by the European Union, because Moldova's membership in the European Union shows that these European efforts are something more than campaigning for funds, for institutions. It is a fight for values. And this European path of Moldova shows that the Russkiy Mir can be overcome, that you can win against Russian services. Against this Goliath, David can win with truth, consistency and determination.

Moldova is a model for us in how to fight oligarchs who try to destabilize our societies, how to fight lies, but also how to fight phenomena such as cryptocurrencies, which in some European Union member states are still used to destroy democracy, to destroy the European Union. Let us take an example from Moldova – a small country, but great in spirit.

Vytenis Povilas ANDRIUKAITIS

Mr President, Commissioner, colleagues, thank you for the excellent report, Sven Mikser. I cannot stress enough the importance of opening all negotiation clusters for Moldova and Ukraine. Article 49 of the Treaty of European Union clearly states that unanimity is required only for the opening and closing of accession negotiations. But what is the European Council doing? The endless unanimity silos for each chapter are like sand that the Council is throwing in the gears of enlargement.

The situation now is that the Member States are undermining European security, delaying the enlargement process, sabotaging our strategic interests and preventing effective, comprehensive negotiations on all clusters with Moldova. Let us do our best to fulfil our promise to start closing all chapters at the beginning of 2027, as promised.

Dear friends in Moldova and Ukraine, please continue your reforms with the same spirit as before. Please trust us, and we will do our utmost to have you sitting in this Parliament among us in the nearest future. Let's do it!

Liudas MAŽYLIS

Mr. President, Commissioner, colleagues. Today, Moldova is demonstrating impressive European momentum: bilateral screening is complete, all six accession negotiation clusters are potentially open, and twenty-four out of twenty-six reform steps have already been implemented. Clear progress is visible in the areas of fundamental values, the internal market, and external relations. Moldova continues to try to move consistently in the directions of resources, agriculture, and cohesion. For us, the European Union, this is an argument to act boldly and open membership negotiations, showing that reforms yield real political results. Of course, Russia's military presence in Transnistria is a violation of international law and a direct threat. The Russians must withdraw unconditionally, and we must help Moldova strengthen its resilience, energy independence, and confidence in the European path.

Gheorghe FALCĂ

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today we are not only deciding on the European path of the Republic of Moldova. We are also deciding how credible the European Union is when a people embraces our values and has the courage to defend them.

The Republic of Moldova is not asking for favors. It comes with reforms, sacrifices, and a democratic choice reaffirmed by its citizens. It comes with dignity and remarkable resilience in the face of Russian pressure and threats. That is why the Republic of Moldova is not just a candidate state. It is proof that the European project inspires, mobilizes, and offers hope. For Romania, this support is a historical responsibility. For the European Union, it is a matter of credibility.

We cannot ask for courage from those who choose Europe and then abandon them. Reforms must continue in Moldova, and we must respond with firm and consistent support. Today, our vote must be directly for Moldova, as well as for a united European Union.

Oliver SCHENK

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, dear colleagues! Moldova is once again at a turning point. The recent political developments in Chișinău show how sensitive the domestic political situation remains and how crucial stability, the capacity for reform, and a clear European course are now.

Against this very background, I consider this report to be particularly important. It clearly shows that Moldova has made remarkable progress in the EU accession process despite enormous external pressure – in judicial and administrative reforms and in economic rapprochement with the European Union.

But we must not be naive. Moldova is under sustained hybrid attack – disinformation, cyber attacks, energy blackmail, and Russian influence aim to break the country's European course.

Our response must be clear: We support Moldova politically, financially, and in terms of security policy. Accession negotiations must be based on performance, not blockades. Those who deliver reforms must see progress. Moldova's European future is not just a Moldovan issue, it is a question of Europe's credibility and security.

Michał SZCZERBA

Mr President! Madam Commissioner! Moldova is a unique candidate country. And I would like to very warmly thank you as well, Madam Commissioner, that from the very beginning you have been betting on Moldova - on a country which, also according to this presented report, has the greatest progress when it comes to preparations for membership. And we want to state this very clearly.

But this is also a country that inspires and motivates also through responsibility for social and democratic resilience, for understanding what security is, what hybrid threats are present around our neighbourhood.

As the rapporteur for military mobility, I proposed that Moldova be one of the close partners to be included in this regulation, because by building military mobility, by building mobility corridors, we also want to include candidate countries. Moldova has its place there.

Nikola MINCHEV

Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, the 2025 report on Moldova sends a clear message: despite an extremely challenging geopolitical and economic environment, Moldova continues to move forward on its European path.

The progress is concrete. Moldova is replacing its Soviet-era standards with European ones. These are not merely technical changes, but tangible steps, improving quality, safety and protection for Moldovan citizens. We also see progress in consumer protection. Moldova has made public services more accessible and effective.

Notably, Moldova has consistently cooperated on foreign policy issues, and aligns with the EU's common foreign and security policy positions. This is done in a very hostile environment, under significant internal and external challenges, such as persistent hostile Russian interference, as correctly noted in the report.

Of course, challenges remain and further work is needed, but today we should recognise the progress achieved. Moldova is making serious efforts, delivering concrete results and demonstrating through action its European ambitions.

These efforts deserve our recognition and our continued support, because we do not see them everywhere, and we value them when we see them.

Alvise PÉREZ

Mr President, I completely do not understand what some MEPs—almost all of them Spanish—are doing, applauding the enlargement of the European Union, earlier in the previous debate on Ukraine and now in this one on Moldova.

That the Germans do it, I can understand, but we Spaniards, have we not read here the leaked internal study from the Council of the European Union itself in 2023, which indicates that Spain is going to be the only country that will go from being a net recipient to a net contributor? Do you know what 3 billion euros less from the CAP means for a farmer in Spain, in Romania, in Portugal, or in Italy?

Do you know what it means to bring in the poorest country in Europe, which is Moldova, with 2.4 million inhabitants—I know this because I have been to Moldova as a volunteer, with refugees from Moldova—and with systemic corruption amounting to 12% of GDP? We are talking about bringing in right now a territory that has 1,500 Russian soldiers inside it, in Transnistria, with a European referendum, by the way, that yielded 50.4%, and thanks to the diaspora vote, because one in three Moldovans lives outside their country.

Anyway, I understand that some do, but for Spanish MEPs to support this seems surreal to me.

Marta Kos

Mr President, honourable members of the European Parliament, it's really good to see that Moldova has so many supporters here in the European Parliament. Some of them are very passionate. Mr Andriukaitis, thank you for your passionate words. I am on your side. I would also like to see Members of the European Parliament from Moldova as soon as possible too.

Moldova has demonstrated determination and delivered meaningful reforms under exceptionally challenging circumstances. It deserves recognition for that progress and our continued support to move forward on its path to EU membership. We have organised the biggest investment conference to date at the beginning of June in Chişinău and the companies from the Member States are already coming. This is the only way to prosperity. So, they have to do the reforms, the investors will come, and then we can speak about the prosperity.

Regarding the question of when Moldova will be able to become a member of the EU: when all the reforms will be done, meaning Moldova has to deliver, but we have to deliver too. I have heard this today many times. So, it is also our responsibility that this will happen as soon as possible. I used to say that Moldova is the best student in my class. Since the last successful way on the reforms, I am saying that Moldova is the best performer in my class.

Sven MIKSER

Mr President, first of all, I would like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs. It was really intellectually stimulating and a very constructive effort that produced this report. I think that all the pro-European groups who negotiated the report were brought together by a great sense of unity of purpose, but also a sense of urgency. I would also like to thank Commissioner Kos for her personal dedication and commitment to supporting, in every possible way, Moldova's very legitimate European aspirations. And I would like to thank all the colleagues for an extremely constructive debate here.

I hope that the report that we are going to be voting on tomorrow – and also tonight's debate – help us to send a very clear message to the Moldovan people and the Moldovan Government: a message of support and solidarity, but also a message of what our expectations are as to the next steps to be taken in this reform path.

I also hope that the report and the debates send a very clear message to our colleagues, the political leaders in our Member State capitals, who periodically meet around the Council table: a message that we expect them to live up to our end of the bargain, as I said, and to actually act with the same sense of urgency, because it is absolutely clear that the Russian pressure on Moldova will not dissipate until the successful completion of this process.

Moldova did not apply for membership and we did not launch this process in order for us to allow them to enjoy the process. It must be a purpose-driven process that will conclude in fully integrating Moldova into our European family without any unnecessary delay.

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

Thank you to the rapporteur and everyone who participated in the debate, as well as to the Commissioner.

The debate on this item is now concluded and the vote will take place tomorrow.
