Commission report on Serbia

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

The next item on the agenda is the report presented by MEP Picula: the Commission's report on Serbia for 2025 (2025/2255(INI)) (A10-0163/2026). I would like to inform honourable members that for this debate there will be only one round of speakers on behalf of political groups. Therefore, the catch-the-eye procedure will not apply, and no blue cards will be accepted. And to begin with, I would ask the rapporteur, our colleague Mr Picula, please go ahead.

Tonino PICULA

Dear Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, this year's report reflects the reality in Serbia during one of the pivotal periods of its recent history. There is hardly any chapter in which progress towards European Union membership has not been assessed as limited or non-existent.

Our mission in Belgrade at the beginning of the year also took place under unusually difficult circumstances. Members of parliament were exposed to verbal attacks by government representatives and pro-government media, and high-ranking officials of Serbia repeatedly made groundless claims that the European Union and some of its member states are inciting or supporting a so-called colored revolution in Serbia.

Overall, Serbia's progress in achieving reforms important for advancement towards European Union membership has slowed down significantly. In several key areas, and particularly in the rule of law, there has even been regression.

This is also reflected through limited progress in the dialogue between Belgrade and Pristina, a continuous lack of alignment with the common foreign and security policy, a lack of genuine political commitment to reforms, aggressive rhetoric towards the European Union, and the deterioration of working conditions for free media and civil society organizations. A continuous failure in the comprehensive implementation of recommendations on electoral reform is noted, as problems persist with the regulatory body and the voter register.

While the authorities in Serbia continue to present European Union membership as their strategic goal, the actions of its political leadership often fail to confirm this. The latest European Commission report also points to continuous democratic regression, insufficient progress in rule of law reforms, and a growing gap between Serbia's stated European aspirations and its political practice. Unfortunately, we also see no progress in the investigation into the collapse of the railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which sparked mass civic discontent.

Due to unfulfilled obligations or a serious lack of results, particularly in the area of the rule of law, the report calls on the Commission to halt future disbursements under the Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans. I also advocate for the reprogramming of existing and future European Union funds in order to strengthen support for judicial reform, anti-corruption efforts, independent media, civil society organizations, and the independent cultural sector.

I would remind you that the policy of stabilocracy and turning a blind eye to autocrats over the past decade or so has stimulated the existing poor conditions across a large part of the Western Balkans.

Therefore, we do not need to wonder how a referendum on Serbia's entry into the European Union would fare today, precisely because of the low support for membership. There are many reasons why this support is the lowest in the region, given that anti-European rhetoric has been used for years. However, an important element in the loss of trust in the European Union and its institutions is certainly the tolerance of the false pro-European narrative of the authorities in Belgrade over all these past years.

Because of this, I am convinced that the insistence on opening negotiating cluster 3, which would resume Serbia's accession negotiations with the European Union after a four-year standstill, is misplaced. That stagnation had its clear and justified reasons, just as restarting it has none today.

The report reflects the continuous collapse of democratic standards in Serbia. Should we reward the lack of alignment with European foreign policy, which is at only 63 percent, despite the fact that other candidate countries have no problem with full alignment? Alongside the strengthening of ties with China and Russia, we also have a case where a government minister visits Iran, and let us not forget how the speaker of the Serbian parliament once even attended the inauguration of Nicolas Maduro.

Furthermore, it is impossible not to react to attempts from Belgrade to undermine the recent holding of the European Union-Western Balkans summit in Montenegro. All of this shows that relations between the European Union and Serbia cannot simply be reset.

The state of the media is also an extremely large problem. The process of takeover is currently underway for the few remaining independent media outlets, which can easily be rendered dependent on a government that has proven it does not tolerate any criticism.

(The President deprived the speaker of the floor)

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

Under the new approach, I have to be stricter – even with the rapporteurs and Commissioners. That's to be fair.

Marta Kos

Mr President, honourable Members, dear rapporteur Tonino Picula, thank you for your comprehensive report and for your work on Serbia. The Commission appreciates the opportunity for a separate debate on Serbia.

Serbia is an important partner in the region, with a clear EU-accession perspective. The European Commission therefore continues encouraging Serbia to seize the current opportunity to advance towards membership.

At the EU-Western Balkans Summit, we heard clear commitments from the Serbian leadership that the EU path is their strategic priority. We now need to see Serbia demonstrate its strategic commitments, address the EU's concerns and continue to deliver on the much-needed reforms.

As said many times, reforms on the rule of law, and respect for democratic principles and freedoms, will remain essential for Serbia's progress on its EU path. Two weeks ago, the Serbian Parliament took an important step in the right direction to correct the judicial laws adopted in January. This helps starting rebuilding the trust.

Serbia also made tangible progress in addressing key audit recommendations by revising legislation relevant for the electoral framework. In May, amendments to four election-related laws, among others, on the election of the Members of Parliament and on the election of the president, were adopted.

Two particularly important and substantial laws that concern the financing of political activities and the prevention of corruption are currently under preparation, meaning still to be done.

The recent invitation to OSCE/ODIHR to conduct the usual needs assessment mission is an important step to ensure, in a timely manner, a fully-fledged international election observation mission ahead of the next elections.

We now need to see Serbia advancing further on the electoral reform, in line with ODIHR recommendations, in a transparent and inclusive manner – strengthening media freedom and pluralism; ensuring respect for fundamental rights and freedoms, including freedom of peaceful assembly and academic freedom; and an enabling environment for civil society.

Recent developments on the formation of the so-called REM Council have been encouraging, and we hope that this regulatory body can start its important work soon. This is a long-awaited step.

Alignment with our EU objectives extends beyond internal policies to our common foreign and security policy. Serbia's European past therefore requires clear strategic choices. This also needs to be reflected in a consistent and high alignment with the Union's common foreign and security policy.

A credible European trajectory also means a commitment to regional stability, to normalisation of relations with Kosovo, and to a shared understanding of the security challenges facing our continent. It means tackling disinformation and abstaining from hostile political rhetoric, including against the EU, its institutions and honourable Members of this Parliament.

Serbia's commitment to the EU path and its political will to implement the required reforms also have to be strengthened via communication and concrete actions – including meaningful engagement on EU reforms – with the relevant stakeholders, including civil society organisations, to overcome the current deep divisions in Serbian society.

Dear honourable Members, with other countries advancing in the accession process, we do not want to see Serbia fall behind. This is why, in light of the recent – some positive – developments, the Commission renewed its recommendation to the Council to open Cluster 3 in the accession negotiations with Serbia.

The Commission will also continue to incentivise further reform progress for the benefit of all Serbian citizens and the whole Serbian society.

Davor Ivo STIER

Mr President, colleagues, EU enlargement has regained its political importance. This is something that, in general, has benefited countries, but not in the case of Serbia. President Vučić made clear that Serbia can implement EU‑related reforms and has appointed a very professional negotiating operational team. But he also said that Serbia will not turn its back on Russia. Serbia does not perceive itself as part of the West, but pursues a non‑aligned policy, which is deeply rooted in society: it existed before Vučić and will probably continue after him.

While the EU should acknowledge this decision, Serbia needs to understand that it won't make progress towards EU membership if it keeps friendly relations with the EU's adversaries. Sometimes driven by a transactional logic, some key Member States have attempted to change Belgrade's policy. However, they have so far failed – sometimes increasing the level of frustration on all sides.

At the same time, Parliament's criticism, while honest and principled, has had little impact so far on changing the course of events. So what can be done? A realistic approach should envisage cooperation and partial and gradual integration in those areas of mutual benefit – from border management, trade, finance, energy and transport. A pragmatic but firm approach can bring results. We saw it with the repeal of the mortgage laws, with better cooperation on electoral reform, even with better cooperation with the Croatian National Council.

Of course, this should be continued and expanded to the benefit of both sides, but we should also be honest with each other: Serbia will not align with the EU any time soon. There is no political will for it, neither in the government nor in the opposition. To that situation, our response should not be appeasement or isolation, but rather a realistic engagement: firm on values and pragmatic on promoting our interests, without false promises about progress in the negotiations, but with a clear vision of a working relationship that serves the cause of peace in...

(The President cut off the speaker)

Andreas SCHIEDER

Mr President, Madam Commissioner, I think it is important to say it again: we all want to see Serbia and especially the Serbian citizens in the European Union.

But there is one problem on this way, and the problem has a name. It's Aleksandar Vučić – because under his presidency, the country is going backwards – going backwards on democracy, on media freedom, on transparency, growing corruption is on the rise, the ministers attending the funeral in Iran. Also, Serbia and Belgrade sometimes is seen as a Moscow proxy. I think these are arguments enough also to discuss seriously to freeze further EU money.

Secondly, I think we have to express very clearly here from the European Parliament 100 % solidarity with the students movement. Every week, ten thousands are going on the street, risking a lot of their life, risking their studies and their future, but fighting for a better, a European future. And they have a simple demand, which is a clear, functioning, modern Serbian State. While they are not waving European flags, I think they expect that the European Union is supporting these students' demands: to have a modern, functional, clean Serbian State.

The last point: Vučić now called for new elections. Nobody knows exactly when. It seems to be another trick of this magician of debate. But we have to say, before it comes to election, we need an electoral law which is fulfilling the need for clear and fair elections. We need that the OSCE or the European Parliament recommendations are implemented, and also we need a clear and fair voter registration process. Otherwise, the elections will result in the same result like the old elections.

Annamária VICSEK

Mr. President! We can all agree that serious challenges lie ahead for Serbia today. Reforms must be continued, social dialogue must be strengthened, and the European integration process must be advanced. At the same time, it is important that we interpret today's debate within the current European political environment. In recent weeks, we have received a clear message: the European Union regards enlargement as a strategic priority. Montenegro is closing further negotiating chapters. Ukraine and Moldova have opened their first negotiating cluster. Yesterday, the European Commission made it clear that it supports the opening of the third negotiating cluster for Serbia in July, because in its view the conditions for this have been met. This is a favorable political moment that neither Serbia nor the European Union should miss.

Shortcomings must be named, but it is equally important to acknowledge the achievements that have been made. In recent months, Serbia has adopted 23 key laws, including EU legal harmonization, judicial, and electoral reforms. This week, the Serbian parliament is discussing further legislation concerning the recommendations of ODIHR, as well as negotiating chapters 23 and 24. In May, the government also adopted the minority action plan. Regrettably, the tone of the report does not reflect this balanced approach. It focuses almost exclusively on shortcomings, while reforms and achieved results appear in it only sparingly.

Even when praise does appear in it, further criticisms relativize the recognition. A credible and merit-based enlargement policy requires not only uncovering shortcomings, but also acknowledging the results of reforms. Only in this way can we preserve the credibility of the enlargement policy, which serves the common interest of Serbia, the Western Balkans, and the European Union.

Şerban Dimitrie STURDZA

Mr President, Commissioner, dear colleagues, Serbia's accession to the European Union must mean real reforms, the rule of law and full respect for national minorities. It is necessary for Serbia to treat the rights of Romanians on its territory with seriousness, without the attribution of artificial identities such as Vlachs. Romanians are Romanians, wherever they may be.

At the same time, we must see good neighbourly relations through deeds and here I refer to the Iron Gates III project on the Danube, because we are talking about an international river, not the exclusive property of a single state. Therefore, any major project that can affect the water regime, energy security, ecological balance or agriculture must be discussed transparently with neighbours, before it becomes a political problem.

European integration means trust, and trust is built through transparency, cooperation and mutual respect.

Helmut BRANDSTÄTTER

Mr President, dear Commissioner, I admire the young Serbian people. They are very brave; they go on the street; they fight for a life in freedom. And then they listen to the Commission, and the Commission says, 'we want to open Cluster 3, we want to continue the process'. No! Right now it's not the moment to continue the process because there is a backlash.

There are no reforms, as I hear now. On the contrary, what does Mr Vučić say? He cannot leave power. He takes Putin as a role model. He says: 'what's fine for Putin is now fine for me, so I want to be again the Prime Minister and not the President'. Here, you see, it's not about democracy; it's not about freedom. But it's our job to say to the Serbian people: 'we are on your side'. The Serbians are Europeans like us; the Serbians should be members of the European Union. But autocracy has no place here.

So I think, yes, Commissioner, you said there should be observation of the elections, but there also should be more than only observation during the elections. We need a long observation. We need contact with the opposition, which is also here, with the students. Serbia: yes! Autocracy: no!

Vladimir PREBILIČ

Mr President, ladies and gentlemen! The European Parliament is not an enemy of the Serbian people. Nor is the European Parliament an obstacle to Serbia on its path to the European Union. However, the European Parliament is an unwavering supporter of democracy and of all those who fight for it.

Media freedom, freedom of expression, the rule of law, respect for those who think differently, and the fight against corruption unfortunately do not have a home in Serbia.

Since the authorities bear the primary responsibility for protecting democracy, the European Parliament is sending a clear message: "No, we are not satisfied with the state of democracy and we will persistently demand the fulfillment of all fundamental democratic values in Serbia."

Serbia deserves fair and free elections as soon as possible. To make this possible, reforms must be implemented, hence the call to the European Commission: "The time has come for action by the holders of power, not for indulgence."

Jonas SJÖSTEDT

Mr President! Serbia is facing a real crossroads. On the one hand, Vučić's authoritarian right-wing government, which actively suppresses the opposition - a rule fundamentally characterized by corruption and abuse of power. We see how the rule of law is being undermined. We see how freedom of the media is restricted.

On the other side is one of Europe's most dynamic, interesting and well-organized democracy movements. The Serbian students have created something unique, a grassroots movement, democratic from the ground up, that challenges power through constant innovative, democratic protests. They carry the seed of a better future for Serbia.

Our task is very clear: It is to do everything we can for a fair election. When it comes to the electoral law, when it comes to the registration of voters and not least when it comes to implementation. That is our responsibility.

Alexander SELL

Mr President! Yesterday in Berlin, Lars Klingbeil presented the federal budget for 2027: 200 billion euros in new debt; the German state can now only be financed on credit. While Germany is going bankrupt, you want to admit more and more members into the European Union here. The CDU's Konrad Adenauer Foundation estimates that Serbia's accession will cost 3 billion euros, and the entire Western Balkans 7 billion euros a year. German taxpayers will have to shoulder a quarter of the costs, which is about 2 billion euros – roughly the amount that the Federal Government wants to save on family caregivers. In other words, Germans who care for their parents have their pensions cut so that the CDU and SPD can squander their tax money in the Balkans. I am surprised that there are still voters who give their votes to these parties.

For two years now, Serbs have been taking to the streets because of corruption in their country. The Serbian president has therefore declared his resignation because, unlike German politicians, he is willing to take responsibility for the mistakes of his government. I find this exemplary; Ursula von der Leyen or Friedrich Merz should take a cue from this and follow his example.

We want a privileged partnership with Belgrade. But before we rebuild the Balkans with German tax money, we must first rebuild Germany.

Marta Kos

Mr President, Mr Brandstätter, dear Helmut, indeed, the election observation is not enough. That's why, for any new elections, we expect them to take place under conditions which ensure free and fair elections, in accordance with the European and international standards.

So the electoral process requires further tangible improvement and reforms. For this, Serbia should build on the first positive steps taken to address concerns about the integrity of the electoral register and the electoral legislation. But work still needs to be done.

So progress on Serbia's path is in the interest of the EU, and when we speak about supporting Serbia, we speak about supporting Serbian citizens.

Tonino PICULA

Mr President, of course, I thank everyone for their contribution to tonight's debate, and especially my fellow shadow rapporteurs for their excellent cooperation.

I believe that today's debate was followed not only by the citizens of the European Union, but above all by the citizens of Serbia. I also believe that the citizens of Serbia want free and fair elections and an opportunity to build a better European future, but after years of democratic backsliding, the European Union must not reward the Serbian authorities with progress on their accession path based on pseudo-reforms.

Serbia is the largest country in the Western Balkans with the greatest capacity for progress on the path towards EU membership. However, instead of opening and closing negotiating chapters, the Serbian government is only opening new dilemmas and new tensions towards its neighbors.

We cannot talk about progress in the dialogue with Kosovo if those responsible for the terrorist attack in Banjska are not brought to justice. We cannot talk about a breakthrough in the rule of law if an attempt is made to correct something that was initially done completely wrongly, because those Mrdić laws, or rather Vučić's laws, should never have been adopted.

We as the European Parliament must be firm in our commitment to respecting values and rules. We cannot remain silent about the backsliding in the rule of law, the erosion of democratic standards, and the destructive impact on regional stability.

If the authorities in Serbia want to progress on their path towards the European Union, they must make a clear strategic choice, carry out key reforms, and fully align with the European Union's common foreign and security policy and the European Union's sanctions against Russia.

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

The debate on this item is now closed and the vote will take place tomorrow.

Kinga GÁL

The European Parliament's annual report on Serbia is more critical and biased than ever before.

The report does not recognize any reform activity or results achieved so far and applies a one-sided, politically motivated approach. Unfortunately, this attitude on the part of the Union is increasingly characteristic of the Western Balkan countries and especially of Serbia, which constantly undermines the European Union's credibility in the region.

This trend is also worrying because Serbia is a key country for the stability of the Western Balkans, and the Union would need a balanced, responsible, and partnership-based approach. The common goal is to preserve the stability of the region, which can only be achieved by a credible, objective EU approach that also recognizes achievements.

As a responsible patriot regarding the report currently under discussion, I see the text as unbalanced. There is no doubt that the country still has much to accomplish in numerous areas, but the Serbian government's European commitment and the efforts it has made so far in energy policy, family policy, visa policy, and minority policy should be appreciated. Instead, the text concentrates on presenting shortcomings and contains severely unjust ideological distortions. There is no room for double standards in enlargement policy, yet current political interests are becoming increasingly prominent instead of neutral, performance-based evaluation.

Serbia's European integration can contribute to curbing illegal migration and ensuring long-term energy supply. A stable Serbia committed to the Union is in the interest of Europe, and thus of Hungary.

Air passenger rights

Where available, remarks are AI-translated into English. Select the language badge to view the original.

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

And first we have explanations of vote on the report by Andrey Novakov: Air passenger rights.

Lefteris NIKOLAOU-ALAVANOS

Mr President, the regulation voted on invokes passenger rights in air transport, while satisfying all the requirements of large industry conglomerates that are recording record profits and are already stuffed with state and European Union subsidies. It further reduces the obligations of airlines, cuts compensation for passengers and paves the way for their final restriction, maintaining the elastic concept of extraordinary circumstances, which gives conglomerates the ability to avoid compensation at will and make a fortune even from cabin hand luggage, as well as from suitcase dimensions.

At the same time, companies, on the basis of the liberated market, have skyrocketed prices and annihilated any services to passengers. Their criterion for action is profit, as of course is that of governments and the European Union, which condemn civil aviation services to operate with outdated infrastructure and scarce personnel under conditions of intensification, jeopardising flight safety. There is no other way: For the people to gain rights and safety, capital must lose.

Juan Fernando LÓPEZ AGUILAR

Mr President, in this July plenary session of the European Parliament, the final vote on the Regulation on air passengers' rights has taken place, and it is a vote that has two extraordinary features that deserve to be highlighted.

The first is the overwhelming majority: almost the entire parliamentary spectrum voted in favour. It received favorable votes from all parliamentary groups. The reason is simple: after thirteen years of deadlock, an agreement has finally been reached with the Council.

The second extraordinary feature is that, at last, progress is being made in the rights of citizens and, particularly, of passengers, and often labor rights—even fundamental rights in the European Union—have gone hand in hand with consumer rights.

At last there is a right to compensation against abuses by airlines, delays, overpricing, and overbooking, at last the recognized right to bring cabin luggage on board, and at last express facilities for people with mobility difficulties, so that they can exercise their rights on equal terms with everyone else.

Coordination of social security systems

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

And now follows the oral explanation of vote on the report by Gabriele Bischoff: Coordination of social security systems.

Lefteris NIKOLAOU-ALAVANOS

Mr President, the regulation serves the needs of capital for a cheaper and more flexible workforce. In practice, it adapts the current framework of individualized and commercialized starvation insurance, with the generalization of occupational funds to the needs of the market, as recently announced by the government of New Democracy through the Bank of Greece. Its pursuit is cross-border mobility, that is, mass migration from country to country, chasing a daily wage.

In the European Union of the war economy and involvement, where one in three workers is officially poor and unemployment is rampant, the regulation proposes stricter conditions for access to and retention of the unemployment benefit. The goal of the regulation is the dismantling of labor rights, and the shifting of state/employer burdens into losses for workers.

For workers to win, capital, the parties that serve it, and its international alliances must lose. They must now organize their struggle for collective labor agreements with decent wages, with full insurance rights, and a reduction in working hours.

Martin HOJSÍK (Chair)

With this, we have concluded the explanations of vote and also today's debates.
